3. All the 4 accused persons were placed on trial before the learned Additional District Magistrate, Kushtia to answer charge under section 467/468/471/34 of the Penal Code. They pleaded not guilty to the charges and claimed to be tried. At the trial, prosecution examined 4 witnesses and the defence none. The defence plea was one of innocence and false implication. Their specific dafence was that the portion of the writing alleged to have been subsequently entered in the kabala was already there at the time of its execution and registration and that it was wrongly omitted in the Balam Book of the Registration Office when it was copied from the kabala deed. The learned Magistrate has on consideration of the materials on record negative the defence plea of misstate by the Registration Office in copying out the deed in their Volume and held that the 3 appellants forged the kabala deed by introducing new things therein including the plot, unsing the forged document for the purpose of cheating and also dishonestly using the same as genuine in the Settlement Office at Kushtia in furtherance of their common intention. He has accordingly convicted and sentenced the 3 appellants as stated earlier. He has however found accused Sahera not guilty of all the charges leveled against her and acquitted her. Against this judgment and order the appellants have preferred this appeal. 

 4. P.W.1 Abdul Gafur Sheikh, the then Inspector D.A.G., Kushtia, has narrated the prosecution case as stated earlier. In his cross-examination he has stated that the document was not examined by any Expert. P.W. 2 Nazimuddin Mollah made an application (Ext. 4) before the D. A. G. for investigation into the forgery and taking necessary steps claiming that plot No. 835 in question belongs to his mother and sister in whose names the record-of-rights had been prepared. He has stated that the accused person filed Dispute Case No. 346 in the Settlement Office and also a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the Criminal Court claiming the land on the basis of purchase by the questioned kabala. He took out certified copy of the said kabala and found that this plot was not mentioned therein. In his cross-examination he has denied the defence suggestion that he does not possess the land nor it belongs to his mother and sister. P. W. 3 Altaf Hossain, Assistant Record Keeper of the Registration Office, Kushtia states that on 17.2.83 the I.O. seized the Balam Book from his office in his presence under seizure list (Ext. 1). In his cross-examination he has pleaded his ignorance as to the ways and for correction of the Balam Book in case of any mistake in copying out there in contents of a registered document or as to whether there was any complaint about any such mistake. P.W. 4 Mokbul Hossain was the Orderly peon of Mr. S. A. Ashraf, Magistrate, 1st Class, Meherput, who has stated that in his presence on 20.1.82 P.W.1 seized from the Court of the Magistrate the kabala deed dated 14.12.57 and the power of attorney dated 29.7.55 under seizure list (Ext. 2). 

 7. It has been stated by P.W.1 that the documents, that is power of attorney and the kabala in question were seized from the Court of the learned Magistrate, wherein they were filed in connection with C.R. 695/C/80 filed by P.W.2 against the accused persons on the allegation that they forcibly reaped away the paddy grown by him on plot No.835 which was fraudulently incorporated in the kabala by means of forgery. This is not disputed on the other side. There is however nothing on record to show what has actually been the fate of that case or at what stage the case was when the documents were seized. Mr. Hafeez submits, though without support of any paper, that since then the proceeding before the learned Magistrate are stayed and no further step had been taken therein for want of the documents upon which the accused persons based their claim to the land. The contention of Mr. Hafeez is that since the document that is the kabala was produced in a proceeding before the court of the Magistrate none else but the learned Magistrate was the person who was competent to make any complaint, if necessary, after conclusion of the proceeding and as such the prosecution launched on the F.I.R. lodged by P.W.1 and the cognizance taken by the S.D.O. in the case thereon were without jurisdiction and void abinitio. The plain reading of the relevant provision of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as quoted above would show that if the document is "produced" or "given in evidence" in the proceeding the only person competent to make a complaint with regard to such document is the presiding officer of the Court itself and none else. The word "or" between the words "produced" and "given in evidence" in the section shows that the 2 things are disjunctive. This means that the law gives authority to the Court concerned to make a complaint not only if the document is given in evidence but also if it is produced in the proceeding. Filing of a forged document in a proceeding before a court amounts to production within the meaning of section 195(1) (c), because "produced" does not mean used in evidence. full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—In this appeal by special leave the question raised is whether the appellant is a "non-agricultural tenant" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 and is entitled to protection under section 7 of the said Act. 

 2. Respondents-plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 51 of 1965 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Jessore, for ejectment of the appellant and recovery of khas possession of the suit land. The suit land lies within the Jessore Municipal Area and it admittedly belongs to the plaintiffs. Their case is that the defendant-appellant was their monthly bharatia-tenant in respect of the structures thereon—a tin shed but and two golpata huts at a monthly rent of Tk. 15/- which was subsequently raised to Tk. 20/- per month. The plaintiffs require the suit land for constructing pucca structures for their own use; in due course they served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon the defendant terminating the tenancy, but he did not vacate the premises. Defendant (No. 1) contested the suit by filling a written statement. His case is that the original bharatia tenancy ceased to exist when the structures were destroyed by fire. He then took lease of the vacant suit land under a written agreement at the monthly rent of Tk. 15/- and constructed a Charge sheet but thereon with his own materials, to which he added a pucca privy later on. The new tenancy, he contends, is in respect of the suit land which is a non-agricultural land, he is not a bharatia tenant in respect of the structures, he has been in possession of the land for ever 30 years and as such he is protected from eviction except on the ground of violation of the terms of the tenancy as laid down in section 7(5) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 3. The trial Court on consideration of evidence found that after destruction of the original tenancy by fire a new bharatia tenancy more or less on the same terms and conditions was created. That suit land was not leased out, but on the vacant suit land the defendant constructed a tin shed with his materials but with "landlord's permission" on condition that he would regularly pay monthly rent for his use and occupation of the huts and would vacate the land and remove the structures whenever the landlord required the land for making pucca construction. On these findings, the trial Court decreed the suit directing his ejectment subject to his right to remove his materials used in constructing the huts. On appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge reversed the findings and held that since the structures were constructed with the tenant's own materials and since the lease Agreement, Ext. B, refers to "lease of the land itself", the tenant was in fact a non-agricultural tenant for a period of over 12 years, and as such he is protected from ejectment under section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. On this finding the appeal was allowed and the suit was dismissed. But the learned Single judge of the High Court Division in second appeal (S,A.No. 894 of 1968) reversed the lower Appellate Court's decision and restored that of the trial Court, thus finally decreeing the suit for ejectment. 

 4. There is no dispute that the suit land belonged to the respondents whose father had raised some structures thereon and inducted the appellant as a bharatia tenant from month to month. This tenancy continued till destruction of the entire structures by an accidental fire, a fact about which there is also no dispute. On destruction of a premises by fire the tenancy ceases to exist at the option of the tenant, as the "doctrine of frustration" under section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act applies to cases of lease. But the respondent's contention is that the monthly tenancy was revived when fresh construction was made and a new agreement was entered into between them. Respondents do not deny that the new structures a tin-shed and two golpata huts were raised with their permission and approval by the tenant using his "own materials" but contend that erection of the new structure did not change the .character of the tenancy when the construction was made by the appellant with their permission subject to the condition that in case they would require the land for making pucca construction, the tenant appellant would vacate the premises after removing his materials. The land itself, it is contended, was never leased out. 

 5. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned Advocate for the appellant, contends that after destruction of the original structures the monthly tenancy ceased to exist, and in support of this contention he has referred to a decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Khitish Chandra Mondal V. Shiba Rani Devi AIR 1956 Cal 441. The principle of law followed in that case is not disputed in the instant case since both the parties are relying upon a fresh agreement entered into by them after destruction of the old structures by fire. Here the tenant is found to have reconstructed the premises with landlord's permission, using his own materials and continued to pay monthly rent though at a higher rate, which was tagged with the value of the land. The question is whether the using of his own materials by itself makes him tenant of the land and not of the structures only. There are two Agreements Ext 2, and Ext. B, bearing the same date, 1st Baishak 1358 B.S. and it is these Agreements on whose true construction fate of the case depends largely. 

 6. Both the Agreements are "bharapatra" . This clearly indicates that tenancy created is a monthly bharatia tenancy. Rent fixed was Tk. 5/- per month likely to be enhanced if the value of the land increased. The rent was raised to Tk. 20/- when a pucca privy was subsequently added to structures. Mr. Asrarul Hossain contends that as Ext B, the suit-land was leased out. But the words used there are that জমি ভাড়া দেওয়া হইল This sounds absurd, for when a land is leased it is called ইজারা বন্দোবস্ত in Bengali. It is not called ভাড়া Secondly if the land were leased out the tenant would not have been subjected to increase in the rate of monthly rent of the structures. In the rent receipts, particularly in the Deposit of rent with the Rent Controller the word monthly "bhara" was used. The land-lords have been paying Municipal taxes, government taxes and their names have been recorded in all official documents. The tenant never paid such dues not ever made any attempt to mutate his name in khatian Municipal Register. Section 2(5) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act provides that "Non-Agricultural tenant" does not include any person who holds any land on which any premises occupied by such person are situated, if such premises have been created or are owned by the person to whom such occupation is liable to pay rent for such occupation. Mere "using of his own materials" does not make the tenant owner of the land as well as the structures. The materials were used because the landlords were not in position to procure or purchase them at that time, but they gave permission for using these materials on specific condition that the tenant would remove his materials whenever the landlords require the land for making pucca construction. Had the land been leased out many other consequences would have followed, such as yearly rent of the land would have been paid by the tenant to Government on state acquisition, his name would have been recorded in Municipal Registrars and Government's Khatians. Mr. Asrarul Hossain has based his arguments on the Agreement, Ext B, which shows that the land along with the structures was leased out. If the land had been taken lease of, landlord's permission for construction would not have been necessary. Secondly, this Agreement, Ext-B, was styled "Bhara-Patra" in Bengali Ext-2, the other Agreement shows that usual monthly bhara-tenancy was created. Both the documents have been considered by the trial Court, but the lower Appellate Court considered only, Ext-B, totally ignoring Ext-2, and other evidence, such as rent receipts, record-on-rights. Non-consideration of the materials evidence by the lower Appellate Court has exposed its finding to attack in second appeal. 

 7. Mr. Asrarul Hossain's argument is based on interpretation of section 7(5) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. I do not think that interpretation of this is very much necessary in this case for fate of this case depends upon the finding as to whether under the Agreement Ext. 2 and Ext B, the land itself was leased out or only the premises thereon was leased out. On consideration of these two documents we have no hesitation to hold that High Court Division correctly held that the land was not leased out but the premises thereupon was leased on monthly basis. Therefore, continuous occupation of the premises for over 12 years by the tenant did not bring him within the category of "Non-Agricultural tenants" and as such the protection under section 7 is not available to him. We find nothing to interfere with the High Court Division's decision.

3. The plaintiff Opposite Parties filed the suit for declaration of title to the suit land on the allegations inter alia that the suit land was the khan land of the defendant No. 1 Hemendra Nath Sanyal and the defendant No. 2 Dwijendra Nath Sanyal. The plaintiff No. 1 took pattan of 2.00 acres of land from the said defendants at a rental of Rs. 15/-on 12th Falgoon, 1352 B.S. Plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 took pattan of another 2.00 acres of land from the said defendants on the same date at a rental of Rs. 15/-. However in the C.S. Khatian only 3.47 acres of land were recorded against the suit plot and the rest. 59 acres of land were tenanted land. The plaintiff no. 1 has been possessing 2.47 acres of land from the south eastern portion of the suit plot and the plaintiff No. 2 has been possessing 1.00 acres of land from the north western portion of the suit plot, though the two plaintiffs took pattan of 4.00 acres of land in total. The suit land has wrongly been recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1 although the defendants have no title and possession in the suit land. The plaintiff filed 2 Miscellaneous Cases for correction of record of rights of the suit land but they withdrew the said Miscellaneous Cases subsequently. The Tahsilder of the defendant No. 3 refused to receive rents from the plaintiffs on 14-11-75. Hence the suit. 

 4. The defendant Nos. 4 and 5, who are the petitioners in this Rule, contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. They admitted that defendant Nos. 1 and .2 were the owners of the suit land. Their case is that the defendant’s petitioners and one Abdul Mazid Talukder took pattan of the suit land from the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on the 25th Aswin, 1345 B.S. by 'virtue of an Amalnama. Abdul Majid Talukder did not pay Nazar money and rent. So these 2 defendant, petitioners paid Nazar Salami and rent of the suit land and have been possessing the same. As the suit land has not been recorded in the names of the petitioners, they filed Title Suit No. 508 of 1976 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Tangail for declaration of their title to the suit land which is still pending. The plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in the suit land. 

 5. The learned Subordinate Judge took into account the pattannama and the dakhilas of the Plaintiff opposite parties and found that those were genuine. He also examined the Amal-nama of the petitioners and found that their Amalnama and dakhilas are fabricated documents. In regard to possession the learned Subordinate Judge discussed the oral evidence on record and found that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land since their pattan in 1352 B.S. in that view of the matter the suit was decreed. 

 7. Inevitably the first point raised by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners is that the Appellate Court below committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by 'passing a judgment of affirmance without any application of mind and without adverting independently to the evidence on record. 

 8. Mr. Mahmudul. Islam, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff Opposite Parties has drawn my attention to the Orders dated 13-12-79, 6-4-81, 2-5-81, 11-5-81 and 16-5-81 passed by the learned Additional District Judge while the appeal was pending before the Court. The order dated 13-12-79 shows that the Plaintiff Opposite Parties filed an Affidavit alleging that the exhibits of the case have been lost from the records and taken away by the defendant Petitioners. They prayer for criminal prosecution of the defendant Petitioners on that ground. A lengly enquiry and hearing followed the allegation and the appellate Court below after hearing all the parties came to the conclusion that the papers might have been taken away by the defendant Petitioners who got frustrated in the Court of the 1st instance. A show cause notice was served on the defendant Petitioners as to why a criminal case shall not be started against them. However, after finding that the Bench Assistant of the Court might have a direct hand and connivance in the fraudulent act of causing the removal of the Court's record for the benefit of the interested party the Court of appeal below decided later on not to proceed with the matter and take up the hearing of the appeal without the connected records. 

 10. Mr. Mahmudul Islam further submits that after the records were called for by this Court, surprisingly the exhibits made their reappearance in. the records of the appellate Court below without the knowledge and behind the back of the Plaintiff-Opposite Parties, which is reflected in the Order No. 39 dated 1-3-83 passed by the appellate Court below. 

 11. It is not only the defendant petitioner's documents but also the plaintiff Opposite party's documents, marked as exhibits in this case, which were spirited away and which were refiled by unknown persons. In these circumstances there was hardly any option left for the appellate Court below but to dispose of the appeal on the basis of the available evidence on record. Considering his predicaments I do not think that his judgment suffers from any error of law apparent on the face of the record. 

 12. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury next submits that the learned Additional District Judge further committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by not considering that the tahsilder who granted the pattan to the plaintiff Opposite parties had no authority to settle the land and that the plaintiffs failed to prove that the said Tahsilder had the requisite authority. 

 Let the records be sent back immediately.

full_judgment:
2. Suit was filed on 13-2-2017 for declaration of title and for further declaration that the RS and City Survey records prepared in The name of the defendants are wrong. 

 3. The case of the plaintiffs is that the CS tenants and their successive heirs in whose names SA record also stands sold 0.49 acres out of 0.55 acres from plot 447 and 0.49 acres out of 0.55 acres from plot 448 to Arab Ali, Romizuddin, Motaleb Fakir, Moyezuddin by registered kabala dated 19-2-1965 and inducted them into possession. The suit land measuring 0.98 acres is a pond in which purchasers maintain joint possession by rearing fish. They while trying to transfer the same came to learn on 5-12-2016 that the suit land was not recorded in their names and upon collecting the printed copies of RS and City Survey records on 22-1-2017 and 23-1-2017 they came to know that those were wrongly prepared in the name of defendant 1. Hence the suit was filed. 

 5. The lower Court framed as many as five issues as to maintainability; limitation; whether plaintiffs have title, interest, right and possession in the suit property; whether the RS record and City Survey record have been wrongly prepared in the name of defendant 1 in respect of the suit property; whether plaintiffs can get the relief as prayed for. 

 7. The Joint District Judge decreed the suit on 10-2-2019 on the finding that the suit is not barred by limitation and plaintiffs have acquired title by purchase and PW 2 supported possession and further found that since transfer was made in favour of plaintiffs before RS operation the subsequent records prepared in the name of defendant 1 are wrong and defence failed to prove the basis of the record so prepared. 

 11. We have heard the learned Advocates of both sides and perused all the materials on record and gone through the impugned judgment and the grounds taken in appeal. 

 12. Plaintiffs filed the suit on the strength of kabala dated 19-2-1965 claiming as transferees from the CS and SA tenants. The true copy of the kabala which is certified by sub-registrar, Islamkati, Khulna on 25-5-1966 with a heading of words like "residential certificate issued by First Class Magistrate duly submitted Khulna" was tendered by the plaintiffs in evidence and marked as Exhibit-9. The document was produced by PW-1 on 13-8-2018 who is plaintiff No. 8 in the snit and the same was admitted without objection. PW 1 was examined on commission on behalf of all the plaintiffs by virtue of a power of attorney, Exhibit-1 dated 26-7-2018. The suit was tiled on 13-2-2017. In the plaint there is no explanation as to why the original of the document could not be filed. Law says that when a party desires to prove a document the best evidence rule requires that the party should produce the original of the primary evidence under section 62 of the Evidence Act. But if he fails to meet such requirement he can file a certified copy of the same under sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act and in such a case it is his duty to explain away in his pleading and evidence as to why he failed to produce the original. In the instant case pleading and evidence do not say so. Law is settled that a party producing 'a secondary evidence of a document is not exempted from explaining why the original could not be produced even though no objection was raised when it was tendered and marked in evidence. It seems that the writing on Exhibit-9 has been lately done on old stamp papers, The document was not at all proved in evidence because either the executants or their descendants or any scribe, attesting witness, identifier came before the Court to -prove the same. Moreover Exhibit-9 shows that the second schedule of the document contains 0.08 acres of land of Police Station Tala of Islamkati sub-registry office of District Khulna but plaint is silent about it and respondents could not submit any document showing the property mentioned in 2nd schedule to the deed belonged to the vendors. Thus it is clear that the document contains fictitious land and is an invalid document being barred under section 28 of the Registration Act. It also appears from perusing the seal given on the reverse side of the second page of the document that the copy was prepared, sealed, signed and delivered on 23-5-1966 but on the last page the date is 25-5-1966. The document was prepared on 25-5-1966 but read over by a person on 27-4-1965. Moreover it is detected with the naked eye that the signatures of sub-registrar differ from each other. The stamps used in the deed have no number at the back side and serious anomalies led us to believe that the deed is forged and fictitious one. We have asked the learned Advocate for the respondent as to why the deed was shown to be registered in the office of sub-registrar, Islamkati, Khulna where there is no averment in the pleading in respect of schedule-2 property but he failed to reply to satisfaction. All those facts and circumstances clearly establish that the deed in question has been manufactured by the plaintiffs in suit. Similarly, another group of people came with an application for addition of party as respondents by showing a true copy of the sale deed. On scrutiny and calling volume from the sub-registry office, Tejgaon it was found that the same was forged one and consequently application was rejected imposing penalty and directing the District Registrar, Dhaka to file criminal case. Exhibit-9 as has been discussed above is a fake, forged, fraudulent document and the same does not confer any title to the plaintiffs. Since plaintiffs failed to prove their title they are not entitled to challenge the subsequent record of rights prepared in the name of defendant 1 under section 144(7) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and such records bear presumptive value under section 144(A) of the same Act and cannot be dislodged until found incorrect. 

 13. Paragraph 6 of the plaint shows that the suit land is pond in nature in which plaintiffs have been maintaining possession by rearing fish. In chief PW 1 also stated the same. Neither plaint nor evidence discloses as to how and by whom such possession was maintained by the plaintiffs. PW 1 admitted in cross that they have not paid rent after the suit land was recorded in RS khatian. The revisional survey was completed in the concerned area before 1976. Plaintiffs even did not file any rent-receipt showing earlier payment since their purchase or by their transferors. PW 2 admittedly lives in a different place and his evidence is not sufficient to prove possession of the plaintiffs being unconvincing and incredible. Plaintiffs have miserably failed to prove their possession in the suit land. Exhibits 10, 11, Kha, Ga are good evidence of possession of defendant 1 and the presumption of such entry in the name of defendant is never dislodged by any cogent and reliable evidence. 

 18. Send down the lower Court's record.

full_judgment:
The opposite parties, as plaintiffs, instituted Title Suit No. 172 of 1995 in the 2nd Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Narayanganj, seeking a decree for declaration of title for 15 decimals of land as described in the schedule to the plaint contending, inter alia, that Nazumuddin was the original tenant. He died, leaving six sons, Rekmat Ali, Hazari, Fazar Ali, Poizari, Yad Ali and Metier Ali. Among them, Fazar Ali died, leaving five brothers before marriage. Rekmat Ali died, leaving two sons, Saman Munshi and Isa Ali, and two daughters, Laxi Bibi and Maleka Bibi. Meher Ali, Yad Ali, Hazari, Poizari, and Isa Ali sold disputed property by registered deed dated 30-3-1972 to Sadak Ali, Mazibur Rahman, and plaintiff No. 2. Thereafter, Mazibur Rahman transferred five decimals of land in favour of his wife Rahatun Nessa by way of Heba-bil-Ewaz deed dated 18-8-1980. Then Rahatun Nessa sold her five decimals of land by registered deed dated 12-5-1988 to plaintiff No. 1, and accordingly, he has been possessing the same by paying rents after mutation. During the revisional survey, the RS record was wrongly prepared in the Government's name, which the plaintiff learned on 28-8-1995 and hence the suit. 

 3. The defendant Bangladesh Government, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Narayanganj, contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint alleging, inter alma, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and barred by law of limitation. The defendant further alleged that the plaintiffs have no right, title, or possession in the suit land. During RS operation, the plaintiffs or their vendors were not in possession, and, as such, RS record-of-rights was rightly prepared in the name of the Government. The deeds in the name of the plaintiffs are false and fabricated. The plaintiffs have filed the suit to grab the suit land with false assertion, and hence, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 5. The plaintiffs examined 6 (six) witnesses as PWs, and the defendant examined 1 (one) witness as DW to prove their respective cases. Besides, both parties produced documentary evidence, which were duly marked Exhibits. The Trial Court, having heard the parties and on consideration of the materials on record, found the right, title, interest, and possession of the plaintiffs over the suit land, but it dismissed the suit on the point of defect of parties only. Against which the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 47 of 1996 before the District Judge, Narayanganj. Subsequently, the record of the said appeal was transmitted to the 1st Court of Additional District Judge, Narayanganj for disposal, who, having heard the parties and on consideration of the materials on record, allowed the appeal on contest against the Government and thereby set-aside the judgment and decree dated 30-5-1996 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj in Title Suit No. 172 of 1995 and thereby plaintiffs title over the suit land has been declared. Against which the Government preferred this revisional application with a delay of 435 days, which was condoned. 

 7. On the other hand, Mr. Md. Ibrahim Molla, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite-parties, submits that the appellate Court, being the final Court of fact, having considered the evidence on record and the provisions of law rightly decreed the suit and declared the title of the plaintiff over the suit land and, as such, such finding of the Court of appeal below need not be interfered with sitting on revisional jurisdiction as the findings of the appellate Court is not perverse. 

 10. 1 have heard the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the petitioner and the learned Advocate for the opposite parties and perused the materials on record, particularly plaint, written statement, oral evidence, as well as the documentary evidence which were duly marked as exhibits and the impugned judgment. Admitted fact is that Nazumuddin was the original tenant, and at his death, his six sons, namely Rekmat Ali, Hazari, Fazar Ali. Poizari, Yad Ali, and Meher Ali, became the legal heirs to inherit their father's property. 

 11. The plaintiffs' definite case is that out of their six brothers, Fazar Ali died, leaving the remaining five brothers. While Rekmat Ali died; leaving two sons, Saman Munshi and Isa Ali, and two daughters, Laxi Bibi and Maleka Bibi. Meher Ali, Yad Ali, Hazari, Fazar Ali, Poizari and the son of Rekmat Ali, i.e., lsa Ali, sold the disputed land by a registered deed dated 30-3-1972 to Sadek Ali, Mazibur Rahman, and plaintiff No. 2. Subsequently Mazibur Rahman transferred his five decimals of land in favour of his wife Rahatun Nessa by a Heb-bil-Ewaz deed who sold the same by a registered deed dated 12-5-1988 to plaintiff No. 1. Sadek Ali sold five decimals of land to plaintiff No. 1 by registered deed dated 16-6-1992. Accordingly, the plaintiff became the owner and possessor of the suit land by purchase. The Government claims that the suit land was rightly recorded in its name during the RS operation. But the Government could not substantiate any document under what facts and circumstances its name has been recorded in the RS Khatian. Both the courts below found plaintiffs' rights, title, interest, and possession over the suit land. In a suit for declaration of title the Trial Court dismissed the suit only on the point of defect of parties. On a bare reading of the judgment of the Trial Court, it is not found under what circumstances the suit was bad for defect of parties or who were left out at the time of framing of the suit. The concurrent findings of both the courts below regarding the possession of the plaintiffs appear reasonable based on evidence. The plaintiffs mutating their names and paying rents have been possessing the suit land. By producing oral evidence, the plaintiffs have been availed to prove the cause of action for filing the suit. On a careful examination of the Exhibited documents namely CS Khatian Exhibit-1, SA Khatian Exhibit-2, rent receipts Exhibit-3 series, deeds dated 30-3-1972, 18-8-1980, 12-5-1988 and 16-6-1993 Exhibits-4, 4(1), 4(b) and 5. It appears that the plaintiffs could prove their chain of title and possession over the suit land vis-a-vis there is no reason to record the suit land in the RS Khatian during RS operation in the name of the Government simply because the Government failed to produce any single paper or document showing its title in the suit land. During the trial, the defendant totally failed to produce the names of the necessary parties in the suit. So, according to Order I, rule 9 regarding misjoinder and non-joinder of parties, the defendant failed to establish its case. From the veracity of the plaint, it appears that the plaintiff claimed title over the suit land only against the defendant's Government. So, there should not be any question of defect of parties, and, as such, the Trial Court, without considering the provisions of law and facts, erroneously dismissed the suit on the point of defect of parties. As a final court of fact, the appellate Court rightly reversed the finding of the trial Court, which need not be interfered with by this Court sitting on revisional jurisdiction. 

 15. Send down the lower court record (LCR) at once.

2. The plaint case, in brief, is that Din Mondal alias Dinu Mondal was the owner of the schedule suit land. Dinu Mondal died leaving behind his wife Dukhi Bewa and 2(two) daughters Sahachari and Gayahwari. According to Dayabhaga System of Hindu Law Dinu's wife Dukhi Bewa got life estate in the suit land left by him. Dukhi Bewa had no son and as such her elder daughter Sahachari was given in marriage with one Shreecharan Mondal and he was kept in her house as domesticated son-in-law. The suit land was recorded in CS khatian 177 in the name of Dukhi Bewa and Shreecharan Mondal to the extent of 8 annas share each but Shreecharan Mondal had no title over the suit land. During her possession and enjoyment Dukhi Bewa sold 0.37 acres from plot 70 to Surendar Chandra Sarker and others for the legal necessity and handed over possession thereof. Accordingly, the said 0.37 acres of land was recorded in SA khatian 346 and RS khatian 49 in the name of Surendra Chandra and others. Subsequently, Dukhi Bewa died leaving behind her 2(two) daughters Sahachari and Gayahwari Mondal. As per Dayabhaga system they got life interest in the land left by Dukhi Bewa except the land measuring 0.37 acres texhibitransferred by Dukhi. Gayashwari subsequently died leaving behind his only son Ashwani Kumar Mondal the father of defendants 1-3 and grandfather of defendants 4 and 5 and her sister Sahachari Mondal. In this way Sahachari Mondal acquired life interest over the property left by Dukhi Bewa measuring an area of 5.25 acres. Sahachari died leaving behind his 3(three) sons Kiron Mondal, Dinesh Mondal and Haripada Mondal and thus Ashwani, Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada Mondal acquired the suit land as grandson of Dinu Mondal in equal shares i.e., each of them got ¼ th of property measuring an area of 1.3125 acres. In SA operation SA khatian 345 in respect of 5.25 acres was recorded in the name of Gayasshari's husband Ananda Mondal and Sahachari's husband Shreecharan Mondal along with titleless Madhab Mondal and Profulla Kumar Mondal. In RS operation, RS khatian 15 measuring an area of 5.31 acres (0.06 acres land) was recorded 8 annas in the name of Gayasshari's son Ashwani Kumar and remaining 8 annas in the name of Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada, the sons of Sahachari. During their possession and enjoyment Ashwani Mondal transferred 0.65 acres to Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada by a registered kabala dated 1-11-1969 from RS Khatian 15 corresponding to SA khatian 345 and handed over possession thereof. Kiron, Dinesh and Horipada got 3.9375 acres by inheritance and also 0.6150 acres by purchase measuring total 4.5525 acres from SA khatian 345 corresponding to RS khatian 15. They sold 0.04 acres to defendants 20 and 21 and remained in possession in 4.5525 acres. During their possession and enjoyment Kiron Chandra died leaving behind his 2(two) sons Parimal and Nirmal plaintiffs 5 and 6; Dinesh, Haripada, Parimal and Nirmol during their possession and enjoyment over 4.5125 acres sold 0.63 acres to defendant 24 and remained in possession over 3.8825 acres. Haripada died leaving behind his 4(four) sons Maran Chandra Sarker, Bimal Chandra Sarker, Kamal Chandra Sarker and Sujan Chandra Sarker. In this way the plaintiffs have been owning and possessing 3.8825 acres by erecting houses thereon and planting trees. In 2004, the son of Gayahwari mutated his name in respect of the suit land showing his share to the extent 8 annas then it came to the knowledge of the plaintiffs and they filed an objection against the said mutation and it was cancelled in 2013. The defendants refused to partition the land showing the shares of the plaintiffs to the extent ¾ share of the total land then they instituted the suit praying for shaham over the land as detailed to the schedule of the plaint. 

 3. The defendants 1-5 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the statement made in the plaint. They contended that the suit is not maintainable in the present form and manner and it is barred by limitation. They further contended that Dukhi. Bewa was the owner of land measuring 5.62 acres. Dukhi Bewa had 2(two) daughters Sahachari and Gayashwari. The husband of Shahachari namely Shreecharan Mondal was kept in her house as domesticated son-in-law. CS khatian 177 was prepared wrongly showing 8 annas share to Dukhi and Sreecharan each but actually Dukhi Bewa was the owner of the total land. The defendant after examination of witnesses on 1-8-2018 amended the written statement and incorporated the fact that the suit property was owned by Dukhi Bewa as Yatuka at the time of her marriage and consequently it will be treated as her Stridhana. They admitted that Dukhi Bewa sold 0.37 acres of plot 70 to Surendra Chandra Sarker and others and during her possession and enjoyment on remaining land measuring 5.25 acres she gave her daughter Gayahwari to marriage with Ananda Mondal and kept him in her house as domesticated son-in-law. In 1940 she partitioned the land between his 2(two) daughters and each of the daughters got 2.625 acres. During possession and enjoyment through the husbands of 2(two) daughters SA record in respect of 5.25 acres was recorded in the name of Shreecharan and Ananda and erroneously the names of Madab Mondal and Profullo Mondal were included in the khatian but they have no title and possession over the suit land. Sahachari Mondal died leaving behind his 3(three) sons Kiron Chandra, Dinesh Chandra and Haripada and they inherited the property left by Sahachari in equal shares. Gayahwari died leaving behind her only son Ashwani Kumar Mandal and he inherited 8 annas share enjoyed by her mother. Ashwani during his possession and enjoyment transferred 0.28 acres to Minor Hossain, 0.15 acres to Montu Shah, 0.13 acres to Chondi Dash, Nipendranath and Raton Mondal and .24 acres to Md Rohman and others. Apart from the above transfer, he transferred 0.615 acres to the 3(three) sons of Sahachari Mondal i.e., the predecessors of the plaintiffs. Aashwani Kumar Mondal further sold 0.04 acres to defendant 3 and 0.285 acres to defendant 24. Thus he totally transferred 1.74 acres from the suit property and had been enjoying and possession of the remaining part. He mutated his name in the year 2004 to the extent of 8 annas share of the suit jote and died leaving behind the defendants 1-5 as heirs. The father of the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.132 of 2003 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Court No.4, Gazipur which was dismissed on 27-10-2005. The plaintiffs have no title and possession over the land measuring an area of 0.885 acres having been enjoyed by the defendants. The suit has been filed on false averments and as such it would be dismissed. 

 4. The trial Court on pleadings framed as many as 5 issues to adjudicate the matter in dispute. Amongst other the issue whether the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree for partition as prayed for. During trial, the plaintiff examined 4 witnesses and Exhibited their documents Exhibits 1-4 series, while the defendants examined 4 witnesses and their documents were Exhibited as Exhibits Ka-Cha. However, the trial Court considering the evidence and other materials on record by the judgment and decree under challenge decreed the suit on the finding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove that Dukhi Bewa enjoyed and possessed the suit land as life estate. The defendant failed to prove that the property was obtained by Dukhi Bewa as Stridhana. 

 5. Mr Uzzal Bhowmick, learned Advocate for the appellants takes us through the materials on record and submits that the plaintiff although claimed that Dinu Mondal was the original owner of the suit land but they failed to lead any positive evidence supporting the contention. Admittedly CS record was prepared in the name of Dukhi Bewa showing his share to the extent of 8 annas. The presumption of preparation of CS record is to be rebuted by the plaintiff through evidence. Subsequently, 2(two) records were prepared in conformity of the CS record. In SA record the names of the husbands of 2(two) daughters of Dukhi Bewa were recorded with the name of some other title less persons and RS record was prepared in the name of Ashwini Kumar Mondal to the extent of 8 annas share which supports that Dukhi Bewa obtained the suit land as Yatuka and it was her stridhana. Although, the said claim of the defendants about Stridhana was incorporated by amended of the written statement at a belated stage but it was nothing but a better statement. The defendants proved their case by Exhibiting CS, SA and RS khatian Exhibits-Ka-Gha. He refers to the deed of purchase of the plaintiffs predecessor Exhibit-5 and submits that through the said documents the plaintiff processor purchased land from 3 plots to the extent of 8 arenas share of each plot. The plaintiffs thus admitted the title of 8 annas share of the defendant Ashwani over the suit land. While the sons of Sahachari admitted the title of the defendant to the extent of 8 annas share, their sons cannot undo those after expiry of long years. He refers to the statement of paragraph-Cha of the written statement and submits that Dukhi Bewa in the year 1940 partitioned of the suit land between his 2(two) daughters which has been admitted by PW2 and supported by the evidence of DW 4. The plaintiff did not deny it by cross-examining DW 4. The title and possession over the suit land has been admitted by the first generation, second generation and third generation, now the plaintiffs being fourth generation cannot disown it. The subsequent 2 records, i.e., SA and RS support the aforesaid partition by Dukhi Bewa. It is admitted position of fact that Ashwani Kumar being the son of Gayashwari transferred more than 4 annas share of the suit land. The plaintiffs' present suit without challenging those documents and claiming title over the suit land and without making any prayer for correction of the record of rights is not maintainable. The facts and circumstances and the transfer by Ashwani Kumar proves that he got the suit land per stripes. The trial Court without entering into the facts and evidence on record erred in law and thereby decreed the suit which is to be interfered with by this Court in this appeal. 

 6. Mr Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondents submits that the defendants totally failed to prove that the property in question was Stridhana of Dukhi Bewa. Their claim to get 8 annas of Dukhi Bewa's property by Ashwani son Gayashwari fails paving the way to success of the partition suit as claimed by the plaintiffs. He submits that in the original written statement the story of Stridhana was not stated but it was incorporated on 1-8-2018 after 7 years of the institution of the suit, i.e. after conclusion of the examination of the plaintiffs' witnesses. It clearly shows that this sort of amendment was afterthought and concocted. He refers to the provision of section 105 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submits that the plaintiff although did not challenge it to the higher Court at that time that and it was merged with the judgment but at this stage they can raise the port of allowing such sort of amendment. The trial Court also found that although the defendants predecessor Ashwani transferred his major share from the suit jote but suppressing those facts he mutated his name in the concerned office showing his share to the extent of 8 annas. He then submits that although in the written statement, the defendants contended that Dukhi Bewa gave the property to her two daughters in equal share whereby the property was partitioned by Dukhi Bewa herself during her lifetime but it has been consistently held by our Apex Court that mutual family arrangement for convenience of enjoyment of the property does not amount to partition. Moreover, since both Sahachari and Gayashwari owned and possessed the property as life estate but after death of both of them the property went to the legal heirs of original owner Dinu Mondal and they are Dinu Mondal's daughters' sons. The property admittedly stands recorded in RS khatian No.15 in the name of both parties. Although showing the shares wrongly in the name of Ashwani to the extent of 8 annas. This contention of the defendants is legally infirm and rightly rejected by the trial Court. He refers to the case of Probir Kumar Rakshit vs Abdus Sabur, 14 BLC (AD) 28; Rajendranath Saha @ Rajendra Pradan Saha and another vs Md Sonaullah Pramanik and others, 42 DLR 393 and Abdul Noor Q Cunnu Miah and another vs Makhan Miah Q Md Laisuzzaman and others, 12 MLR (AD) 347 and relied on the ratio laid therein. Mr Neogi then submits that earlier the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.132 of 2003 which was dismissed for default on 27-1-2005 and the cause of action for a partition suit being recurrent which exists till the property is partitioned by metes and bounds, the present partition suit is therefore squarely competent and maintainable. In the aforesaid premises the trial Court correctly decreed the suit which may not be interfered with by this Court. 

 7. We have considered the submissions of both the sides and gone through the materials on record, particularly the plaint, written statement, the oral evidence lead by the parties and the documents submitted. It is admitted that Dukhi Bewa was the wife of Dinu Mondal. It is also admitted position of fact that CS record was prepared in the name of Dukhi Bewa and Shreecharan Mondal to the extent of 8 annas share each. It is further admitted that SA record was prepared in the name of Shreecharan and Ananda Mondal along with the name of some other titleless persons. It is also admitted that Dukhi Bewa died leaving behind his 2(two) daughters Sahachari and Gayashwari and it is further admitted that Sahachari died leaving behind her 3(three) sons Kiran, Dinesh and Haripada and Gayashwari leaving behind his only son Ashwani Kumar. The claim of plaintiff-respondent is that Dinu Mondal was the original owner of the suit land measuring an area of 5.62 as detailed to the schedule of the plaint. After his death Dukhi Bewa got life estate over the suit land. On the other hand, the defendants claim that Dukhi Bewa obtained the suit land as Yatuka from her father and she partitioned the land between 2(two) daughter Sahachari and Gayashwari in the 1940. The defendants did not disown that Dinu Mondal was the husband of Dukhi Bewa. It appears that if the fact of partition of the land by Dukhi Bewa in the year 1940 it taken as true the SA record published in the year 1963 finally would have been prepared in the name Sahachari and Gayashwari but it was prepared in the name of Shreecharan and Ananda along with other titleless persons. It proves that Dukhi Bewa got the suit property as life estate on the death of her husband Dinu Mondal and since she had no son her two domesticated son-in-law Shreecharan and Ananda enjoyed the suit land on behalf of them as they acquired life estate in the suit land. The fact of obtaining the suit land by Dukhi Bewa was incorporated in the written statement after conclusion of the examination of plaintiffs' witnesses. On scrutinizing the record we do not find that any evidence was led supporting the claim of the defendants of Yatuka. The fact of obtaining the suit land as Yatuka from the father of Dukhi Bewa is also proved false by the evidence of DW1. In evidence PW1 he stated that “বিয়ের পর দুখি বেওয়া সুত্রাপুর আসে সত্য”. It mines that after the marriage Dukhi Bewa came to the place, where her husband resided and the suit property situated. Therefore, the suit land cannot be Yatuka property of Dukhi Bews. 

 9. In this case, as per the evidence of plaintiffs and defendants we find that Sahachari and Gayashwari got life estate in the suit land and after their demise the 3(three) sons of Sahachari namely Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada and one son of Gayashwari namely Ashwani would get equal share in the suit land as grandsons of late Dinu Mondal. Although, in the record we find that defendant Ashwani son of Gayashwari had owned has been owning and possessing more than the share he is entitle to and he has transferred more than his 4 annas share which he is bound to part with as per the decision reported in 12 MLR (AD) 347. The submission of Mr Bhowmick that the son of Sahachari admitted the title of Ashwani to the extent of 8 annas share of the suit land by purchase from him each plots and now their sons or grandsons cannot disown the title of the defendant cannot be accepted because principle of estopple does not lie against law. The property shall be devolved upon the Dinus grandson as per Hindu Dayabhaga System per capita. The submission of Mr Bhowmick that the heirs of Sahachari and Gayashwari will receive the property left by them per stripes is not correct because Sahachari and Gayashwari enjoyed and got the suit property as life estate and therefore, the main heirs of Dinu Mondal being the sons of his 2(two) daughters will get the suit property per-capita i.e., Kiron, Dinesh, Haripada and Ashwani each will get 4 annas share of the suit property and the present plaintiff being the heirs of Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada will get 12 arenas of the total property left by Dukhi Bewa and one son of Gayashwari namely Ashwani will get 4 annas of the total land. The trial Court on correct assessment of fact and law, considering the Dayabhaga System of the Hindu Law decreed the suit finding plaintiffs' title and ejmali possession over the suit land. 

 Communicate the judgment and send down the lower Court records.

19. Mr A.M. Aminuddin, learned Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, itself bars filing a suit in a civil court questioning legality of the order passed or any action taken under this Act and thus, the decree passed by the Courts below is a nullity and the High Court Division committed an error of law in maintaining the decree for derequisition. He further submits that in view of section 5(7) of the (Emergency) Requisition Property Act, 1948, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is the owner and possessor of the said quantum of land acquired in LA Case No.30 of 1958-1959 out of which 0.71 acre of land was allotted to the appellant by way of lease agreement in the year 1975 as required for nursery and opening a sale center in the greater interest of the citizens of the Dhaka Metropolitan City. He then submits that there is no scope to say that the suit land is unused and unutilized and the appellant is not the requiring body, and it has been done without jurisdiction. Therefore, the High Court Division committed error of law in affirming the concurrent judgments of the Courts below. He continues to submit that the burden of proof lies upon the plaintiffs to prove the case as alleged and the question of non-service of notices under sections 5(A), 5(C) and 7 of the said Act and non-receiving the compensation money incorporated in the plaint by way of amendment long after 12 years of filing the suit are required to be proved by the plaintiffs which they have utterly failed and, as such, the High Court Division committed an error of law in failing to consider that the amendment was made after a long lapse of time incorporating of those facts with a view to simply making out a case and those facts, as it appears has not been proved. 

 "That section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, itself bars filing a suit in a civil court questioning legality of the order passed or any action taken under this Act and thus, the decree passed by the Courts below is a nullity and the High Court Division committed an error of law in maintaining the decree for derequisition; that the view of section 5(7) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act,1948 the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was the owner and possessor of the said quantum of land and out of which 0.71 acre of land was allotted to the petitioner by way of lease agreement in the year 1975 as required for nursery and opening sale center in the greater interest of the citizens of the Dhaka Metropolitan City and in such circumstances it cannot be said that the land is unused and unutilized and the petitioner is not the requiring body, and it has been done without jurisdiction; that the settled principle of law that the burden of proof lies upon the plaintiffs to prove the case as being alleged and the question of non-service of notice under sections 5(A), 5(C) and 7 of the said Act, 1948 and non-receiving the compensation money incorporate in the plaint by way of amendment long after 12 years of filing the suit and the High Court Division committed an error of law in failing to consider that the amendment was made after a long passage of time incorporating of those facts with a view to simply make out a case and those facts, as it appears has not been proved."

The Rules were issued to examine the legality of order dated 17.8.2011 passed by the Zonal Settlement Officer, Comilla in Miscellaneous Case Nos.12-13 of 2011 under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 (in brief Tenancy Rules) allowing the cases and thereby canceling D.P. Khatian Nos. 1712 and 1713 prepared in the names of writ petitioners in compliance with a common order passed in Appeal Nos.6282 and 6284 of 2010. 

 Facts relevant for disposal of the Rules, in brief, are that the land measuring 69 decimals or thereabout appertaining to C. S. Khatian No. 180, Plot No.595 and 04 decimals of Bata Plot No.1331595 originally belonged to Krishna Chandra Saha, Harish Chandra Saha, Balaram Saha and Khetra Mohan Saha in four equal shares. The petitioners are their descendants and successors-in-interest. Their predecessors or any of them did not sell any land to any other person. As the D. P. khatians were wrongly prepared including their land in the names of respondents, they prayed for correction of the record by filing Appeal Nos.6281-6284 of 2010 under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, which were ultimately heard by the Assistant Settlement Officer, Comilla. The said appeals were preferred against orders passed in Objection Case Nos.1736-1739. The Assistant Settlement Officer, Comilla heard the appeals analogously and dismissed Appeal Nos.6281 and 6283 of 2010, while allowed Appeal Nos. 6282 and 6284 of 2010 by a common order dated 21.9.2010 directing preparation of separate khatians in the names of appellants (herein writ petitioners) curtailing 28 and 44 decimals of land from D. P. Khatian Nos.1524 and 948 respectively. Accordingly D. P. Khatian Nos.1712 and 1713 were prepared in their (petitioners’) names on 19.12.2010 for 28 and 44 decimals of land respectively in Plot No.3298, 33193814 , 3305; 3306 and 3319. (annexes-B and B -1) 

 Thereafter, respondent Nos.6-7 again filed the present Miscellaneous Case Nos.12-13 of 2011 against the same order dated 21.9.2010 passed in Appeal Nos.6282 and 6284 of 2010. The Zonal Settlement Officer by order dated 26.5.1991 started the said cases on receipt of a report filed by a Preliminary Committee for Scrutiny and subsequently passed an order on 6.6.2011 for analogous hearing of the two cases. A five member inquiry committee was formed by order dated 22.6.2011 and on receipt of the inquiry report, he allowed the miscellaneous cases by order dated 17.8.2011 reducing 28 and 44 decimals of land from D. P. Khatian Nos.1712 and 1713 respectively and thereby virtually cancelled the said D. P. Khatians prepared in the names of writ petitioners. 

 Mrs. Nahid Yesmin, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that respondent Nos. 6 and 7 had filed the applications under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules on vague allegations of fraud, which were liable to be rejected summarily. Instead, the Zonal Settlement Officer allowed the cases to proceed on a report of a Preliminary Committee for Scrutiny and ultimately cancelled the D. P. Khatians duly prepared in the names of writ petitioners on the basis another inquiry report, which did not establish even disclose any fraud in preparing the D. P. Khatians in the names of writ petitioners. 

 Mr. Moinuddin, learned Advocate appearing for respondent Nos.6 and 7 submits that the miscellaneous cases were filed by these respondents on clear allegations of fraud. The cases were started on the basis of a report of the Preliminary Committee for Scrutiny, wherein it was found that the writ petitioners interpolated their appeal numbers on D. P. Khatian Nos.1524 and 948, and suppressed the facts relating to disposal of earlier Appeal Nos. 4906, 5110 and 5112 of 2007 on the same land. During proceedings of the cases, there was another inquiry by a five member committee, wherein title and possession of the land in question was found in favour of the respondents and as such the impugned order was rightly passed under section 42A of the Tenancy Rules. There is nothing to interfere with by this Court exercising its authority of judicial review under article 102 of the Constitution. 

 We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates and examined the record including the impugned orders. It appears that on the same D. P. Khatian Nos.1712 and 1713 respondent Nos.6-7 earlier had filed Miscellaneous Case Nos.8-9 of 2011 under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules before the Zonal Settlement Officer, who rejected the same by order dated 4.4.2011 because of tampering on documents and warned the responsible employees of the Settlement Office. It further appears from order No.1 dated 26.5.1911 in Miscellaneous Case Nos.12-13 of 2011 that after filing of the applications under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, a Preliminary Committee scrutinized the records and submitted a report with prima facie finding inter alia, that the writ petitioners had committed fraud in obtaining the D. P. Khatian in their names by interpolating their appeal numbers on D. P. Khatians Nos.1524 and 948 prepared in the names of respondents 6-7. On the basis of the said report, the Zonal Settlement Officer started proceedings of the miscellaneous cases. During the proceedings another inquiry was held by a five member committee. The said committee furnished its report on 29.6.2011 with findings of title and possession in favour of respondent Nos.6-7 and recommended reduction of land from D.P. Khatian Nos. 1712 and 1713, but without any affirmation or reference to the prima facie finding of fraud which was found earlier by the Preliminary Committee for Scrutiny. Ultimately the Zonal Settlement Officer allowed the miscellaneous cases by the impugned order dated 17. 8.2011 mainly on the basis of the inquiry report dated 29.6.2011 furnished by the Five Member Inquiry Committee. The impugned order or the inquiry report dated 29.6.2011, basing which the impugned order has been passed does not disclose any finding of fraud, but has been passed on reappraisal of title and possession of the respective parties. 

 In order to appreciate the submission of learned Deputy Attorney General on abatement of the Rules, we have examined section 13 of the BCe, 2001. It provides abatement of suits or proceedings claiming title to any vested property or any proceedings for release of the same pending before the Custodian of Vested Property on the date of publishing the list of vested property in official gazette. The present miscellaneous case under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules in no way affects the alleged vested character of the land in question and no question of seeking any relief regarding vested character of the land arises and as such it does not come within the scope of section 13 of the Ain. We are, therefore, unable to accept his submission that the Rules have already been abated. Moreover, it is not clear as to how the Government-respondents’ interest would be served if D. P. Khatian Nos. 1524 and 948 prepared in the names of respondent Nos.6 and 7 remain unchanged.
