2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in brief, are that the suit property along with other properties originally belonged to one Ram Krishna Sarker, Sree Krishna Sarker and Bijoy Krishna Sarker. By amicable family arrangement the suit property had been in exclusive share and possession of Ram Krishna Sarker. Ram Krishna Sarker setting up idol of the deity, Radha Ballav Deb Thakur in his dwelling house had been performing daily worship (Deb puja) and other rituals with utmost devotion. At the age of 71 years Ram Krishna Sarker dedicated the suit property as described in the schedule of plaint as debuttar property to the plaintiffs by a registered deed of endowment (Arpannama) dated 13' Karthik, 1349B.S. corresponding to 30' October, 1942 A.D (exhibit-5) and he himself as shebait had been performing Deb puja and other religious rites. As per terms of the deed of endowment, after the death of Ram Krishna Sacker his son Kanakadri Krishna Sacker became shebait and continued to perform Deb puja of the plaintiff's deity regularly. In 1945 Kanakadri Krishna Sarker left this country for India. Thereafter Niladri Krishna Sarker became shebait and has been performing Deb puja and other rituals of the plaintiff deity regularly. The further case of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners is such, that the suit property was wrongly recorded in the names of Niladri Krishna Sarker and his brothers in S.A. Khatian. But Niladri Krishna Sarker has been performing functions as shebait and enjoyment and possession of the suit property by the plaintiff deity had never been affected or obstructed in spite of such wrong recording. In R.S. Khatian the suit property has been recorded in the name of plaintiff deity, but in remark column of the R.S. Khatian it has been noted as 'Vested Property'. On 05.09.1979 A.D. the local tahsilder threatened to lease out the suit property as vested property necessitating institution of the suit. 

 7. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the impugned judgment and decree is neither proper nor in accordance with the provisions of law. The learned lower Appellate Court during disposal of the appeal committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and both the courts below illegally decided the merit of the suit against the plaintiffs and in favour of the defendants on the basis of surmise and conjecture. The learned Advocate Mr. Prabir Neogi on behalf of the petitioners further submits that the trial court as well as the appellate court were totally failed to assess the evidence on record properly and appreciate the actual position of law and there has-been no sifting of evidence rightly by the learned trial court as well as lower appellate court. The learned Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi committed error of law in not considering that Trust Board as mentioned in exhibit-5 and all the members of Trust Board either died or left this country the last shebait Niladri Krishna Sarker being died during the pendency of the suit his son Samirandra Krishna Sarker having all the qualifications of becoming a shebait performed Deb puja of Sree Radha Ballav Deb Thakur and looked after and managed the affairs of debuttar properties and others since of late shebait Niladri Krishna Sarker also having performed Deb puja & all the 6(six) sons of late shebait were substituted in his place. The learned counsel for the plaintiff-petitioners also submits that Ram Krishna Sarker got the suit properties in his `Saban' by amicable settlement and as such he had legal rights to endowment the suit properties as debuttar for the purpose of `Deb sheba and Deb puja' as described in the deed of endowment (exhibit-5) and as such the findings of the lower appellate court that Ram Krishna Sarker had no legal right to donate the suit properties as debuttar is absolutely baseless. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the learned- lower appellate court erred in law in not considering that from the evidence on record Radha Ballav Deb Thakur is still in the `Mandie at the residence of Rant Krishna Sarker at `Baneswar' and as such even if anyone of all the shebaits have migrated for India the properties of the bigraha cannot be declared as an enemy or vested and non-resident properties. It is from the evidence of the plaintiff's witnesses that Samarendra Kumar Sarker with other brothers has been possessing the suit properties on behalf of Radha Bailey Deb Thakur and the defendants have hopelessly failed to prove the possession of the defendants by giving lease. The learned counsel for the plaintiff-appellant -petitioners has drawn much emphasis to the following submissions that Sub-Section (6) of Section 9 of Act No.16 of 2001 (as amended by অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ (সংশোধন) আইন, ২০১১, (Act No.23 of 2011) which provides that the properties which is not enlisted in the `Ka' or `Kha' schedule of Bangladesh Gazette cannot be treated Vested and non-resident properties and in the said properties the Government has no manner of title, interest, right and liabilities as contemplated by law. The suit properties excepting .08 acres of land in R.S. khatian No.44/2 in Plot No. 296 out of total 14.80 acres of land is not enlisted in the `Ka' or 'Kha' schedule of the respective localities and the Government (Ministry of Land) published the list of `Ka' schedule vested properties of the concern Puthia Upazilla under Rajshahi District by Notification dated 08° February, 2012 in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary Issue, dated 08° April, 2012. In the said list in Serial No.102 only .08 acres of land appertaining to A.S. Khatian No.44/2, R.S. Plot No. 296 has been included out of 14.80 acres of land which is the subject-matter of the instant suit. The Government published list of "kha" schedule vested properties of the concern Puthia Upazilla by Notification dated 08th March, 2012 in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary Issue, dated in May, 2012 wherein the suit Property is not at all included. Act No. 16 of 2001 provides that under Section 13 Sub-section 1(kha) the suit which is pending in respect of such properties which is not enlisted as vested property in the Official Gagette is automatically abated to the extent of that portion of land. 

 8. As against the submissions of the learned counsel for the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners the learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Copal Chandra Saha on behalf of the Govemment opposing the Rule submits that the suit of the plaintiffs is concocted and manipulated and papers produced are forged, created and not acted upon. The plaintiff's title paper i.e. the 'Arpannania' is a forged document which is not acted upon and by virtue of this 'Aipannama' no possession was delivered in favour of the plaintiffs as alleged and in fact, both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff-petitioners are not able to prove its case of possession of the suit property and there exist defect of parties in the suit which is apparent from the face of the records. The learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Gopal Chandra Saha for the opposite parties further submits that there is no scrap of paper and a single witness from the side of the plaintiff-petitioners to substantiate that the plaintiffs have got possession in the disputed properties and it is evident from the papers on records that there are some left out parties whose presence are necessary for proper adjudication of the suit and both the trial court as well as the appellate court rightly decided that the suit is not maintainable under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for want of possession and defect of parties. The learned Assistant Attorney General in support of his submissions referred some decisions of our Apex Court reported in 43 DLR (AD) 87 upon maintainability of the suit, 47 DLR (AD) 95 upon Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 4 BLT (AD) 150 upon Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 56 DLR 427, 39 DLR (AD) 237, 43 DLR 551 upon identification of the suit property, 28 DLR (AD) 57 and 51 DLR (AD) 55. The learned Assistant Attorney General lastly submits that the alleged shebait as stated from the side of the plaintiffs since not functioned properly the property in dispute is under the control and possession of the Government and the Government by leasing out the property to its lessee managing the some rightly and the learned trial court & the appellate court during disposal of the suit and appeal after proper sifting of evidence and appreciation of law decided the merit of the suit and appeal respectively and the Rule having no substance is liable to be discharged. 

 9. Heard the learned Advocates of both sides, perused the case records, deposition of the witnesses, exhibited documents and all other connected papers including the series of decisions referred from both the sides of the respective parties. 

 10. On perusal of the case 'record it transpires that the learned trial court during disposal of the original title suit being no.25 of 1990 decided the merit of the suit against the plaintiffs on the plea  that there exist defect of parties in the suit and two necessary parties namely Kanakadri Krishna Sarker and Amadri Krishna Sarker, 2(two) sons of Ram Krishna Sarker who are residing in India has been left out from the pleadings and the plaintiffs did not implicate them as parties to the suit whose presence are necessary to adjudicate the matter in dispute. In the last portion of the decision the learned Assistant Judge, Puthia opined that as per evidence adduced from the side of the plaintiffs the plaintiff's title to the disputed properties appears to be proved but only because the suit is bad for defect parties the plaintiffs are not entitled to get declaration of title. The learned appellate court vide the impugned judgment and decree upheld the decision of the trial court and it was further observed by the learned lower appellate court that the plaintiffs had no locus standi to file the suit as their title document the 'Arpannama' was not properly acted upon and since the suit is bad for defect of parties there is nothing to interfere with the judgment and dismissal decree of the trial court. It was also observed by the lower appellate court that after payment of rent no rent receipts were obtained year to year and submitted to prove the bonafide of the appellant-petitioners and the property in dispute cannot be treated debuttar for want of proof. 

 11. In the aforesaid context from the papers on record it appears that it is the specific case of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners that the suit property by amicable family arrangement had been in the exclusive share and possession of Ram Krishna and Ram Krishna setting up idol of the deity Radha Ballav Deb Thakur in his dwelling but had been performing daily worship there. At the age of 71 years he dedicated the suit properties as debuttar property in favour of the plaintiff deity by a registered deed of endowment (Arpannama) on 13u Karthik, 1349 B.S. corresponding to 30th October, 1942 A.D. (Exhibit-5), After the demise of Ram Krishna his son Kanakadri Krishna Sarker became the shebait and continued to perform 'Deb puja' of the plaintiff deity regularly. In the year 1945 A.D. Kanakadri left this country for India and thereafter, Niladri Krishna ,Sarker became shebait and has been performing 'Deb puja' and other rituals of the plaintiff deity regularly. It is also the specific case of the plaintiff-petitioners that despite during the S.A. Operation the S.A. khatian was wrongly recorded in the names of Niladri Krishna Sarker and his brothers but in the R.S. khatian the suit property has been recorded in the name of plaintiff deity, but in the remark column it has been noted as 'vested property' and for that noting while the concerned Tahsilder tried to lease out the property in favour of third party plaintiff's title to the suit properties has been clouded. To dispel that cloud plaintiff instituted the original suit for declaration of title. The very documentary evidence as adduced from the side of the plaintiff-petitioners marked as exhibit-3 series supports the contention of the plaintiffs. In the concern R.S. khatian in it's remark column the property is mentioned as vested property but the names of the plaintiffs has been duly recorded. The prayer for relief by the plaintiffs as cited in the prayer portion of the plaint is for declaration that the schedule properties appertaining to:C.S. khatian no. 164 and R.S. khatian no. 187 including other khatians as described in the schedule of the plaint comprising an area of 14.80 acres is liable to be declared 16 (sixteen) annas title in favour of Sree Sree Radhaballabh Deb Thakur seen as plaintiff no. 1 in the plaint and the time of cause of action cited therein is 05.09.1975 A.D. while the concerned Tahsilder tried to lease out the property in favour of third party. To substantiate the case of the plaintiffs they have adduced 5(five) witnesses. The witness no, 1 is Samarendra Krishna Sacker son of late Niladri Sarker. This witness deposed in support of the plaint case and the witness no. 2 Md. Ekramul Hoque is a `Maharar of the concern District Registry Office who after getting summon of the court brought the concerned volume book to prove the title document of the plaintiffs which is identical with the suit properties marked as 'exhibit-5'. The witness no. 3 for the plaintiffs is Vhim Charan Paul who deposed corroborating the case of the plaintiffs. The witness no. 4 Debendra Nath also states supporting the plaintiff's case. The last witness Suvash Kumar being one son of Niladri Kumar specifically states in his deposition that the suit properties are being possessed and looked after by proper management and they are as sons of Niladri Kumar Sarker being full-brothers do possess the property in dispute and they are performing all the religious activities concern to deity within the knowledge of all. 

 12. On the other hand the witness no. 1 is the sole witness on behalf of the defendant-opposite parties namely Md. Abdul Ezaj who is a Tahsilder of Baneswar Tahsil Office. This witness states in his deposition that in the S.A. record of rights the land has been recorded in the names of Niladri Sarker and others and in the corresponding R.S. record it has been recorded in the name of Radha Ballav Deb deity which is not correct. In his cross-examination it was admitted by the witness for the defendants that the C.S. recorded tenants possessed the suit property in 'Ejmali' and it is within his knowledge from his predecessors. He also admits that no paper has been produced from their side showing the property as enemy or vested property. This witness at a stage of his deposition specifically states to the effect that he does not know the suit properties personally and never went there and as such, he cannot say whether there is any deity in the suit property. 

 13. I have come across from the connected papers that the learned trial court in his judgment and decree opined that the plaintiffs have successfully proved title in the disputed properties but for defect of parties they are not entitled to get the relief as prayed for. In this context the learned Advocate Mr. Probir Neogi on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners referred some decisions of our Apex Court reported in 49 DLR (AD) 151 & 10 BLC (AD) 41 and regarding burden of proof under the purview of Evidence Act's Sections 102 and 103 the decision reported in 1987 BLD (AD) 103 and 54 DLR (AD) 26. Consulting the relevant decisions of our Apex Court it is obvious to note that it is a settle principle of law that the suit shall not fail for reason of mis-joinder and non-joinder of the parties. No suit can fail by reason merely of non-joinder of parties. Order I Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes this legal position clear. Apart from this on careful scrutiny over the case records it is evident that Abdul Latif and Elahi are not the necessary parties of the suit. As lessee under the defendant No.1 their presence is not required for proper adjudication of the matter in dispute and it is within record that the defendant Government of Bangladesh is well within the plaint of the suit and they are contesting the case. The exhibited documents as it appears go to show that the rent receipts starts from Puthia Zomindari Estate upto the Government which has been duly marked as Exhibits 4-4(35) from the side of the plaintiffs. In view of the materials on record it is a glaring misconception of law as to onus probandi in a civil proceeding. Cumulatiye effect of Section 101, 102 and 103 of the Evidence Act is that unlike criminal cases, the fate of a civil suit is decided by the preponderance of evidence, in other words, comparative weight and worth of evidence led by the parties. In the instant case, the plaintiffs have established their case by producing unimpeachable documentary and credible oral evidence. All the documents forming the basis of the claim of the plaintiffs on the suit property were admitted into evidence and marked exhibits without objection. The testimony of P.W. 1 was corroborated by four other competent, credible and independent witnesses whose testimony remained unshaken in cross-examination. 

 14. On the contrary the sole witness for the defendant-Government is the witness no. 1 Tahsilder, Baneswar Tahsil Office who had no personal knowledge about the suit properties. He could produce the official records, if any, relating to the suit property, but admittedly he could not produce any scrap of paper. As I have stated earlier that the burden of proof to discharge onus of proving the respective case lies entirely on the concern party and the decision as referred from the side of the petitioners carries much weight to arrive at a correct decision. In the case of Chinivash Pramanik Vs. Md. Nurul Hossain Molla reported in 1987 BLD (AD) 103 it has been held, when both the parties adduced evidence in order to set up their respective cases, the question of onus losses significance and the provisions laid down in Section 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act is required to be judged. Consulting the nature and character of each and every suit when both the parties lead evidence question of onus as well as the matter in dispute is to be decided on the evidence adduced from the sides of the respective parties. 

 22. Having regard to the facts, circumstances arid evidence referred to above I have every reason to inclined such a view that both the courts below were totally failed to assess the evidence on record properly and appreciate the actual position of law. There is no sifting of evidence in the true perspective of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The appellate court during disposal of the appeal misread and misconstrued the evidence on records and misinterpreted the material evidence specially the exhibited documents which is an apparent error in law on the face of the papers. This submissions with regard to the respective case of the Plaintiff-Appellant-Petitioners from the side of the learned Advocate Mr. Probir Neogi carries much weight as well as consistent with the nature & facts of the suit and I have the reason to appreciate the decisions referred to but the case laws cited from the side of the learned Assistant Attorney General have got no nexus in the instant suit due to different facts & circumstances. 

 28. Send back the Lower Court's Record immediately.

Surendra Kumar Sinha J : These appeals and civil petition involve public importance on the environment and human rights, protection and preservation of environment, and the construction of certain provisions of the tenancy laws applicable in the country, the town Improvement Act, 1953, the Paribesh Sangrakhan Ain, 1995 and Jaladhar Sangrakhan Ain, 2000 and as the disposal of these matters would have impact on the implementation of various housing projects by individuals and private companies, I would like to express my opinion on the questions separately. 

 14. Clause (e) of section 3(4) says that tenants holding lands directly under rent-receivers with effect from the date on which the notification under section 3(1) have been served shall become tenants directly under the Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate to the Government. Clause (f) speaks of rent-receivers themselves who shall be liable to pay rent to the Government with regard to lands not acquired by the Government under section 3(2). Clause (ff) provides that where final publication of record-of- rights under section 19(3) or determination of rent under section 53 was yet to be made or, in other words, pending the same, the tenants referred to in proviso in clause (e) and in clause (ft) shall pay rent to the Government at the rates shown in the preliminary record of rights. 

 Resource Maps-record existing infra- structure locations, along with public and private sector development commitments; 

 52. BELA filed a supplementary affidavit against the said alleged permission stating that MMDL created it by resorting to forgery. Under such circumstances, the High Court Division called for the record of RAJUK for ascertaining the genuineness of this endorsement and ascertained that though a copy of the letter was kept with the file, there was no such permission. The High Court Division thereupon came to a definite finding that "This copy contains the signature of the issuer Mr. Zakir Hossain, Town Planner (Director), just after the finish of the main con- tents of the letter but Annexure-X-l contained the same signature at the bottom of the alleged paragraph and as such it can be safely said that the issuer of the letter dated 29.7.1995 superfluously included this portion in Annexure-X-l for the reason best known to him. Therefore, we hold that the allegation of forgery on the part of Modhumati in inclusion of that part in Annexure-X-I, has no basis". 

 61. It is contended on behalf of the appellants in Civil Appeal No. 254 of 2009 that they are bonafide purchasers for value and exercised due diligence when purchasing the plots from MMT and thus their interest cannot be denied. Accordingly, it is contended that the High Court Division has rightly held that their interest shouid not be interfered with. It was also contended that they being purchasers, their right is guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution. Mr. Azmalul Hossain, added that MMDL has a contractual and legal obligation to provide the infracture facilities as promised to the third party-purchasers such as roads, bridges, culvert, water channels, open spaces, recreation areas and other facilities on the common land of MMDL. They being purchasers for value without notice to any illegality or wrong doing, it would be expecting too much from lay- men that they should have known the law, and the private property right of purchasers should not be taken away by a decision of this Division where a substantial number of them are not even involved in this dispute. Article 102 cannot be used to take away fundamental rights to be treated in accordance with law under Article 31 and the right to property under Article 42. These are express rights which can be protected under Article 102. 

 63. In the ETV case, this Division observed "the third party rights exist(s) and fall with Ekushey Television since their interest merged with that of ETV. The substantive legal principle in this regard is that every person is subject to the ordinary law within the jurisdiction". In Sharif Nurul Ambia, the Government gave to the Dhaka City Corporation certain plots for construction of car park as earmarked in the Master Plan but the City Corporation constructed shops on the said plots and allotted the shops to the shop keepers taking salami. This Division in the attending circumstances refused to recognize the alleged right of the "bona fide" allottees and ordered stoppage of construction and demolition of existing structure. The statements of law argued on the question of bonafide purchaser for value without notice of any restriction is based on sound principle of law and I find no reason to depart from them. In view of the above, I find merit in the contention of Mr. Mahmudul Islam that these purchasers cannot acquire any better right in view of the statutory barrier to make development in areas earmarked as SPZ173. 

 Environment and Human Rights 

 66.	The environmental problems of the day damage our natural environment and life on earth. Protection and preservation of the environment has been integral to the culture and religious ethos of most human communities. The international community has increased its awareness on the relationship between environmental degradation and human rights abuses. The international community has assumed the commitment to observe the realization of human rights and protection of environment. Thus there is no gainsaying that the protection of the environment and internationalized-human rights are presented as universal and protection of the environment appears as everyone's responsibility. Human rights and environmental law have traditionally been envisaged as two distinct independent spheres of rights. Now- a-days, the peoples perception is aroused to the notion that the cause of protection of the environment can be promoted by setting it in the frame-work of human rights, which has by now been established as a matter of international law and practice. 

 67. To avail the benefits of environmental law and human rights one must give protection to environmental law that would help ensure the well-being of future generations as well as the survival of those who depend immediately upon natural resources for their livelihood. Secondly, the protection of human rights is an effective means to achieving the ends of conservation and environmental protection. The focus is on the existing human rights. There exists a raging debate on whether one should recognize an actual and independent right to a satisfactory environment as a legally enforceable right. This would obviously shift the emphasis on to the environment and away from the human rights. Thirdly, in the Stockholm Conference in 1972, it was argued by the delegates that international environmental law has developed to such extents that even the domestic environments of states have been inter- nationalized. Environmental law has in many parts of the world, be it at the international or domestic level, suffered from the problem of standing. Because of this barrier, it is often difficult for individuals or groups to challenge infringements of environmental law, treaties or directives, as the case may be. 

 68.	The right to a healthy environment is now to be found in a number of regional human rights instruments around the globe. Article II of the Additional Protocol to the Inter-American Convention of Human Rights (1994) popularly known as the San Salvador Protocol, states; (1) everyone shall have the right to live in a healthy environment and to have access to basic public services; (2) the state parties shall promote the protection, preservation and improvement of the environment. The convention of the Rights of the Child, 1989, article 24(2)(c) requires state parties in the matter of combating disease and malnutrition to take into consideration, "the damage and risks of environmental pollution". The African Charter on Human and People's Rights 1981 pro- claims in Article 24(1) a right to "a general satisfactory environment favorable to their development". In the final report on Prevention of Discrimination and Protection of Minorities listed amongst other including: (a) the right to freedom from pollution, environmental degradation and activities which threaten life, health or livelihood; (b) protection and preservation of the air, soil, water, flora and fauna; (c) healthy food and water; a safe and healthy working environment. 

 69.	In the Stockholm Declaration 1972 as mentioned above, it was declared "Man has the fundamental right to freedom, equality and adequate conditions of life, in an environment of a quality that permits a life of dignity and well being, and he bears a solemn responsibility to protect and improve the environment for present and future generations". In the United Nations General Assembly, resolution No. 45/94 recalled the language of Stockholm, stating that all individuals are entitled to live in an environment adequate for their health and well-being. All global and regional human rights bodies have accepted the link between environmental degradation and internationally-guaranteed human rights. The European convention on Human Rights has also been invoked in environmental matters. In Europe, most of the victims invoke either the right to information or the right to privacy guaranteed under the Convention. Under the said Convention and Protocol, it has been recognized that pollution or other environmental harm can result in a breach of one is right to privacy and family life. 

 74.	The Brundtland Commission defined sustainable development as development which was formally known as the World Commission of Environment and Development (WCED). The Commission's report defines sustainable development as "development which meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of the future generations to meet their own needs". The principle envisages, firstly, that each generation should be required to conserve the diversity of the natural and cultural resource base, so that it does not unduly restrict the options available to future generations in solving their problems and satisfying their own values, and should also be entitled to diversify comparable to that enjoyed by previous generations. This principle is called 'conservation and options". Secondly, generation should be required to maintain the quality of the planet so that it is passed on in no worse condition than that in which it was received, and should also be entitled to planetary quality comparable to that enjoyed by previous generations. Thirdly, each generation should provide its members with equitable rights of access to the legacy of past generations and should conserve this access for future generations. This is principle of 'conservation of access". 

 75.	The Supreme Court of India in a later case in Me Mehta vs Kamal Nath, (1997) 1 see 388 added that "it would be equally appropriate in controversies involving air pollution, the dissemination of pesticides, the location of rights of ways for utilities, and strip mining of wetland filling on private lands in a state where governmental permits are required". The facts of that case are that Kamal Nath's family has direct links with a private company, Span Motels Private Limited, which owns a resort- Span Resorts-for tourists in Kullu-Manali Valley. The problem is with another ambitious venture floated by the same company- Span Club. The club represents Kamal Nath's dream of having a house on the bank of the Beas in the shadow of the snow-capped Zanskar Range. The club was built after encroaching upon 27.12 bighas of land, including substantial forest land, in 1990. The heavy earth-mover has been used to block the flow of the river just 500 meters upstream. The bulldozers are creating a new channel to divert the river to at least one kilometer downstream. The tractor-trolleys move earth and boulders to shore up the embankment surrounding Span Resorts for laying a lawn. According to the Span Resorts management, the entire reclaiming operation should be over by March 31 and is likely to cost over a crore of rupees. Last September, these caused floods in the Beas and property estimated to be worth Rs 105 crores was destroyed. Once they succeed in diverting the river, the Span management plans to go in for landscaping the reclaimed land. The District Administration pleads helplessness. Rivers and forest land, officials point out, are not under their jurisdiction. 

 88. As regards bonafide purchasers, I found earlier that the purchasers could not claim any right on the plea of bonafide purchase since their vendor could not acquire lands exceeding the retainable ceiling provided in Act, 1950, PO 98 of 1997, and Ordinance X of 1984, they could not acquire any better right than their vendor. The fundamental rights of the third party purchasers cannot override the fundamental rights of the overwhelming number of residents of the metropolis under Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution. Further, no person can claim protection of law, and of right to life and personal liberty in violation of law. Both in Articles 31 and 32 protect those rights and liberty if he does not violate the law. Equal protection embraces the entire realm of state action, it would extend not only when a person is discriminated against in the matter of exercise' of his rights or in the matter of imposing liabilities upon him, but also in the matter of granting privileges. The principle of equality does not mean that every law must have universal application for all persons who are not by nature, attainment or circumstances in the same position, as the varying needs of different classes of persons-often require separate treatment. If a law deals equally with members of a well-defined class, it is not obnoxious and it is not open to the charge of denial of equal protection on the ground that it has no application to other persons. Right of the State to charge its policy in respect of the retainable lands from time to time under the changing circumstances can not be questioned. The High Court Division has ignored this aspect of the matter. 

 a)	after the acquisition of rent receiving interests, there should be only one class of tenants under the Government and all such tenants should have occupancy rights and have option to commute the rents of their holdings and become free peasants; 

 93. It should be remembered that no person or firm or company can acquire by way of purchase or otherwise any land which exceeds the ceiling and therefore, before the permission is sought for from RAJUK, the said person or firm or company is required to obtain permission from the Revenue Officer if the Project exceeds 100 standard bighas. Putting lands in excess of the required ceiling to residential use would be clearly contrary to the restrictions which the MMDL has undertaken the development plan without prior approval. The common law rights of the owners must give in to the statutory restrictions. The common law use and enjoyment of the ownership rights should, therefore, be subject to the requirements of the statutory law prevailing in the country. 

 94. These laws require conducting the elaborate survey of the civil needs of the citizens and feasibility and practicability of the various land uses and the prospective growth of the city before demarcating the land for different purposes. According to the Master Plan, the development plans should define various Zones into which the area sought to be developed may be divided and should also indicate the manner in which the land in each Zone is proposed to be used. The dominant intention of the aforesaid statutory provisions is to plan for the present and future development of the whole area under the plan by restricting and regulating the use of ownership rights of the owners under the common law.  104. The factual matrix involved in these appeals as it is placed before this.  (3).  132. By filing a supplementary affidavit, BELA alleged that this portion of Annexure-X-1 was an act of forgery on the part of 'Modhumoti Model Town'. The impugned judgment shows that the High Court Division called for the records of RAJUK for the purpose of ascertaining the genuineness of Annexure-X-1. Having gone though the file, the High Court Division found that a copy of Annexure- X -1 was retained in the file but that did not contain the paragraph alleged to have indicated according of development permit. The copy kept in the record contained the sig- nature of Jakir Hossain, Town Planner (Director) just after furnishing of the main contents of the letter.  "The third party rights exist and fall with the Ekushey Television, since their interests are merged with that of ETV.  167. BELA in its writ petition prayed for (I) direction to protect the Sub-flood Flow Zone of Bilamalia and Bailarpur mouzas within Savar Police Station of Dhaka near Aminbazar from illegal earth filling and (II) declaration that Madhumati Model Town project is unauthorized and in violation of Jaladhar Ain,2000.  5. The opposite party No. 1 St. Francis Xavier's Girls High School being represented by its Head Mistress and Secretary as plaintiff laid a suit being Title Suit No. 156 of 1997 in the Sixth Court of Assistant District Judge, Dhaka against the defendant petitioners Lakshmi Bazar Shahi Masjid Committee represented by its Chairman and another for a decree of permanent injunction with respect to the suit property detailed in the schedule to the plaint restraining the defendants from invading plaintiffs right and also from interfering with its enjoyment of the suit property with the averments that the said school was established in the year 1912 and was being run in accordance with the Secondary and the Higher Education Board Regulation, 1977. One Sree Rajendra Chandra Dey Singh was the owner of the suit property along with other properties and one PJ Harth, Bishop of Roman Catholic Church purchased the suit property by way of deed of conveyance registered on 1-4-1902. PJ Harth established plaintiff school, St Gregory's Boys High School and a Roman Catholic Church. The plaintiff school has been running since the year 1912. The School is situated on State Acquisition Plot No. 802 and the area of the suit property is 2.75 acres and during the all previous Record of Rights plaintiff School's name was recorded: The plaintiff School has been exercising acts of ownership and possession on the suit property on regularly paying rents to the Government and also taxes to the Municipal Corporation now City Corporation, Dhaka. The defendant Lakshmi Bazar Shahi Masjid is situated on State Acquisition Plot No. 803. The Plaintiff School and the defendant Mosque are situated on two different plots. On 10-12-1996 in the morning when the Plaintiff School engaged labourers to cut a tree, the President and Secretary of the Masjid Committee and some outsiders obstructed the cutting of the said tree and claimed the suit property t6 be the property of Mosque. The Plaintiff School asserts that it has exclusive right, interest and the defendant got no right title, interest and possession thereon. The defendant on 25-5-1997 again attempted to dispossess the plaintiff. School from the suit property and GD Entry being 1475 was registered with Sutrapur Police Station on 25-5-1997.  7. The defendants has been resisting the suit by presenting a written statement traversing all the material allegations madein the plaint contending, inter alia, that one pious Muslim built a Mosque during the Mughal period for offering prayer by religious Muslims and dedicated his property in the name of "Allah". There was Hujrakhana for Imam of the Mosque and Imam used to stay there. During Cadestral Survey Record of Right 0.0784 acre of land was recorded in Khatian No. 8941 in the name of Moulvi Ibrahim, the Mutwalli. The stand taken by the defendants is that during the State Acquisition Record of Right 0.0180 acre of land stood recorded in the name of the Plaintiff School wrongly and the Record of Right had been prepared by the plaintiff in collusion with the settlement officers. Further positive averment made by the defendants is that, the Hujrakhana is on 0.078 acre of land of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 3 and the plaintiff St Francis Xavier's Girls High School is on Cadestral Survey Plot No.2. It is also averred that the land of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 2 and the land of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 3 and the structure standing thereon are absolutely different. 2. Fact relevant for the disposal of the present Rule is that, the plaintiff-opposite parties filed the aforesaid title suit for a declaration that the order of mutation passed in Mutation Case No. 193(11) Bau-68-69 and order dated 18-11-86 passed in Miscellaneous Case No.32 BPL/83-84 are illegal and not binding on them alleging, inter alia, that they are the heirs of the SA recorded tenants and are all along in possession of the suit land. The plaintiff opposite parties for the first time came to learn in 1984 from the local Tahsildar that the suit lands were mutated in the names of the defendant-petitioners. Accordingly, plaintiff-opposite parties made an enquiry into the matter and came to know that the defendant-petitioners managed to mutate their names in respect of the suit land in the aforesaid Mutation Case No. 193(11) Bau-68-69 on the basis of some false and manufactured documents showing that the defendant-petitioners auction-purchased the suit land pursuant to Mortgage Execution Case No. 32 of 1951 on the basis of a mortgage decree in Title Suit No. 102 of 1949 and that the mutation was done without serving any notice on them. Accordingly, the plaintiff-opposite parties filed Miscellaneous Case No. 32 BPL/83-84 before the Revenue Authority concerned for reconsideration of the aforesaid mutation order. But the Revenue Authority refused to reconsider its earlier order passed in favour of the defendant-petitioners in 1969. The plaintiff-opposite parties asserted that the aforesaid mortgage suit, mortgage decree and auction-purchase of the suit land and delivery of possession thereof in favour of the defendant-petitioners were all false and manufactured and the defendant-petitioners did not have any possession of the suit land at any time. 

 8. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits opposing the Rule that since the impugned order of mutation passed by the revenue authority in 1969 purportedly under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was without jurisdiction the appellate court below rightly decreed the suit by reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The learned Advocate also submits that the plaintiff-opposite parties being the heirs of SA recorded tenants in respect of the suit land had locus standi to file the suit for declaration to the above effect and in view of the nature of declaration sought for there was no necessity to pay for any further or consequential relief. 

 9. Admittedly, both the SA Khatians as well as RS Khatians in respect of the suit land stand in the names of the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff-opposite parties and also in some of their names. It is true that the SA records, in view of section 19(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, do not provide conclusive evidence as regards title but it provides conclusive evidence as regards their preparation and revision. But entries in the SA records; in my opinion, provide a prima facie evidence as regards title. In order to maintain a suit for declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff is required to have prima facie evidence showing that he has a legal character or right to a property in respect of the subject matter of the suit and granting or refusal to grant a decree in such suit shall always depend on final adjudication thereof on evidence. Since the SA records vide Exts 3 and 3(Ka) stand in the names of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-opposite parties and also in some of their names it should be taken to be a prima facie evidence of title of the plaintiff-opposite parties in respect of the suit land and, as such, the plaintiff-opposite parties were competent to file the present suit. I do not dispute the legal principles deduced in the aforesaid cases cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners. Since the present suit was not for a declaration of title but for a declaration of the act of the revenue authority namely, the order of mutation outside the purview of law as illegal the same is certainly maintainable. Reference may be made in this connection to the case reported in 16 DLR 298. 

 11. In terms of the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act the court shall in exercise of its discretion refuse to grant any declaration if the plaintiff being in a position to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title fails to do so. Because the object of the proviso is to avoid multiplicity of suits and to prevent a person from getting a mere declaration of his rights in one suit and to resort to any remedy which was already available to him. A consequential relief is one which directly flows from the decree passed. A consequential relief within the meaning of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, however, must fulfil another condition namely, the relief must be asked for as an incidental to the declaratory decree. In the present case the plaintiff-opposite parties being SA recorded tenant merely sought for a declaration that the mutation order which was passed in 1969 affecting their proprietary right in respect of the suit lands was bad in law. If a decree is passed to the above effect the purpose of the plaintiff-opposite parties would be served and they are not required, in my view, to ask for any consequential or further relief by way of recovery of possession. Because such further relief is not at all necessary in view of the declaratory relief granted in this case. 

 12. A suit for declaration simpliciter in a case, such as the present one, is maintainable without any further or consequential relief by way of recovery of khas possession, since the mutation order was challenged as made in excess of jurisdiction in the interest of maintenance or preservation of legal and proper act namely, the preparation of SA record. 

 13. The Revenue Authority in this case is palpably without jurisdiction in disturbing the entries in the SA record in the name of mutation at the instance of the defendant-petitioners in purported exercise of powers under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 14. Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is attracted only when clerical mistake is required to be corrected or a mutation of names is to be made as a result of transfer or inheritance. It is not attracted when the record of right is to be corrected after a finding to be given as to the title of holders or challengers. The examination of title deeds for the purpose of determining title to the holder of record of rights is not permissible under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The word ''transfer'' in Clause (a) of section 143 of the said Act is limited to transfer by the recorded tenants and not by other persons. In the present case the mutation was sought for by the defendant-petitioners not because of the transfer by the plaintiff-opposite parties, but on account of auction sale at the instance of the court due to a mortgage decree. In that view of the matter, the impugned mutation order in favour of the defendant-petitioners by the revenue authority was without jurisdiction. Moreover, all the four PWs as well as DWs 1 and 2 have stated in their evidence that the plaintiff-opposite parties are in possession of the suit land. The appellate Court below has, therefore, rightly decreed that suit in favour of the plaintiff-opposite parties.

 "Periphery of hat or bazar was within the bounds of any land of hat or bazar. But the land which is not physically attached to the hat or bazar nor shown as such in any settlement record could be treated as within the periphery of the hat or bazar. If the hat is separated by an intervening space from the plot on which the bazar is situated the word 'periphery' cannot be constituted to have brought the appellant's plots within the definition of hat or bazar." 

 10. The learned Advocate submits that in this case the learned Subordinate Judge misread and misconceived the words “এইখানে বাজার শুরু হইলে” as it means where bazar was started in the locality or area because the bazar was started within the aforementioned 4 plots as specified by DW 1 in his deposition and the disputed plot which was recorded in the name of the predecessors of the plaintiff was on different plot under a different khatian intervened by another plot under another khatian as mentioned above. So he totally misread and misconstrued the pleadings of the plaintiff in the plaint. In delivering judgment the learned Subordinate Judge erred in holding that: 

 12. So in view of the above submissions and the decisions cited by the learned Advocate I find that the case of the plaintiff is, that the suit land since the predecessors-in-interest of the deceased plaintiff was in his possession and he possessed the same by constructing a hat on the land and thereafter when the Madhukhali hat was started- in the locality or in the nearby area he built a shop on the plot. He paid rent by Ext I series and released the land from auction sale on payment of certificate dues by LCR Ext. 2 The pleading of the plaintiff does not contain within the few lines of the plaint but it comprises the entire of it and to clear any ambiguity the plaint should be read entirely. The said plot does not fall in the hat plots and this is specific plot and nor even it is within the periphery of the hat as it is intervened by another plot and not within the circumference of hat plots. So, the notice under section 5 of the Ordinance XXIV of 1970 is illegal and the land was wrongly recorded in the khas khatian of the Government. 

 13. The learned Advocate appearing for the Government submits that under Order VII rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code plaintiff is required to specify and describe the suit plots. So there is no ambiguity in respect of the suit plot and there would be no difficulty if a decree is passed and more so the deceased plaintiff and his heirs are in possession of the suit land and living there by constructing hat and' a grocery shop attached to his residential house. 

 Next point raised by the learned Advocate is that the suit is barred by limitation because the suit was not filed within 6 years of the date of knowledge from the Tahsil office when his rent was not accepted as the land was recorded in khas khatian of the Government 

 17. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the material evidence which were not considered by the courts below and in view of the above discussion and the rulings cited above, I am of the view that the learned lower appellate Court and the trial Court totally misconceived the facts and circumstances of the case and also material evidence on record and so they came to an erroneous decision in the disputed plot and the plots where hat is situated.

Mr Subrata Kumar Saha, learned Senior Advocate appearing with Mr Kamal Hossain, learned Advocate for opposite party Nos. 1, 2 and 4 submits that by proposed amendment the plaintiffs are trying to introduce an alternative and completely different kind of plea which will have the effect of introducing a new controversy between the parties. Learned Advocate further submits that the application for amendment was filed after the commencement of trial but without explaining due diligence and, as such, it was liable to be rejected with cost in view of the provision under the provisos to rule 17 of Order VI of the Code of Civil Procedure. Learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiffs did not state in the application that in spite of due diligence, they could not have raised the matter before the commencement of trial. Learned Advocate further submits that by proposed amendment the plaintiffs changed the cause of action of the suit which is not permitted under law. Learned Advocate further submits that without assigning any reason the trial Court allowed the application and the revisional Court, upon proper appreciation of the materials on record and considering the case of the parties, came to definite finding that the parties have no community of interest in the subject matter of the suit and accordingly, rightly allowed the revision by setting aside the order of the trial Court and, as such, interference is not called for by this Court. 

 10. I have heard the learned Advocates, perused the plaint, written statements filed by the defendants, the application for amendment of the plaint, the orders passed by the Courts below and other relevant documents available on record from which it reveals that the application for amendment of the plaint was filed after the commencement of trial of the suit i.e after examination of PW 1 in-part and closing of the evidences PWs 2 and 3. 

 13. in the instant case, the plaintiffs in their plaint stated that they have title to and exclusive possession in 0.0950 acre suit land out of 0.19 acre land of RS Plot No. 620 of RS Khatian No. 243 but by proposed amendment they sought to introduce facts that they are owning and possessing the suit property in ejmali with the defendants. By proposed amendment the plaintiffs sought to introduce a new schedule in the plaint adding some other plots and land in the plaint. They proposed to introduce 'Ka' schedule measuring an area of 1.06 acre land of several CS plots including the suit plot. This application for amendment was filed after completion of evidence of PWs 2 and 3 who in their examination-in-chief and cross-examination clearly stated that defendant No. 1 is owning and possessing entire 0.19 acre suit land of RS Khatian No. 243. Moreover, in paragraph No. 7 of the plaint the plaintiff stated that on 5-2-2018 the plaintiff went to the Tashil Office for mutating their names and learnt from the Tashilder that RS record was not prepared in their names or their predecessor and refused to take rent from them but in the application for amendment the plaintiffs sought to introduce the fact that on 4-2-2018 the plaintiffs learnt about the wrong record-of-rights when they requested the defendants to demarcate the suit land but without doing so they disclosed that RS Khatian has not been prepared in the names of the plaintiff. By proposed amendment, the plaintiffs are trying to introduce an alternative and completely different kind of plea and different kind of cause of action which will have to the effect of introducing a new controversy between the parties which cannot be allowed as per settled principle of law, as discussed above. 

 14. The trial Court while allowing the application for amendment did not appreciate above factual and legal aspect of the matter, as discussed above, passed a non-speaking order which is illegal apparent on the face of the record. The Court of revision though rejected the application for amendment on other grounds, but came to correct decision and, as such, committed no error of important question of law resulting erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice in setting aside the order of the trail Court and accordingly, interference is not called for by this Court.

2. The facts, relevant for disposal of this petition, are that the plaintiff, Girin Ghosh (now deceased), predecessor of the present respondents, filed Land Survey Tribunal Case No.1268 of 2010 for correction of the record of rights of land measuring 8.50 decimals under Dhaka City Survey Khatian No.693, Plot No.9308 on 05.05.20 0, stating, inter alia, that land measuring 2.08 acres appertaining to CS Plot No. 177, Mouza No.297 Begunbari, Police Station-Tejgaon, presently Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka originally belonged to Brojonath Dhupi. which later devolved on his son, Sharat Chandra Dhupi who transferred 1.25 acres land out of 2.08 acres land to Madlona Di Rozario vide registered deed dated 12.06.1950 and after the death of Madloan Di Roziario, her heirs inherited the said land. Subsequently, one Shakhawat Hossain purchased 8.50 decimals land from the heirs of Madlona Di Rozario on 03.12.1988 and accordingly, the land was mutated in his name in 1990. On 25.03.1999, the said land was sold out to the plaintiff, Girin Ghosh and accordingly, the mutation khatian was prepared in his name. The plaintiff established a motor car show room thereon and also by mortgaging the same obtained loan from Janata Bank Limited. Earlier the Government acquired the said land from Madlona Di Rozario on 03.03.1957 and subsequently, derequisitioned the said land in favour of Madlona Di Rozario on 09.07.1962. Thus, the land was enlisted as vested property and at the instance of Madlona Di Rozario, the Government by notice dated 17.12.1989 informed that the land was released from the list of vested property. At the time of City Survey, the khatian of the land was wrongly prepared in the name of Bangladesh Railway, instead of the name of plaintiff, Girin Ghosh; hence the case. 

 3. The present petitioner, namely, Wega Fashions Sweaters (Pvt) Limited, being added as defendant No.9 on 02.05.2013 contested the case by filing written statement therein contending, inter alia, that the land in question measuring 1.25 acres was acquired by the Government through LA Case No.16 of 1959-60 along with other lands for the purpose of excavation of earth for Bangladesh Railway and accordingly, the Gazette Notification was published on 28.03.1968. After completion of the excavation work, the Government decided to lease out the land for industrial purpose and the present petitioner filed an application to the Ministry of Housing and Public Works for getting the allotment of land and the Ministry vide Memo No.6/1 L-3/95/62 dated 20.10.1996 allotted the said land to the petitioner. Subsequently, the Ministry of Housing and Public Works vide Memo No.Sha-7/L-Tej-18/99/1049/1(2) dated 11.10.2000 directed the concerned Executive Engineer to hand over possession of the said land to the present petitioner as the allottee. Accordingly, the Chief Engineer, Directorate of Public Works vide Memo No.2303/1 dated 12.10.2000 handed over the physical possession of the said land to the petitioner and upon accepting the consideration money, the Government executed the lease agreement on 01.11.2000 and the same was registered in favour of the petitioner. Plaintiff, Girin Ghosh (now deceased), filed Writ Petition No.8741 of 2013 challenging the order dated 02.05.2013 passed in Land Survey Tribunal Case No.1268 of 2010 allowing the application for addition of party of the present petitioner and a Rule was issued on 08.10.2013 and also an order of stay of the operation of order dated 02.05.2013 was passed. But in spite of such stay order, the proceeding of the Land Survey Tribunal case continued. In such facts and circumstances, the petitioner filed an application for stay of the proceeding of the said Land Survey Tribunal Case in Writ Petition No.8741 of 2013 and the said application was allowed by order dated 24.06.2015. Subsequently, the Rule Nisi issued in the said writ petition was discharged for non-prosecution on 14.10.2015. In the meantime, the plaintiff, Girin Ghosh, died on 18.09.2014. But without taking any step for substitution of the heirs of Girin Ghosh, his constituted attorney, Kishore Kumar Saha, PW1, proceeded with the said case by suppressing the fact of death of the sole plaintiff. Bipul Kumar Ghosh, son of the deceased-plaintiff. Girin Ghosh, was substituted on 12.10.2015 as the heir of the deceased-plaintiff in Writ Petition No.8741 of 2013. In the meantime, another writ petition being Writ Petition No.1600 of 2016 was filed by one Akanda Sanowar Murshed and another challenging the order dated 18.10.2012 passed in the said case against the rejection of their application for addition of party and by order dated 22.02.2016, a Rule Nisi was issued and an order of stay of all further proceedings of Land Survey Tribunal Case No.1268 of 2010 was passed. Subsequently, the Rule Nisi in subsequent Writ Petition No.1600 of 2016 was discharged for non-prosecution on 03.08.2016. After disposal of Writ Petition Nos.8741 of 2013 and 1600 of 2016, the proceeding of land survey tribunal case was started. Thereafter, the petitioner filed an application on 25.07.2016 under Order XXII, rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the Code) for recording an order that the suit has been abated stating, inter alia, that after completion of the deposition of the parties, the case was posted for argument on 15.03.2016. But the heirs of the sole plaintiff were not substituted within the statutory period of 90 days. Then, Bipul Kumar Ghosh, son of late Girin Ghosh, tiled an application on 17.08.2016 for sub-stitution as the heir of sole plaintiff in the said case and both the aforesaid applications for recording the order of abatement of the case and the application for substitution were heard together and the Land Survey Tribunal by order No.47 dated 04.10.2016 allowed the application for substitution and rejected the application for abatement of the case and fixed the matter for argument. 

 7. Mr. SK. Md. Morshed, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submits that after completion of the proceedings of Writ Petition Nos.8741 of 2013 and 1600 of 2016, the petitioner filed an application for abatement in Land Survey Case No.1268 of 2010 and along with an application for taking necessary steps against the constituted attorney of Girin Ghosh. Thereafter, present-respondent No.1, Bipul Kumar Ghosh, filed application for substitution in the case on 17.08.2016. He further submits that the case abated automatically under Order XXII, rule 3(2) of the Code in absence of substitution of the legal heirs within the statutory period of 90(ninety) days, but the Tribunal without considering this aspect allowed the substitution petition without any prayer by a separate application for setting aside abatement under Order XXII, rules (2) and (3) of the Code though the same is mandatory requirement of law and as such, the impugned order passed by the Land Survey Tribunal and the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division are liable to be set aside. He further submits that in case of abatement, a formal order of the Court is required for setting aside the said abatement as per Order XXII, rule 9(2) of the Code, but the Tribunal without setting aside the abatement of the said suit allowed the application for substitution of the legal heir of the plaintiff in violation of the provisions of Order XXII, rules 9(2) and (3) of the Code and as such, the impugned order passed by the Tribunal and the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division are liable to be set aside. He further submits that writ-respondent No.8 in his application for substitution filed in Land Survey Tribunal Case No.1268 of 2010 neither made any prayer for setting aside the abatement nor made any explanation for delay in filing the said application and therefore, the impugned order passed by the Tribunal and the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division are liable to be aside. He further submits that the learned Judge in allowing the application for substitution wrongly held that “বাদীপরে দাবী হল মহামান্য হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে রীট পিটিশনের আদেশ এর প্রেক্ষিতে অত্র মোকদ্দমার যাবতীয় কার্যক্রম বন্ধ থাকার কারণে গিরিণ ঘোষের পুত্রকে স্থলাভিষিক্ত করা হয় নি” though there was no order of stay regarding further proceeding of the said case from 18.09.2014 to 24.06.2015 in Writ Petition No.8741 of 2013 and as such, the impugned order passed by the Tribunal is liable to be set aside. He further submits that the application for abatement of the case was filed by the present petitioner on 25.07.2016 and on the other hand, the application for substitution of the sole plaintiff was filed on 17.08.2016, but the learned Judge of the Tribunal failed to take into consideration the mischievous conduct and approach of writ-respondent No.8 before the Court and as such, the impugned order passed by the Land Survey Tribunal is liable to be set aside. He further submits that all the disputes raised by present respondent No.1, Bipul Kumar Ghosh, and his predecessor with regard to the property in question has been resolved in Civil Appeal Nos.62-64 of 2004 and Civil Review Petition Nos.77- 78 and 84 of 2006 and lastly in First Appeal No.371 of 2011. Therefore, continuation of Land Survey Tribunal Case No.1268 of 2010 tiled by Girin Ghosh, father of present respondent No.1, Bipul Kumar Ghosh, regarding correction of the record of right in relation to the said property has become fruitless litigation. 

 9. We have heard the learned Advocate for both the parties and perused the materials on record. 

 11. It appears from the application for substitution that the explanation of delay has been furnished but no prayer for setting aside the abatement has been made. The Tribunal allowed such application treating the same as an application for substitution upon setting aside the abatement and on the other hand, it rejected the petitioner's application for recording the order of abatement. The learned Judges of the High Court Division having considered the aforementioned enunciation endorsed the same view upon holding that the Tribunal rightly exercised its discretionary power. The impugned judgment also shows that the learned Judges also disapproved the decision enunciated in the case of Bhupati Biswas-Vs-Niranjon Biswas reported in 40 DLR 517 where no explanation of delay was furnished. We are inclined to hold that the Courts below rightly exercised its discretionary power upon proper appreciation of fact, the superior Court shall not interfere therewith. 

 12. It may be mentioned further that the heirs of Girin Ghosh have been substituted in Writ Petition Nos.8741 of 2013 and 1600 of 2016, where the legal representatives of a party to a proceeding have already been brought on record which is connected and inter dependent proceeding even though in superior Court, side by side the preceding of the case before the Tribunal was stayed in the aforesaid writ petition. Thus, it is totally unnecessary to insist upon a repetition of the same process in the lower Court and in such a case, the question of abatement does not arise. 

 13. Having considered those facts and circumstances, evidence on record, we find no illegality and infirmity in the impugned judgment.

After hearing the parties and upon considering the evidence and materials on record the learned Assistant Judge, Rajshahi Sadar, Rajshahi by his judgement and decree dated 5-9-2001 decreed the suit. Then the defendant filed Title Appeal No. 226 of 2001 before the District Judge, Rajshahi. On transfer the appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Third Court, Rajshahi, who by his judgement and decree dated 25-3-2003 allowed the appeal reversing the judgement and decree of the trial Court. Being aggrieved, the plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No. 2852 of 2003 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was made absolute. 

 8. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgement of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

 9. It is apparent from the record that the appellant and respondent No. 2 purchased the property in their joint names and enjoyed the same in equal share. As long as they were living together, there can be no doubt that it was their matrimonial property. We accept the submission of Mr Samad that respondent No. 2 is an educated lady, and we find from the copy of the deed itself, which has been shown to us, that the deed clearly bears endorsement that it is a deed of gift. That endorsement appears on the top page in clear and legible writing. Hence it cannot be said that respondent No. 2 signed the document believing the same to be a power of attorney. 

 11. In such facts and circumstances as discussed above, we are of the view that this would be an appropriate case where we should exercise our authority under article 104 of the Constitution for doing complete justice in the matter before us. The evidence and materials on record do not disclose the real reason behind the gift by the wife to her husband. The fact remains that the property was purchased jointly and was in their joint possession and enjoyment in spite of the gift. The third party has purchased the property for valuable consideration. There was no evidence that the defendant mutated the record of rights to his name after the acquisition of legal title to the property by virtue of the gift. The third party purchaser would not have been aware of the transfer of title.

full_judgment:
2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that one Eklas Hossain Khan, predecessor of respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed an implication under section 24 of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption of the case land measuring 0.0206 acre of CS and SA Plot No. 565 appertaining to SA khatian No. 612 and mutation khatian No. 474/18. The case of the pre-emptor was that the case land along with other land originally belonged to Jogesh Chandra Majumder and others and the CS record of rights was accordingly prepared and published in their names. Golam Mortuza Khan, father of the pre-emptor and respondent Nos. 3-11 purchased 5 kathas of land by registered deed of sale from the said tenants and lived there by constructing dwelling house and paid rents on mutation of his own name. Golam Mortuza Khan died leaving behind the pre-emptor and respondent Nos. 3-5 as four sons and respondent Nos. 6-11 as six daughters and the said heirs possessed the land jointly by way of inheritance. Respondent No. 4 Golam Mostafa Khan by registered deed of sale dated 18-2-1988 transferred his share to his brother Moslemuddin Khan-respondent No. 3 and delivered possession. Respondent No. 3 transferred the said land by a deed of sale executed on the same date to the pre-emptee-Harunur Rashid and the deed of sale was registered on 13-8-1988. In spite of the fact that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the joint tenancy, no notice was served upon him. The pre-emptor was a stranger and a tenant under respondent No. 3. The pre-emptee declined to re-convey the land to the pre-emptor. Hence, the pre-emptor was constrained to make the application for pre-emption. 

 3. The pre-emptee appeared and opposed the application for pre-emption. His case was that the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters got their inherited lands and properties amicably partitioned by a family arrangement executed on 5-5-1978. The case land was recorded in the name of Moslemuddin Khan, the vendor in the Dhaka Municipal Corporation in separate holding. The pre-emptor and his brothers and sister were paying rents in two separate jamas. The pre-emptee after purchase of the case land got his name mutated without any objection from any quarter in mutation khatian No. 474/18/1 and has been paying rent since then. The price of the land was settled at Taka 1,56,000 and the pre-emptee paid the said amount as consideration, but the price of the land was written as Taka 50,000. After purchase the pre-emptee had invested huge sum of money to construct a semi pucca building and obtained electricity, WASA and gas connection, thereby he had to incur a cost of Taka 1,15,000. 

 9. Mr Abut Kalam Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the respondent made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division. He further submitted that both the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division after thorough analysis and assessment of the pleadings and the evidence adduced by both the parties found that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the holding and the said pre-emption case was not barred by limitation and, as such, allowed the pre-emption case. He further submitted that the High Court Division found that no notice was ever served upon the heirs of Golam Mostafa Khan and no power of mutation has been given to any other authority including Dhaka Municipal Corporation; that mutation of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation to be valid must be based on an order in writing of the revenue authority concerned under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act); that the heirs of Golam Mostafa Khan are still enjoying the joint tenancy left by the father and that amicable partition amongst the co-sharers even if recorded in writing or even a decree passed in a partition suit, cannot subdivide the joint tenancy of Golam Mostafa Khan and, as such, the pre-emptor did not cease to be a cosharer in the tenancy left by him. He submitted that the High Court Division held that Exhibit. 'Uma (O)' series were issued during the pendency of hearing of the pre-emption case and that subdivision without notice upon a co-sharer of joint tenancy could not affect the right of pre-emption and admittedly both the appellate Court and High Court Division held that no notice was served upon the co-sharer for subdivision of the holding and, as such, the respondents are the co-sharers as well as the pre-emption was filed within time from the date of registration under section 60 of the Registration Act. He submitted that the Senior Assistant Judge committed error of law resulting in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the order dated 21-6-1998 in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.85 of 1988. 

 10. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgement of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

 11. In essence the only substantive issue is one of maintainability of the application for pre-emption of non- agricultural land under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in the facts and circumstances of the case. The claim of the pre-emptor is that he is a co-sharer of the case plot by inheritance. In fact we find from the records that the vendor of the case land and the pre-emptor are full brothers. On the other hand, the claim of the pre-emptee is that the pre-emptor and his siblings are living separately having mutated their names in municipality records. The pre-emptee, therefore, claims that the pre-emptor and the vendor are no longer co-sharer. The learned Advocate for the appellants categorically submit-ted that by mutation, the property ceased to be in joint ownership and, therefore, the application for pre-emption cannot be maintained. 

 "In a case of pre-emption filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy' Act if a co-sharer tenant owns a portion of land in any plot, he is to be treated as co-sharer in the entire plot even if the land of that plot is recorded in more than one khatian. Therefore, in the event of transfer of a portion of land of that plot appertaining to another khatian a co-sharer tenant can file a pre emption case under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act notwithstanding the fact that he does not have any interest in that khatian. The words "one or more co-sharer tenants of such land" occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act means a co-sharer in the plot not the holding as mentioned in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act." 

 14. We note further from the evidence on record that the pre-emptor is the full brother of the vendor of the case land. One should not lose sight of the intention of the legislature behind the provisions of law for pre-emption. Essentially the provision exists to prevent any stranger from buying land which form a part and parcel of jointly owned property. The aim of the legislature is to give opportunity to the co-sharers to buy the case land thereby excluding incursion by strangers. In the facts of the instant case, clearly the pre-emptor and the vendor being full brothers, the pre-emptor is entitled to prevent any stranger from entering into what was their joint family property. It has been rightly held that separation of the jama is not effective since the provisions of section 117(1)(c) of the Act have not been complied with; simply having a separate municipal holding does not sever the joint ownership of the property unless the mutation takes place in accordance with the provisions of the Act.
