full_judgment:
2. Facts necessary to dispose this appeal are that respondent Nos. 1-21 as the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 116 of 1992 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka for declaration of title to the suit land on the averment that Saroda Proshad Roy Chowdhury was the owner of the suit land and on his death, his legal heirs were continuing to possess and enjoy the suit land who settled 1.00 acre land to the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs by an amalnama who paid rents for a long time and after his death, the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. The plaintiffs came to know from a reliable source that defendant No. 4 was trying to record 1.66 acres land in his name. As on 26.06.1989, defendant No. 4 with the help of some other unruly persons, tried to take possession of the suit land by applying force, the plaintiffs were compelled to institute the suit. 

 3. The suit was contested by defendant No. 4 (hereinafter referred to as the defendant) by filing written statement denying the material statements of the plaint contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs had no cause of action to file the suit, the suit was barred by limitation and was also barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The plaintiffs had neither any right nor any title in the suit land. The defendant had been enjoying the suit land along with other lands by taking settlement from the Zamindari State of Kashimpur. The then landlords accepted rents from him and his name was recorded in the S.A. Khatian, but due to mistake only .66 acre land out of 1.6 acres was recorded in the name of the Government. After the S.A. record the defendant filed an appeal being No. 4493/69/70 before the Settlement Office. Thereafter 1.00 acre land was recorded in the R.S. Khatian in the name of the defendant. The defendant filed Title Suit No. 266 of 1991 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title in respect of .66 acre land since his name was not recorded in respect of the said area of the land which was pending. The defendant did not pay rents because the case was pending. The defendant paid the rents to the landlord and he had been possessing the suit land. 

 "The learned Counsel submits that the High Court Division as well as the appellate Court being the last Court of fact committed an error of law in relying on the Ext.2, the amalnama of the plaintiff ignoring the fact the "প্রদর্শন-২ ঐ কাগজটিতে যে ০৫-০৯-৯৪ বাংলা তারিথ লেখা আছে তাহা ভিন্ন কালিতে এবং ঘষামাজা আছে।” as found by the trial Court. Thus both the Court of appeal below as well as the High Court Division on misreading the material evidence on record arrived at an erroneous finding that the plaintiff opposite party has been able to prove his title and possession in the suit land. He further submits that the appellate Court below as well as the High Court Division fell into an error of law in finding that the plaintiff opposite party is in possession of the suit land totally ignoring the S.A. and R.S. Khatians of the suit land which are documents of possession and collateral documents of title. He next submits that in decreeing the suit and affirming the appellate decree by the High Court Division, both the Courts fell into an error of law in not noticing the material fact that the plaintiff Nos. 1-16 are heirs of Gani Munshi but how the suit land is possessed by them have not been described in the plaint nor there is cogent oral evidence to show that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land rather P.W.1, the plaintiff No. 1 in his deposition stated that he used to possess the suit land through his father in law. He lastly submits that the finding of the High Court Division as well as the appellate court below that the suit is not barred by law is also based on non-consideration of material evidence on record inasmuch as P.W.1 in cross candidly admitted that "১৯৭৮ সনে খাজনা দিতে গিয়াছিলাম তহসিল অফিসে। কিন্তু তহসিল অফিস খাজনা নেয় নাই।" This P.W. 1 in his chief also stated that " নালিশী সম্পত্তির খাজনা প্রদানের জন্য তহসিল অফিসে গেলে তহসিল অফিস খাজনা গ্রহণ করে নাই। পরে জানিতে পারি যে নালিশী সম্পত্তি ৪নং বিবাদীর নামে রেকর্ড হইয়াছে এবং .৬৬ শতক জমি ভূল দেখানো হয়েছে।”" Thus it is clear that the suit is barred by limitation inasmuch as in 1978 at least the plaintiff Abdul Hai came to know that the land is not recorded in their name." 

 8. From the judgment and decree of the trial Court, it appears that it dismissed the suit on the findings, inter alia, that amalnama exhibit-2 which was the basis of the plaintiffs' case was dated 05.09.1924 B.S., but the date was written as " প্রদর্শন-২ ঐ কাগজটিতে যে ৫/৯/২৪ বাংলা তারিখ লেখা আছে তাহা ভিন্ন কালিতে এবং ঘষামাজা আছে।” the two witnesses, who deposed to prove the amalnama, the evidence of PW6 was wishful and false, because the documents filed by the plaintiffs, such as, amalnama, the rent receipts appeared to have been created subsequently; no proof was filed to show that PWs 5 and 6 used to serve at Kashempur Zamidari Estate; the story that the (PWs 5 and 6) knew the hand writing of the persons who granted dhakhilas and that they used to serve with them was also wishful and false; after the abolition of the zamindari system in 1950, the plaintiffs did not pay any rent in respect of the suit land and the SA and the RS records were also not prepared in their names; the plaintiffs failed to give any reason of non recording of their names in the SA and the RS khatians; therefore, he cause of action on which the plaintiffs filed the suit was also wishful one and false; the areas of the suit land was 1.66 acres. The plaintiffs claimed to be the heirs of one Sheikh Goni Munshi, but they did not say in the plaint how did they possess the suit land as the heirs of Gani Munshi and nothing was also stated by the witnesses who tried to prove their possession in the suit land; PW 1 stated that he used to possess the suit land through his father-in-law, Ghughur Ali, but they said fact was not stated in the plaint. The PWs. Stated in their deposition that for the last 4/5 years, the plaintiffs stated possessing the suit land, but actually no such witness was examined in Court; from the deposition of the witnesses, it appeared that the plaintiffs' side used to look after the suit land, but possession and looking after were not the same thing; amongst the defendants, defendant No.4 got the suit land by way of settlement and exhibit- 'Kha' and 'Kha(1) showed that the suit land was recorded in his name in the SA and the RS records in respect of 1 acre land. So it was proved that defendant No. 4 got 1 acre land by way of settlement; DWs 2 and 3 proved that defendant No. possessed the suit land; no document was filed to prove that the suit land was the Government land; no document was also produced to show that the Government possessed the suit land through its lessees; besides defendant No.4 also filed Title Suit No. 16 of 1993 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in respect of .66 acre land out of 1.66 acres land which was pending. The trial Court concluded that from the facts and circumstances of the case, it was proved that the defendant was the owner of the suit land and that the plaintiffs had no title and possession therein. The trial Court further found that the plaintiffs had no cause of action to file the suit inasmuch as from the plaint, it appeared that the defendant with his cohorts tried to dispossess the plaintiffs on 26.06.1989 which gave the cause of action to file the suit. Whereas, in paragraph 2 of the plaint, it was stated that the plaintiffs came to know from the reliable source that the defendant was trying to record his name in the khatian which gave cause of action to file the suit. The trial Court further held that the SA record was finally published in 1961-62 and long thereafter the suit was filed and as such, the same was barred by limitation. 

 9. From the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, it appears that it after noting down the submissions of the learned Advocate of the respective party found title of the plaintiffs in the suit land on the basis of amalnama, exhibit-'2'. The Appellate Court did not at all reverse the finding of the trial Court in respect of amalnama, exhibit- '2'. The Appellate Court did not also reverse the finding of the trial Court as to the competence of PWs 5 and 6 in proving the rent receipt and the amalnama. The Appellate Court did not also reverse the finding of the trial Court that the documents filed by the plaintiffs, such as, the amalnama and the rent receipts appeared to have been created subsequently. The Appellate Court in one sentence said that on sifting the evidence of the plaintiffs, it was found that the plaintiffs were in possession of the suit land without discussing the oral evidence and also considering the fact that the SA and the RS records were prepared in the name of the defendant. The Appellate Court found that the suit was not barred by limitation in as much as the plaintiffs filed the suit after coming to know about the record of rights in the name of the defendant; it did not consider the fact that the Tahsilder refused to accept rent from the plaintiffs in 1978, whereas the suit was filed only on 18.07.1989, i.e. after 11 years. 

 10. Let us see first whether the Appellate Court was correct in holding that the suit was not barred by limitation as the same was filed by the plaintiffs after they had come to know about the wrong recording. It is by now a well settled legal proposition that mere non-recording of a suit land in the name of the plaintiff or party concerned does not extinguish his title and a cause of action to file a suit would arise when title is invaded and the fact of invasion of title of the plaintiff in the suit land has to be gathered from the facts and circumstances of a particular case. In the instant case, plaintiff No. 1 as PW1 in his examination-in-chief stated that they went to Tshsil Office in 1978 to pay rent, but the Tahsil Officer did not accept the rent. This clearly shows that the plaintiffs very much knew about the wrong recording of the suit land, in 1978, in fact, was clear invasion on their title in the suit land, but they filed the suit only on 18.07.1989, i.e. after 11 years of the refusal of rent from them by the Tashil Office. Therefore, the knowledge of wrong recording as stated by the plaintiffs was not correct and in the facts and circumstances of the case, the trial Court rightly found the suit barred by limitation.

3. The case of the plaintiff, in brief, is that suit properties belonged to Shatish Mohon Roy who has two sons namely Sushil Mohon Roy and Narayon Chandra Roy, 4 daughters namely Purno Shashi, Chara Bala, Swadesh Bala and Bina Bala. Purno Shashi was married with Subol Chandra Das, son of Subodh Chandra Das. Except Purno Shashi Das, sons and others daughters left for India where they started residing as their permanent abode and in spite of earnest request by Shatish Mohon Roy, they did not return to Bangladesh. Purno Shashi Das and her Husband Subol Chandra Das came to the homestead of Shatish Mohon Roy and started to reside there taking care of Shatish Mohon Roy. Subsequently Shatish Mohon Roy executed a will in favour of Purno Shashi Das on 3-1-1963 appointing Subol Chandra Das as executor of the will. Puma Shashi Das and her husband Subol Chandra Das continued to reside with Shatish Mohon Roy by looking after him. Thereafter Shatish Mohon Roy passed away and subsequently Subol Chandra Das, executor of the will initiated a Probate Case being Probate Case No. 19 of 1963 and learned District Judge granted Probate on 1-7-1963 in favour of Purno Shashi Das. Subsequently, Subol Chandra Das, transferred the suit land to plaintiff Nos. 1-3, Jatendra Chandra Majumder, father of plaintiff Nos. 4-6 and grand father and father-in-law respectively of plaintiff Nos. 7-8 vide five (5) sale deeds and delivered possession thereof. The plaintiffs mutated their names in the record of rights, paid rent and continued to hold and possess the same by themselves and through Bharatias. The defendants were monthly ejectable tenants but they were habitual defaulter in payment of rent and in spite of repeated demand they didn't pay rents. Subsequently, on being approached, Marshal Law authority issued notice to defendants to quit suit properties. 

 7. Both the parties examined 3 witnesses from each side and also submitted documentary evidences. The trial Court, after hearing the parties and upon perusal of the evidences held that the plaintiffs submitted the certified copy of the Probated will dated 1-7-1963 whereby it is proved that Shatish Chandra executed will in favour of daughter Purno Shashi which has been duly probated and record of right has been prepared in the name of Purno Shashi. The trial Court further found the defendants contention that the sons and daughters of Shatish Chandra did not go to India has not been substantiated. The trial Court further found that Purno Shashi through the executor transferred the suit properties to the plaintiffs and they mutated their name in the record of right and paid all utility bills to the authority and the defendants being tenants under the plaintiffs subsequently claimed title by creating registered documents denying plaintiffs title and accordingly decreed the suit. 

 9. On the other hand Mr AM Aminuddin, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents submits that the plaintiff purchased the suit property from the lawful owner namely Purno Shashi who has got the suit properties from her father Shatish Chandra Roy by virtue of will which was duly probated and also record of right was prepared in her name. Purno Shashi transferred the suit property through her husband Subol Chandra Das by registered sale deeds and after purchase, the plaintiffs have mutated their names in the record of right, paid utility bills and while owning and possessing through tenants i.e. the defendants, they denied title of the plaintiffs for which the plaintiffs have been constrained to file the instant suit and, as such, the suit is maintainable. He further submits all the reliefs are required to be sought in a suit for proper adjudication. He further submits that as the defendants by creating documents regarding the suit properties denied title of the plaintiffs, their varatia right has been forfeited and the trial Court rightly and reasonably decreed the suit. Mr Aminuddin in support of his contention referred a decision reported in 1 BLC (AD) 156 wherein it has been reiterated that the tenant cannot set up title to a property in which he is monthly tenant, without surrendering possession to his landlord. 

 11. The plaintiffs, after purchase mutated their name in the record of right, paid rents and other utility services which also proved that plaintiffs documents have been acted upon. It is curious that no heirs of Shatish Chandra Roy challenged the probate proceeding at any point of time and also they did not challenge the documents executed and registered in favour of the plaintiffs which also prove that plaintiffs are owner of the suit properties. 

 Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the concerned Court. Send down the Lower Court Record.

lawyer:
A.J. Mohammad Ali, Advocate, instructed by Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record ---------  For the Petitioner 
Awlad Ali, Senior Advocate instructed by, Md. Abu Siddique, Advocate-on-Record ---------- For Respondent No. 1

parties:
Al Haj Md. Ghiasuddin ------- Petitioner
Vs.
Ali Ahmed Dewan and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
02. Facts, relevant for disposal of the civil petition for leave to appeal are that 36 acre of land of Khatian No. 16 was recorded in the name of Ahmed Ali Dewan, Ismail Dewan, Abdul Dewan and Harmus Dewan as Charagi subtenant (চেরাগী মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী) I And 1.20 acres land of C.S. Khatian No. 21 was also recorded in the names of above mentioned as sub-tenant under the চেরাগী পীরসূত্রে মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী। With the above claim the respondent Ahmed Ali and other filed Miscellaneous Case No. 110 of 1980 and Kutub Uddin Dewan filed Miscellaneous Case no. 50 of 1996. The respondents had previously partitioned the said property vide Title Suit No. 981 of 1933 and obtained preliminary decree on 23.4.1934 which was made final on 21.2.1935 and their names were recorded in the S.A. Khatian accordingly. The possessive interest was shown as "Cheragi" in one khatian and "occupier as mutwalli" in another. Later on in R.S. Khatian No. 74, out of 1.20 acres of homestead land. 08 acre was recorded as mosque and the remaining 1.12 acres was recorded as the homestead of the petitioners. The land of C.S. Khatian No. 16 was recorded in the name of the petitioners under R.S. Khatian No. 167. 

 03. In spite of the above, one Fariz Uddin Miah filed a petition being No. 49/76 before the Waqf Administrator for enlisting 1.20 acres of the property within Khatian No. 21 as waqf property. The said petition was rejected declaring only. 08 acre of the property as waqf property and the remaining 1.12 acres as under personal ownership. Against the said order Fariz Uddin filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 352/76 before the District Judge, Dhaka, which was disposed of by order dated 30.10.1976. Against that order Osman Gani Dewan filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 21 of 1976 before the High Court Division, Which remanded the matter to the Wakf Administrator by order dated 22.8.1976. Thereafter, the Waqf Administrator included the whole property, i.e. 1.20 acres of land of khatian No. 21 as waqf property. Against that order Ahmed Ali Dewan filed Miscellaneous Case No. 110 of 1980 which was dis-missed on 20.08.1984 for want of tadbir. Against that order Ahmed Ali Dewan and others filed First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 183 of 1984 before the High Court Division which remanded the aforementioned Miscellaneous Case No. 110 of 1980 for disposal in accordance with law after taking evidence. 

 04. A huge number of cases, counter cases and appeals have been filed by various parties, the up-shot of which is as to whether the land, save and except the 08 acre containing Mosque, Graveyard and Mazar, has the character of wakq property or not, or whether the remaining 1.12 acres of land is secular property of the Dewan family. The Waqf Administrator declared the whole property as waqf property, against which Kutub Uddin Dewan filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 53 of 1985 before the District Judge, Narayangonj. By judgement and order dated 16.11.1989 the appeal was allowed declaring. 13 acre of land of plot No. 16 under Khatian No. 21 as waqf property and the reaming property as secular land of Dewan family. Against the Said judgement Miscellaneous Appeal No. 145 of 1999 was filed before the High Court Division. 

 06. Presently, the respondents claim that the suit land is 1.20 acres of land of dag No. 16 under Khatian No. 21 of Kutubpur Mouza and 36 acre of land of dag Nos. 142/143 of Khatian No. 16 in total 1.56 acres of land. The suit land originally belonged to Syed Kha and under him Ayesha Akter was in possession. The land of C.S. Khatian No. 21 was possessed by Ahmed Ali Dewan as Mutwalli as "Cheragi Madhasattadhikari". In this way Ahmed Ali Dewan and others also possessed the land of C.S. Khatian No. 16 Out of Dewan family, Ahmed Ali Dewan in 1955 created Wakf of 1.56 acres of land of aforesaid khatian and that was entered in E.C. No. 3083. In the Wakf property there is Mosque, Mazar, open space as field and homestead. On the other hand the petitioner claims that excepting. 08 acre of land, the remaining land is self acquired secular land. In the case both the parties examined one witness each and exhibited some documents as Exhibit 1-7 and Ka-Ga. The Wakf Administrator declared the property as Wakf property and the District judge affirmed the said order. 

 07. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, Learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submitted that the High Court Division misdirected itself and erred in declaring 1.12 acres out of 1.20 acres of the suit property to be secular property of the Dewan Family and treating only. 08 acre as wakf property. The learned Advocate also submitted that the suit land is described in the record of rights as Cheragi Pir Suter Madhyasattadhikari (চেরাগী মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী) which manifestly demonstrates that it is a rent free grant for the purpose of defraying expenses of lighting lamps in the Mosque, Mazar and Dorga and as such the High Court Division was in error in holding that the property was being enjoyed as secular property. He further submitted that in Miscellaneous EC. No. 49 of 1976 (EC 3083) the Administrator of Waqf by order dated 24.5.1980 after detailed discussion of all the facts and circumstances and taking into account the meaning of the words Cheragi Madhyasattadhikari Chirosthai "(চেরাগী মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী)" and Cheragi Pir Dayal Mutwalli Sutre Madhyasattadhikari Chirosthai "(চেরাগী পীর দয়াল মোতওয়ালী সূত্রে মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী চিরস্থায়ী)" came to positive decision that the properties of two khatins are waqf by user and took the view that the entire property of C.S. Khatian Nos. 21 and 16 was Waqf property and that the enrollment of the property to EC case No. 3083 was valid and legal. 

 10. The crux of the cases relate to the character of the suit property namely 1.20 acres of plot No. 16 of Khatian No. 21. The High Court Division considered the fact that the district Judge considered the properties as waqf property because 18 persons failed affidavit supporting the property to be waqf property. And since the waqf administrator was not a party in Title suit No. 981 of 1933 that decision was not binding upon him. However, the High Court Division observed that the property was declared as waqf by custom and there was no deed made for the dedication. In such view of the matter, the High Court Division decided that only 0.8 acre of the suit land on which the mosque and mazar was situated was waqf property and the remaining property was secular property.

full_judgment:
5. Against the said judgment and decree, the defendant preferred appeal being Title Appeal No. 114 of 2004 before the learned District Judge, Comilla, which was transferred to the Court of the learned Additional District Judge, Brahmanpara, Comilla. After hearing the parties and considering the materials on record the learned Additional District Judge, allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 "(I). The witness of the plaintiffs, during trial, admitted the possession of the defendant in the suit land, and the appellate Court, the last Court of facts, quoting the portions of those evidence, held that the plaintiffs have no exclusive possession in the suit land, but the High Court Division without arriving at a finding as to possession on the basis of evidence on record erroneously decreed the suit and the plaintiff being out of possession, the suit was not at all maintainable without a prayer for recovery of khas possession. 

 (II). Since the genuineness of the kabala dated 15-2-1944 was seriously challenged the appellate Court called the concerned Index Register and on perusal of the same and on considering the evidence on record, particularly the evidence as discussed by it, came to the conclusion that the above kabala dated 15-2-1944, the basic document of the plaintiffs for his title, is forged one and the High Court Division committed error in interfering with the above finding of fact as to genuineness of the kabala dated 15-2-1944, and further observation of the High Court Division that since the plaintiffs produced the certified copy of the kabala dated 15-2-1944, so it is to be presumed that the kabala dated 15-2-1944 is genuine, but such presumption is never intended to extend to the genuineness of the transaction specially when there is no evidence regarding the execution of the above kabala dated 15-2-1944 and; 

 9. Mr Bivash Chandra Biswas, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the appellant made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. The learned Advocate upon placing before us the evidence of the defendant's witnesses pointed out that PWs 2, 3 and 4 admitted the possession of the defendant in their cross-examination. He also pointed out that the appellate Court considered the evidence of CW 1 and came to the conclusion that he could not come to any positive finding that the predecessor of the plaintiffs had title in the suit land. He pointed out that CW 1 the Mohorar from the record room of the District Registry Office categorically stated that the certified copy of deed No. 2031 of 1944 neither contains the seal of the SR Office nor the signature of the Record Keeper, and also the signature of A. Rashid appearing above true copy is not the signature of the then Sub-Registrar A. Rashid. He finally submitted that it is true that the production of a document more than 30 years old raises a presumption of genuineness, but that presumption has been reverted through the evidence of CW 1 that the Index Volume for the year 1944 of that Registry Office did not contain the document in question. Also the evidence of CW 1 raised serious doubt about the genuineness of the certified copy, which was produced in support of the existence of the sale deed of 1944. 

 11. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned and perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

 12. It is apparent from the evidence on record that the plaintiffs witnesses, namely PWs 2, 3 and 4 all deposed in their cross-examination admitting the possession of the defendants in the suit land. The suit of the plaintiffs was for a declaration of their title in the suit land and also for a declaration that the record-of-rights in respect of RS Khatian No. 380 was collusive, fraudulent, ineffective and not binding. Therefore, the appellate Court rightly held that in such circumstances the trial Court fell into error in decreeing the suit only on the prayer for declaration of title simpliciter. 

 13. When the lower appellate Court, being the last Court of fact, comes to any finding based on the evidence on record, the power of the revisional Court to interfere with such finding is limited to cases where the finding of the appellate Court is perverse, or based on wrong appreciation of the evidence. It appears from the judgment of the High Court Division that the aspect of possession of the defendant in the suit land has not at all been dealt with or reversed by the revisional Court. Hence, the impugned judgment is not sustainable on that account. 

 15. The High Court Division observed that "section 55(3) of the Registration Act provides that Index No. II shall contain such particulars mentioned in section 21 relating to every such document and Memorandum as the Inspector General from time to time directs in that behalf. Section 21 provides that no non-testamentary document relating to immovable property shall be accepted for registration unless it contains a description of such property sufficient to identify the same. Though it appears that in page 59 of Index No. II the description of the property in question was not found but there is nothing on record to show that it was only in page 59 the description of the property in question ought to have been recorded." 

 16. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned and perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

 17. It is our view, that the observation of the High Court Division is rather misconceived. The Index of registered documents will not have the description of the property. In our view, the fact that the number of the deed alleged to have been registered on 15-2-1944 is absent from the index is sufficient to indicate that it is not a genuine document. The judgment of the appellate Court appears to be sound and based on proper appreciation of the evidence and materials on record. 

 18. It is also apparent from the records, as found by the appellate Court, that the plaintiffs witnesses admitted possession of the defendant in the suit land. This finding of fact was not addressed by the High Court Division. In our view, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the appellate Court rightly held that a suit for declaration of title simpliciter was not maintainable.

full_judgment:
2. The preemptor-respondent No.1 herein filed Miscellaneous Case No.45 of 1985 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Boalkhali, Chittagong both under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the case land on the averments that he was a co-sharer of the case holding while the purchaser-opposite party was a stranger to that. That on 25.09.1973 the vendor opposite party No.2 sold the case land to the purchaser-opposite party No.1 by a registered kabala dated 25.09.1973 beyond the knowledge of the petitioner. That no notice of that kabala was ever served upon the petitioner and the purchaser-opposite party No.1 also did not take possession of the case land and the son of the vendor-opposite party remained in possession of the case land as before. That on 17.07.1985 when the purchaser-opposite party No.1 came to the case land for constructing a house thereon the petitioner, for the first time, could know about the case transfer. Thereafter, he obtained the certified copy of that kabala on 31.07.1985 and being thus confirmed about the sale in question filed the preemption case on depositing the requisite amount within the statutory period of limitation from the date of his knowledge. 

 3. The purchaser-opposite party No.1 and the respondent Nos. 2, 18 and 19 contested that case by filing separate written objection. The material case of the purchaser-opposite party No.1 was that he purchased the case land within the full knowledge of the father of the petitioner-who was co-sharer of the case holding and that the petitioner was not at all a co-sharer of the case holding at the time of sale in question. That after purchasing the case land the purchaser-opposite party mutated the case land in his name and the B.S. record of rights in respect of the case land also was duly prepared in the name of the purchaser-opposite party. The further case of this purchaser opposite party No.1 was 1 that after his purchase of the case land the opposite party No. 2 the son of the vendor filed Other Suit No. 70 of 1982 in the Court of Munsif, 1st Court, Potia, Chittagong against him for declaring the case kabala collusive and void and that in the plaint of that suit, in para-3, the opposite party No. 2 stated clearly that his Advocate Mr. Sunil Kumar Sarker (the present preemptor-petitioner) obtained the certified copy of the present case kabala for him. That the opposite party No.2 filed another case being No. 18 of 1982 in the Court of Union Parishad against this purchaser opposite party and in that case also the present preemptor-petitioner was a witness. This purchaser-opposite party, in his written objection, stated also that he exchanged 15 decimals of land out of the case land with some other land of Jogeshwar Shil in the year 1982 and thereafter he sold out 96 decimals of land to Jogeshwar Shil in the year 1983 and now he is in possession of only 5 decimals of land out of the case land. 

 9. Mr. M. A. Quiyum, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the preemptee-appellant has mainly submitted before as that this case for preemption filed long 14 years after the case transfer is hopelessly barred by limitation, that there are ample evidence on record and facts and circumstances to prove that this preemptor-petitioner knew about the case transfer from the very beginning; that the appellate court below and the High Court Division committed great error and injustice in allowing the case for preemption ignoring this inordinate delay in filing this preemption case and also the evidence and facts and circumstances telling that the preemptor-petitioner knew about the case transfer from the very beginning. The learned Counsel has made argument to the effect also that the trial court duly considered all these evidence and facts and circumstances and rightly came to the decision that this preemption case was hopelessly barred by limitation, but the appellate court below and the High Court Division without reversing these findings and decision of the trial court whimsically allowed the case for preemption on misinterpretation and misappreciation of the evidence on record. The learned Counsel has pointed out also that in this case there is a strong fact to prove that this preemptor-petitioner knew about the case transfer from the very beginning. Elaborating this argument the learned Counsel has stated before us that in the very written objection filed before the trial court this preemptee-appellant stated clearly that immediate after the case transfer the opposite party No.2-the son of the vendor-opposite party filed Other Suit No.70 of 1982 before the 1st Court of Munsif, Potia, Chittagong challenging the genuineness of the case kabala and in the plaint of that suit the opposite party No.2 stated clearly that this present preemptor-petitioner was his engaged lawyer and he obtained the certified copy of the case kabala for him. The learned Counsel has pointed out also that this preemptee-appellant, in, support of this case, filed the certified copy of the plaint of Other Suit No.70 of 1982 which was duly marked as exhibit-P, and the trial court though rightly took into consideration   this exhibited-P, but the appellate court below and the High Court Division ignored this exhibit-P and most illegally and erroneously allowed the case for pre-emption. The learned Counsel for the pre-emptee-appellant has contended that the judgment of the trial court was a correct one and the judgments of the appellate court below and the High Court Division are wrong. 

 10. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Advocate for the preemptor respondent has made submissions supporting the impugned judgment. He has argued that in this case it is rather an admitted fact that the son of the vendor-opposite party is still in possession of the case land and that the purchaser-opposite party never took possession of the case land before the alleged date of knowledge of the petitioner as stated in the petition for preemption and in the circumstances the appellate court below did not commit any wrong in allowing the case for pre-emption and the High Court Division also rightly affirmed the judgment and order of the appellate court below. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan has argued also that the exhibit-P is not a conclusive proof of the defence case that the preemptor-petitioner knew about the case transfer from the very beginning. The learned Counsel has argued that this exhibit-P is not at all a statement of the preemptor- petitioner himself and that the preemptor-petitioner, during trial of the case, clearly denied the alleged fact that he obtained certified copy of the case kabala for the opposite party No. 2. The learned Counsel for the pre-emptor-respondent has argued that both the appellate court below and the High Court Division, on proper appreciation of evidence on record and other facts and circumstances rightly allowed the case for preemption and in the circumstances this appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

 12. Admittedly, this preemption case was filed long 14 years after the case transfer. It is also an admitted fact that at the time of case transfer the preemptor-petitioner was not a co-sharer to the case holding since his father was alive at that time and at the death of his father the preemptor-petitioner became co-sharer to the case holding. So, the preemptor-petitioner was not entitled to get any notice of the case transfer. Admittedly, the father of the pre-emptor-petitioner-who was the co-sharer of the case holding-did not file any pre-emption case. The purchaser-opposite party, in his written objection, stated clearly that the father of this preemptor-petitioner knew about the case transfer very well. However, the preemptor petitioner has contended that after the death of his father the registration of the kabala in question as per section 60 of the Registration Act was completed and as such the preemptor petitioner, who became the co-sharer of the case holding before that, was entitled to get preemption of the case land. However, the main question in this case for preemption is whether the case for preemption is barred by limitation or not. 

 13. It has already been mentioned above that this case for preemption has been filed long about 14 years after the case transfer. The preemptor-petitioner though has pleaded that he had no knowledge about the case transfer before his alleged date of knowledge-as mentioned in the application for preemption-but on examining the evidence on record we do not find that this case of the preemptor-petitioner was proved. Though, admittedly, the opposite party No. 2-the son of the vendor was in possession of some portion of the case land but this fact alone cannot be a proof of the petitioner's case that he could not know about the case transfer before his alleged dated of knowledge. In this case there are, rather, sufficient evidence and facts and circumstances to prove that the preemptor-petitioner had knowledge about the case transfer from the very beginning. In this case the documents filed from the side of the contesting opposite parties have proved that after his purchase the purchaser opposite party transferred some of the case land to the opposite party No.18 and later the opposite party No.18 transferred some of the case land to opposite party No.19 and both these subsequent purchasers have deposed in this case claiming their possession in the case land. Over and above, there is another strong evidence which proves that the preemptor-petitioner knew about the case transfer from the very beginning. This is exhibit-P-about which I have already mentioned above. Admittedly, the opposite party No. 2-the son of the vendor-filed Other Suit No.70 of 1982 challenging the genuineness of the case kabala immediate after the execution and registration of the same. It should be mentioned that the said Other Suit No.70 of 1982 was ultimately dismissed. However, in the plaint of that suit the opposite party No.2 stated clearly that this preemptor-petitioner was his engaged lawyer and he obtained a certified copy of the case kabala for him. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel for the pre-emptor-respondents has argued that during trial of the case the preemptor-petitioner clearly denied this statement of exhibit-P that he obtained certified copy of the case kabala for the opposite party No.2. But on scrutiny of the deposition of this preemptor-petitioner we find that the preemptor-petitioner while deposing before court, though denied this alleged fact that he obtained the certified copy of the case kabala in the year 1982 for the opposite party No. 2, but he did not deny the fact that he was the engaged lawyer of the opposite party No. 2. The opposite' party No. 2 filed Other Suit No. 70 of 1982 challenging the genuineness of the impugned kabala. In the circumstances it is not believable at all that the preemptor-petitioner could not know about the case kabala before his alleged date of knowledge. From the facts and circumstances stated above it is rather proved beyond any doubt that the preemptor petitioner / knew about the case transfer in the year 1982. In the circumstances the trial court rightly dismissed the case for preemption. The appellate court below and the High Court Division committed wrong in allowing the preemption case.

Short facts leading to this Rule are that one Niamat Ali was granted lease of the House No. C/69 of 3rd Colony, Mirpur, Dhaka(hereinafter referred as case property), by the then Government of East Pakistan by executing a registered deed of lease dated 10-02-1956 for the purpose of rehabilitation as refugee from India. After the death of Niamat Ali his only son Gauhar Ali and daughter Nurunnahar inherited the case property. Later on they transferred the same to the petitioner by executing a registered sale deed dated 15-08-1978. The petitioner also mutated his name in the record of rights in the Revenue Office and has been in peaceful possession of the same by paying rent but the Government illegally included the case property in the "Kha" list of abandoned buildings published in Bangladesh Gazette Extra Ordinary dated September 23, 1986, against Serial No. 13 at Page 9764(23). 

 7. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the Court of Settlement failed to weigh and sift the materials on record as required by law and evidently fell in an error, in coming to his ultimate decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 9. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels, we have gone through the writ petition along with other materials on record and given our anxious consideration to their submissions. 

 12. On perusal of the materials on record, we find that the Court of Settlement in it's judgment referred a decision dated 16-04-1989 passed in Case No. 254 of 1987, wherein it appears that one Dr. A. Matin and another being petitioners, claimed ownership in the case property and prayed for it's exclusion from the list of abandoned properties, contending that after the death of lessee Niamat Ali, his only son Abdul Gaffar transferred the case property to them on 02-04-1979 by a registered kabala deed. In the said case, Court of Settlement observed that they could not prove that lessee Niamat Ali died in Bangladesh, leaving behind Abdul Gaffar as his only heir, so they have not acquired any right, title and interest in the case property by virtue of kabala dated 02-04-1979. The original owner was neither available nor lived in this Country as Bangladeshi national and he left the case property uncared after President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force. The case No. 254 of 1989 was dismissed on 16-09-1989, with the findings that the case property is an abandoned property within the meaning of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 read with Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. 

 14. On critical analysis of the materials on record, we find that the Court of settlement considered all points, there is no misreading or non consideration of the material documents and violation of principle of natural justice, which may affect the merit of the case. 

 15. The Court of Settlement, it appears, rightly considered the crucial point that lessee Niamat Ali was not present in Bangladesh and his whereabouts were not known on 16-02-1972 when President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force. The Court of Settlement upon thoroughly considering the evidence on record found that the petitioner failed to prove that the lessee Niamat Ali was present in Bangladesh as aforesaid, far less proving that his claim of title to the Case property has immune from the perilous effect of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. 

 16. On careful consideration of the materials on record we also hold that the original owner of the case property was not present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were not known or he ceased to manage or occupy the property at the time when President's Order No.16 of 1972 was promulgated on 16-02-1972. Moreover the High Court Division in exercising it's writ jurisdiction, can only interfere with the finding of facts of the Court's below when it appears that the Court acted without jurisdiction and failed to consider the materials on record, which are found absent in the instant case. 

 22. Send down the case record at once.

2. The plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of right, title and interest in the suit land and for recovery of khas possession by evicting the defendant no.1 therefrom stating, inter alia, that the suit land along with its northern 1380 sq. fit appertaining to the settlement plot No. 7808 and Municipal holding No. 884 of Sylhet Municipality originally belonged to Birendra Lal Das and others popularly known as "Lal Brothers" in their Maliki right, one Sital Proshad Choube was a lessee under them in respect of that land. After taking lease from them he constructed a shop house and residential quarters over the land and possessed the same accordingly. He then gifted the land and the structure standing thereon to his grand sons Durga Proshad Tribedi and Mahabir Proshad Tribedi equally by a registered deed of gift dated 21.1.1927. On the basis of this gift Tribedi brothers began to own and possess the premises equally in ejmali as lessees under Lal Brothers. At the time of the gift Mahabir was minor and used to live with his elder brothers Durga Proshad who later on constructed new houses by removing the old one at his own cost and provided therein electric connection, water line, etc. Tribedi brothers continued to own and possess the premises in ejmali and there was no partition between them at any point of time. After the expiry of the lease they apprehended ejectment by Lal Brothers. So, they executed a registered kabala dated 27.3.1942 in favour of Kanailal Surma and his brothers. Then Lal Brothers brought a suit for ejectment being Title Suit No. 169 of 1944 in the First Court of Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet against the Tribedi Brothers. During the pendency of that ejectment suit Mahabir executed a kabala dated 4.4.1944 in favour of Harendra Nath Chakravorty for his 8 annas share though he had no saleable interest in the property at the relevant time. This kabala dated 4.4.1944 is a collusive document and it was never acted upon. Harendra Nath never claimed any right, title and possession on the basis of that kabala. Lal Brothers then obtained a decree in the ejectment suit on 6.4.1945 against the Tribedi Brothers and put the decree into execution being Execution Case No. 14 of 1946. But during the pendency this execution case, Kanailal Surama and others, on the basis of their kabala dated 27.3.1942 from Tribedi Brothers, filed Title Suit No. 29 of 1947 in the First Court of Sadar Munsif, Sylhet for declaration of their title and confirmation of possession over the premises against Lal Brothers impleading Durga Proshad Tribedi, Mahabir Proshad " Tribedi and Harendra Nath Chakraborty, but subsequently the name of Tribedi Brothers and Harendra Nath were struck off from the plaint and the suit was compromised on 9.7.1946 amongst Surmas and Lal Brothers, and thereby Surmas retained their right in the structures they purchased. In the said Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1946 Tribedi Brothers filed an objection being Misc. Case No. 145 of 1947 on 28.4.1947 wherein they asserted that they are not liable to be rejected as per provisions of Sylhet Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act of 1947 as they completed 12 years of possession of the premises. Their contention was upheld upto the High Court in the 2nd   Appeal being Appeal No. 14 of 1947 vide judgment dated 9.12.1952 and it was decided that the Tribedi Brothers had a protected interest and they were not liable to be ejected. Mahabir Proshad Tribedi then executed and registered a Nadabi Patra dated 18.1.1956 in favour of Lal Brothers in respect of his 8 annas share in the property. This Nadabipatra is a collusive document. After execution of this document by Mahabir Durga Proshad filed a case for pre-emption being Misc. Case No. 116 of 1956 under section 24 of the E.B. Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in the 1st Court of Sadar Munsif, Sylhet in order to save the property from further burbles. That case was allowed in part on 24.8.1956. Durga Proshad then preferred Misc. Appeal No. 119 of 1957 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet. The present defendant No.2 also preferred another Misc. Appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 126 of 1957 against the said order dated 24.8.1957 passed by the learned Munsif. The appellate Court allowed the Misc. Appeal No. 119 of 1957 and dismissed the Misc. Appeal No. 126 of 1957 on 13.11.1958. Thereafter two revision cases numbering C.R. 1301 and 1302 of 1958 were preferred before the High Court where in was held that no transfer was effected by the said Nadabipatra vide judgment dated 21.1.1959. In the meantime Lal Brothers created a kabala in favour of the defendant no.2 showing the sale of 8 annas share in the property. But in spite of all this maneuvers neither Harendra Nath nor Lal Brothers nor the defendant no. 2 ever acquired any right, title, interest or possession in the property. Durga Proshad continued to possess the entire property. During the last S.A. operation he was found in possession of the property and the same was record in his name. The Municipal holding standing exclusively in his name remained unaltered during his life time and the taxes were paid by him. Thereafter it was converted in the name of his son the plaintiff and he has been paying taxes in his own name. In the meantime, the defendant no.1 being colluded with the defendant no.2, filed the objection case No. 215 of 1963 under section 50(1) of the E.B.S.A. and T. Act for correction of the record of rights alleging his jote right under the defendant no.2, but the said Misc. case was rejected on 13.3.1963. Subsequently the plaintiff got his name mutated by Mutation Case No. 61/69-70. The defendant no.1 then submitted to the terms of Durga Proshad and began to continue his business in the ground floor of the suit premises agreeing to pay him Taka 5.00 per day as compensation for use and occupation of the same. Durga Proshad then died on 3.2.1963 leaving behind his son the plaintiff as his only heir. The plaintiff then gradually felt inconvenience to reside in the 1st floor of the suit premises and so he arranged to shift to his present address at Kalighat situated within the Sylhet Municipality. But before he left the premises, he let out the same to one Abdul Quddus and his brother Md. Abdul Khalique through a Bharanama dated 10.12.1966. Subsequently they purchased the northern 1380 sq. feet from the plaintiff by two registered kabalas dated 24.4.1969 and shifted there by vacating the 1st floor of the suit premises in favour of the plaintiff in February 1973. Since then he was in exclusive possession of the 1st floor of the suit premises. In the meantime, the suit premises became dilapidated and requires rebuilding. So, the plaintiff requested the defendant no.1 to vacate the ground floor of the same, but the defendant no.1 did not pay any heed to it. He later put obstruction to the passage of the first floor. So, the plaintiff brought a criminal case under section 144 Cr.P.C. being Misc. Case No. 199 of 1976 in the Court of S.D.O. Sylhet against the defendants. In that case the defendant nos.1 and 2 filed separate objections on 2.8.1976 and 24.7.1976 respectively wherein they denied the title of the plaintiff in respect of the suit premises most illegally. The defendant no. 1 then at the connivance of the Lal Brothers and the defendant no.2 stopped payment of Tk. 5.00 per day as compensation for use and occupation of the ground floor to the plaintiff. Thus he put obstruction to his rightful enjoyment of the same. Hence is the suit filed on 30.11.1976. 

 6. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners submits that the plaintiff not having adduced any evidence other than that of the plaintiff himself and that there being no evidence of possession in favour of the plaintiff for suit land, the Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit for recovery of possession. The learned Counsel further submits that there being no evidence where Durga Proshad continued in possession of the suit land even after execution of Na-dabi Patra in favour of Lal Brothers by Mahabii Durga Proshad and where Lal Brothers got possession of the suit land on or before the deed of execution of Na-dabi Patra of 18.1.1956 by Mahabir Durga Proshad and where defendant no. 8 from Lal Brothers on 25.5.1956 and there being no evidence on record to that effect, the Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit. 

 "We have perused the said documentary evidence as above. It is undisputed that by judgment of this Court dated 9.12.1952 in S.M.A. No. 17 of 1949, this Court hold that Trebedi Brothers had occupancy right in the suit property and that they were not liable to be evicted from the suit property in view of the provisions of the Sylhet Non-Agricultural Urban Area Tenancy Act as they were in possession of the suit property over 12 years by making constructions thereon. This case arise out of Title Suit No. 169 of 1944 instituted by Lal Brothers for eviction of Trebedi Brothers which was decreed and Title Execution No. 14 of 1946 was started. On the basis of objection filed by Trebedi Brothers being Miscellaneous Case No. 145 of 1947, their objection was sustained as mentioned above. We find from the materials on record that at the time of disposal of S.M.A. No. 17 of 1949 Mohabir Proshad had already executed deed dated 4.4.1944 Ext. A-1(3) but they could not establish their title on the strength of the said deed by which Lal Brothers allegedly got/8/-interest in the benami of Harendra as submitted by the learned Advocate and failed to maintain the decree for eviction we are therefore convinced that Lal Brothers has acquired no title and possession on the basis of Ext.A-1(3) and that the said deed was not acted upon. It further appears from the Judgment dated 20.1.59 in Civil Revision No. 1301 and 1302 of 1958 Ext.7, that this Court hold that no transfer was affected in favour of Lal Brothers on the basis of Nadabi Patra executed by Mohabir Proshad on 18.1.1956 and this Court dismissed the pre-emption case filed by Durga Proshad on that ground alone. We further find that Lal Brothers did not got possession on the basis of compromise decree dated 9.6.1946 passed in Title Suit No. 29 of 1947 as submitted by Mr. Moksudur Rahman inasmuch as in spite of such compromise decree they failed to uphold the eviction decree in S.M.A. No. 17 of 1949. Further we find that the said compromise decree was not binding upon Durga Proshad as he was not a party in that suit. On perusal of these documentary evidence we are satisfied that Lal Brothers had acquired no saleable title nor possession in the suit premises on 29.5.1956 on which date they transferred the same in favour of defendant no. 2. The defendant no.2 has also acquired no title in the suit premises on the strength of Ext. A-1(1). In the premises the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants that Mahabir Proshad had recognized the transfer of his /8/- share in the suit property by deed dated 4.4.1944 Ext.A-1(3), by executing Nadabi Patra on 18.1.1956 Ext.A-1(4) merits on consideration. 

 11. We have perused the impugned judgment which is concluded by concurrent finding based on evidence on record, both oral and documentary and accordingly find no merit in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the defendant-petitioners.

3. The case of the plaintiffs respondents, in short, is that the suit property originally belonged to Dhirendra Mohan Chowdhury, Niranjan Kumar Chowdhury and Monindra Kumar Thakur who acquired the property by inheritance and accordingly, record of right was prepared in their names. Dhirendra Mohan Chowdhury and Monindra Kumar Thakur died in the then East Pakistan and Niranjan Kumar Chowdhury left this country for India and their properties were made Khas under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 4. The plaintiffs filed an application to Sub-Divisional Officer, Munshigonj for settlement of the suit land in their favour as landless cultivator and upon an enquiry the government granted settlement. Thereafter, plaintiffs executed a registered Kabuliat in favour of the government on 3-11-75 for a period of 15 years. The plaintiffs-respondent thereafter constructed house in the suit land and in some portions thereof they also grew different crops. But behind the back and knowledge of the plaintiffs Naimuddin and two others got the suit land settled in settlement case Nos. 52 of 69-70 and 94 of 69-70. The plaintiffs then brought Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 18, 19 and 20 of 1969-70 in the court of ADC (Rev) Dhaka and after due inquiry and upon submission of report the aforesaid Settlement Cases were cancelled. Thereafter, another man named Mosharraf filed an application for settlement of the self-same suit land for constructing a Health Complex and prayed for cancellation of the settlement of the plaintiffs and accordingly, Miscellaneous Case No. 75 of 75-76 was started; the plaintiffs appeared in that case to contest but on 13-11-76 Mosharraf Hossain Khan managed to obtain an ex parte order in his favour; the plaintiffs thereafter preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 37 of 1976 before the ADC (Rev), Dhaka which was disposed of in favour of the plaintiffs and against which the said Mosharraf Hossain filed appeal being Appeal No. 152 of 1980 before the Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka and the said appeal was also dismissed. It is further alleged that in order to grab the plaintiff’s property another person named Abdul Kashem claimed himself to be the President of Medini Mondal Primary School and he also filed another Miscellaneous Case No. 262 of 1981 before the ADC (Rev) Dhaka praying for settlement of the suit land in favour of that school. The plaintiffs also contested the said case but Abdul Kashem having appeared personally denied to have filed the said miscellaneous case. However, the said Miscellaneous Case was fixed for hearing on 8-12-82 and in place of said Abdul Kashem another person name Anwar Chowdhury appeared in the said case and prayed for settlement of the suit land in favour of the said girls' school. The ADC (Rev) Dhaka on the basis of a report cancelled the settlement of the plaintiff-respondents and passed an order of settlement in favour of the said girls' school on that date, that is on 8-12-82. 

 10. We have heard the learned Counsel for the petitioner and perused the judgment of the High Court Division. Admittedly, the plaintiffs-respondents being landless cultivator were granted settlement by the then Sub-divisional Officer, Munshiganj by registered Kabuliats for a period of 15 years upon proper investigation and enquiry. There is nothing on record to show that the plaintiffs violated any terms of the kabuliat of the settlement. 

 11. It appears that the trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs took settlement as nal land for 15 years but, as a matter of fact, the land is not a nal land and, as such, the settlement taken on false statement is not a legal settlement. The trial Court has however found possession of the suit land with the plaintiffs on consideration of evidence on record. The appellate Court being the final court of fact having considered the materials on record rightly found that the plaintiffs took settlement legally and have been possessing the suit property and they have not violated the terms of the settlement. Upon the aforesaid finding the appellate Court decreed the suit holding that the orders dated 29-11-86 and 29-3-88 passed by the defendant No. 1 are illegal and without jurisdiction. 

 14. It appears that the plaintiffs filed the instant suit challenging the two orders passed by the Chairman, Board of Land Administration, Dhaka and that suit cannot be said to be a suit relating to their granting or cancelling of plaintiffs' settlement of land by the government. The plaintiffs got the settlement of land from the government upon proper investigation and enquiry and they have been possessing the same by mutating their names in the record of right. The government has neither cancelled the settlement nor the mutation granted in their favour. The High Court Division also considered the provision of section 85 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. From aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case we are of the view that contention of the petitioner that the plaintiffs' suit is barred under section 76(2) of the said Act is without any substance.

The brief facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the instant Rule are that the predecessor of the petitioners, as plaintiff, instituted Title Suit No. 2 of 1959 in the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Pirojpur, now Assistant Judge's Court, Nesarabad, Pirojpur, praying for declaration of Title of the suit land. The plaintiff contended, inter alia, that the suit land measuring 0.01 acre appertaining to CS Khatian No. 261 and CS Plot No. 19 corresponding to RS Plot No.313 recorded in RS Khatian No. 243 and SA Khatian No. 447 of Mouza Kourikhara, PS Nesarabad, District Pirojpur was acquired by the predecessor of the plaintiffs by oral lease in the month of Baishak, 1360 BS. It is further stated that the RS and SA record of rights having been wrongly prepared in the name of defendant No. 1, who claimed false title to the suit land on 20th Kartick 1365 BS, the predecessor of the petitioners was constrained to file the suit for declaration of title. The said suit was decreed ex parte on 2-6-1959 by the learned Munsif, now Assistant Judge and the plaintiffs title to the suit land was declared. However, the suit land, although it was described correctly in the body and the prayer portion of the plaintiffs plaint, the current Plot No. 313 was wrongly written in schedule "kha" to the plaint as plot No. 331. Hence the petitioners, as heirs of the plaintiff to the earlier suit for declaration, filed the application for correction under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 27-11-1993. The learned Senior Assistant Judge by his impugned order was pleased to reject the said application on the grounds that the plaintiff has sought correction of the plaint after 35 years from the date of the decree, which is not acceptable in law and is beyond the jurisdiction of his Court. Thus he rejected the application, which is now challenged before this Court. 

 6. I have heard the learned Advocate and perused the materials on record. Upon close scrutiny of the petitioner's plaint, Annexure-B to this revisional application, it appears that the suit plot is referred therein as former settlement Plot No. 19 and present settlement Plot No. 313, which is the disputed land described in schedule "Kha". But schedule "Kha" states that the Plot Number is old 19 and present 331. Clearly there is an. incongruity. In my mind, there is no doubt that this is a typing or clerical error. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, in the impugned order, has rejected the application for correction because of the lapse of 35 years from the date of the decree. The learned Judge felt that he was unable to accept the application, which was beyond his jurisdiction.

3. On 21-3-2000 opposite party No.1 made an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code for addition. His case, in short, is that neither the plaintiff nor opposite party No. 2 has any right, title or possession in the suit land. Moreover, opposite party No. 2 migrated to India long ago and died there. By way of pattan and purchase his grandfather and father acquired the suit land at various times from 1925 and possessed. Lastly, the suit land was recorded in the name of his father during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and they have been in possession on payment of rents. In the present revenue survey also, his name was correctly recorded. In order to grab the suit land the plaintiff created the Bainapatra. He accordingly, prayed that for disposal of such suit, his presence is necessary. 

 6. Mr Harendra Nath Nondy, learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1, submits that opposite party No. 1 is on the land as a successive owner in possession. His father's name was recorded in the SA Khatian and they have been possessing the suit land all along on payment of rents. Opposite Party No. 1 has also got his homestead on the land. Having come to know that the alleged vendor opposite party No. 2 migrated to India long ago and died the petitioner instituted the suit and if a decree is obtained, naturally ex parte, in such suit it will be very difficult for opposite party No. 1 to protect his possession in the land. He, therefore, submits that in order to avoid multiplicity of the proceedings and also for ends of justice presence of opposite party No. 1 is necessary at least to prove that the vendor of the petitioner migrated to India long ago and died there long before the execution of Bainapatra on 12-6-1995. In support he cites decisions in the case of Muhammad lshaq vs Jamila Begum and others reported in PLD 1955 Lahore 644, in the case of Surjya Kanta Majhi and another vs Aswini Kumar Debnath and others, 16 DLR 238 and that of Barjang Lal Agarwala vs Aksed Ali Shaikh & others, 35 DLR 110 and that of Md Toafazzal Hossain vs Sunil Kumar Basak & ors 7 BLT (AD) 103. 

 15. As stated above that the opposite party No. 1 claims that opposite party No. 2, alleged vendor of the plaintiff, migrated to India long ago and died there and that the Bainapatra dated 12-6-1995 was created for the purpose of the suit. He also claims that for generations opposite party No. 1 has been living in the suit land on payment of rent on the basis of record of rights. Opposite party No. 2 has not yet appeared in the suit. According to opposite party No. 1, there is no chance of any appearance on behalf of said opposite party No. 2. In such circumstances, appearance of opposite party No. 1 in the suit at least to see whether the 'Bainapatra' of the plaintiff is genuine or not will be an invaluable assistance to the Court. On the facts and in view of the ratio of above decisions, we find that the learned Subordinate Judge did not commit any error or illegality in the exercise of his discretion in allowing the application for addition. No failure of justice has occasioned thereby.

Vs
Md Saber Ali Mia ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
3. Both the Courts below after considering the material evidence on record decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff holding that he has got the right and title over the 4 suit plots. 

 5. The facts appearing from the records are that one Abdul Kader was the owner of SA Plots Nos. 167, 223, 222, 234, 250 and 235. By a registered sale deed that Abdul Kader sold his aforesaid lands showing plots Nos. 1805, 224, 221, 233, 250 and 235, plots Nos. 250 and 235 are correct but plots Nos. 1805, 224, 221 and 233 was incorrectly written in the deed of sale dated 26-5-1965 instead of plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234. That Abdul Kader was not the owner of plots Nos. 1805, 222, 221 and 233. So, it appears that out of 6 plots, plot number is correct in respect of SA plots Nos. 250 and 235 and incorrect plots numbers were given as plots Nos. 1805, 224, 221 and 233 in the registered document dated 26-5-1965. The selfsame vendor Abdul Kader sold 4 plots showing plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234 in the sale deed dated 14-7-1978 in favour of Md Saber Ali Mia namely, the present plaintiff. Being embodied with the aforesaid sale deed dated 14-7-1978 he instituted the present suit namely, OC Suit No. 211 of 1982 on 29-7-1982. Now both the Courts held that since the deed of Abdur Rahman Mia did not contain the correct plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234 no title of the aforesaid plots passed to Abdur Rahman Mia and since the sale deed of Md Saber Ali Mia contained plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234, the title passed to this Md Saber Ali Mia by a deed dated 14-7-1978 and as such, the title of the plaintiff has been declared. 

 6. Mr Abdul Majid, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has referred to section 95 of the Evidence Act and tried to show that though mistaken plots number were given in the deed as regards 4 plots, yet the vender Abdul Kader actually delivered possession of plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234 in favour of the present petitioner by a registered sale deed dated 26-5-1965. Since that date the present petitioner had been possessing the lands of the aforesaid 4 plots together with lands of plots Nos. 250 and 235. The defendant petitioner mutated his name in the record of rights and have been paying rents to the Government and in this way he has been enjoying the suit properties along with 2 other plots. With regard to plots Nos. 250 and 235 there was no dispute and Abdul Kader was the owner of these two plots. By the selfsame document Abdul Kader sold plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234 showing wrongly plot Nos. as 1805, 224, 221 and 233. This transaction of 6 plots was made by one and same registered document. 

 11. Now let us see whether this was done by mistake or it was done with malafide intention to defraud the defendant petitioner Abdur Rahman Mia. From the evidence on record it appears that it was done by vender Abdul Kader not out of any bonafide mistake but it was deliberately done by vender Abdul Kader with malafide motive and intention to defraud the vendee Abdur Rahman Mia. It is clear from the fact that by a separate registered sale deed this Abdul Kader sold the aforesaid 4 plots to opposite party plaintiff Md Saber Ali Mia giving correct number of plots in the document dated 14-7-1978. Had Abdul Kader no malafide intention to defraud Abdul Rahman Mia, he would not sell the disputed 4 plots of lands to Md Saber Ali Mia the plaintiff by a registered sale deed in the year 1978. It shows that with clear malafide motive and intention Abdul Kader gave incorrect numbers of 4 plots and after a long time he sold the selfsame lands giving correct plot numbers to plaintiff Md Saber Ali Mia. So, it appears that this transaction vide registered sale deed dated 14-7-1978 was absolutely a malafide one in order to deprive and defraud Abdur Rahman Mia. So, the person committed fraud should not be allowed to enjoy the fruits of his own fraud. So, I hold that the plaintiff Saber Ali Mia had not acquired any right and title in the suit properties out of such a fraudulent transaction by a deed of sale dated 14-7-1978. As such, the plaintiff has not acquired any right and title in the suit properties. I further hold that right and title in respect of the 4 plots of lands which belonged to Abdul Kader passed to the defendant petitioner by virtue of the registered sale deed dated 26-5-1965. 

 14. I have gone through the judgments of both the Courts below. It appears that they considered the whole case from a wrong angle and misconstrued the material evidence on record and as a result they committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice and, as such, the judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below are liable to be set aside. The Courts below just considered the facial value of the two sale deeds executed and registered by Abdul Kader but the intention of the vender could not be gathered by them out of these two sale deeds since the intention of the vendor Abdul Kader was to sell his 6 plots of lands, though wrong numbers were given in respect of 4 plots, yet actual possession of his own lands were given to the purchaser Abdur Rahman Mia by virtue of a registered sale deed dated 26-5-1965. On good faith and honest belief he purchased the lands on 26-5-65 at a valuable consideration and got possession on 26-5-65. 

 Send down the LC records immediately.

3. The defendant Nos. 8 and 9 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that 2.54 acres of land of khebat No. 251 was in possession of Arab Gazi and for arrear of rent the superior landlords Syed Asmat Ali and others filed Rent Suit No. 1192/32 and obtained a decree in execution whereof they purchased the entire land in the auction sale and on getting Bainama got possession of the suit land through Court on 25-8-37. Thereafter, Mohammad Gazi got settlement of 1.98 acres of land by executing a registered kabuliyat in favour of Syed Asmat Ali and others and thereafter by executing another registered kabuliyat in 1349 BS Mohammad Gazi took settlement of 0.75 acres of land and thus Mohammad Gazi being owner and possessor of the land by way of settlement transferred his entire interest in the land in favour of contesting defendant Nos. 8 and 9 by four different registered kabalas and inducted the defendants into possession and the defendants are possessing the land in purchase by paying rents, cultivating the land and enjoying its usufructs to the knowledge of the plaintiffs and the neighbouring people. 

 8. The plaintiffs in support of their claim that the land measuring 2.54 acres of CS khabet No. 252 was mortgaged by Tomej Gazi in favour of Nassarjan Bibi and Nassarjan Bibi in execution of the mortgage decree purchased the suit land on 15-5-1937 and obtained Bainama (Exhibit 2) and possession through Court on 26-2-1938 (Exhibit 3) has filed the same. In the said Bainama and the writ of delivery of possession the land of CS khebat No. 251 in the kaim karsha has been shown under khebat No. 234 in the mirash karsha under Howla CS khebat No. 216 in respect of the suit plot measuring an area of 2.51 acres has been taken delivery of vide Exhibit 3. It further appears that Mohammad Gazi took settlement by way of patta in respect of 1.46 acres of land from said Nassarjan Bibi on 2-10-1937. It further appears that Wazed Ali while purchasing the superior interest also purchased the remaining land of Nassarjan Bibi on 22-12-1937. Thus acquired the superior interest of the tenant Mohammad Gazi. Wazed Ali filed rent suit against Mohammad Gazi and obtained a decree and in execution thereof in Rent Execution Case No. 413/42 Wazed Ali himself auction purchased the interest of Mohammad Gazi on 3-10-1942 and took delivery of possession through Court on 31-4-1945. Thereafter, Wazed Ali settled 2.22 acres of land in favour of Mohammad Gazi and his sons on 25-3-1953. Mohammad Gazi in his turn sold 0.63 acres of land to Aptabuddin Sardar, the predecessor of the plaintiffs on 13-9-1956. The plaintiffs also claimed 0.57 acres of land by way of oral gift from Wazed Ali. As against the plaintiffs' claim the defendant have alleged that admittedly the suit land belonged to Arab Gazi in kaim karsha right but the mirash karsha belonged to Syed Arshad Ali, Syed Asmat Ali and Syed Asgar Ali in khabat No. 234 who filed Rent Suit No. 1192/32 against kaim karsha Arab Gazi and obtained rent decree and in execution thereof the landlord auction purchased the suit land and took delivery of possession on 25-3-1937. Thereafter, settled 1.98 acres by way of patta in favour of Mohammad Gazi in Baishak, 1346 BS. The said landlord also settled 0.75 decimals of land in favour of Mohammad Gazi by kabuliyat of 1349 BS. Thus, being owner of 2.73 acres of land Mohammad Gazi sold 1.80 acres of land in favour of defendant Nos. 8 and 9 on 27-10-56, 26-6-57, 18-8-59 and 26-10-59. In view of the rival claim of the parties the plaintiffs have been able to file the writ of proclamation and delivery of possession in respect of the suit plot under CS khebat No. 251 mentioning the khatian and the suit plots but the defendants though alleged that the suit land was auction sold and purchased in Rent Execution Case No. 308/34 by the landlord Syed Asmat Ali and others and filed the writ of proclamation but the said writ does not mention the khabat in kaim karsha and Mirash karsha numbers and do not mention about plot numbers so as to see that the suit plots were auction sold. Nevertheless, the defendants could not prove the delivery of possession by filing the writ of delivery of possession. On the contrary, the plaintiffs have been able to file the writ of proclamation and delivery of possession in respect of the sale in execution of the mortgage decree (Exhibits 2 and 3 respectively) and also the writ of delivery of possession in respect of Rent Execution Case No. 413/42. Both the writ of proclamation and the writ of delivery of possession mentioned about the suit plots together with the kaim karsha khebat No. 251 under mirash karsha in khebat No. 234 under CS khebat No. 216 as is also evident from the CS khebat No. 216 (Exhibit A). Both the Courts below on consideration of evidence on record have found support in the plaintiffs' case of auction purchase and ultimately devolving the suit land to the auction purchaser Wazed Ali. On perusal of the evidence on record and the impugned judgment, I am also of the view that the plaintiffs, have been able to prove that the suit land ultimately devolved on Wazed Ali on the basis of his auction purchase in Rent Execution Case No 413/42 and taking delivery of possession through Court on 31-4-45. Mohammad Gazi, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs also purchased in his name and also in the name of his son 2.22 acres of land on 25-3-53 who in turn sold 0.63 acres of land to Aptabuddin Sardar, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs, on 13-9-56 (Exhibit 7) and, as such, there being no delivery of possession by the alleged landlord Syed Asmat and others as has been recorded in the CS khebat, Mohammad Gazi did not acquire any interest in the suit land on the basis of his purchase from said Syed Asmat Ali and others so as to confer title on defendant Nos. 8 and 9 on the basis of their purchases on 27-10-56, 26-6-57, 18-8-59 and 26-10-59 and accordingly, the recording in the RS and SA Khatian in the name of defendant Nos. 8 and 9 has no basis. The plaintiffs' predecessor having purchased 0.63 acres of land from Mohammad Gazi has acquired title in respect of said quantum of land.
