2. The facts giving rise to this Rule are that the plaintiff petitioners instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 53 of 1990 against the defendant opposite parties for a declaration of their title to the suit land described in the schedule to the plaint and for a further declaration that the order passed in Mutation Case No. 96/81-82 is illegal, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff petitioners and also for a direction to the defendants to hand over possession of the suit land to the plaintiffs. The case of the plaintiffs, as it appears by a reading of this application and the counter affidavit of the defendant opposite parties and the impugned judgment of the learned District Judge, is that the plaintiffs became owner of the suit land by purchase on the basis of registered kabalas but that the defendant No. 1 was trying to lease out the suit land to some other persons and then the plaintiffs filed a non GR Case No. 11 of 1983 under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure wherein the property was attached and a receiver was appointed by the learned Magistrate under section 146 CrPC. Thereafter, the plaintiffs filed the above mentioned Title Suit No. 53 of 1990 against the defendants. The defendant opposite parties contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint. The defendants case as it appears from the counter affidavits is that the suit land was the excess khash land of the Shariatulla Waqf Estate which on being surrendered under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act vested in the Government and the record of rights was prepared in the name of the Government and that the plaintiffs' documents of purchase are collusive ones and not according to the provisions of law. 

 9. Mr. Moazzam Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the defendant appellant opposite parties, has argued that the ex parte judgment passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Title Suit No. 53 of 1990 does not conform to the provision of law in view of the fact that the learned Subordinate Judge did not state in the judgment properly as to how the plaintiffs suit was proved. In this connection, the learned Deputy Attorney-General referred to a decision in the case of Bangladesh Vs. Israil and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 371 wherein it has been held that the court to observe minimum legal requirements, judgment should show application of Court's judicial mind as to whether the plaintiffs witnesses and the papers produced proved the plaintiffs case. The learned Deputy Attorney Attorney-General said that the learned Subordinate Judge did not apply his judicial mind before coming to the conclusion that the plaintiffs have approved their case and therefore, the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge being not in conformity with the minimum requirement of law, the learned District Judge is justified in appointing the receiver by his impugned judgment and order dated 19.11.92 till the hearing of the appeal. 

 14. By a perusal of the impugned order of the learned District Judge dated 19.11.92, it appears that the plaintiff petitioners started non-GR Case No. 11 of 1983 in which the property in dispute was kept under attachment and then the learned Magistrate appointed a receiver for the management of the property and that the plaintiffs' mutation case No. 96/81-82 was also rejected. From this fact it appears that the plaintiffs were not in possession of the suit land since after their purchase till the date of disposal of the Title Suit No. 53 of 1990 and that the plaintiffs did not try to prove their possession under section 145 CrPC in the court of the learned Magistrate. Further, it appears from the impugned order of the learned District Judge that the learned Subordinate Judge did not state in her ex parte order how she came to the finding that the plaintiffs have proved their case. On the other hand, it appears that the learned GP after deposition of the PW 1 had appeared and prayed for cross examination of the PW 1 but that the learned Subordinate Judge did not allow the prayer of the learned GP. The learned District Judge on this point observed that the learned Subordinate Judge being over zealous has inquired into the reasons whether the learned GP actually was engaged in other courts as stated in his petition and then she rejected the prayer of the learned GP. Further, it appears from the impugned order that the learned District Judge observed that the plaintiffs did not enter into physical possession of the suit land although they stated that they were trying to grow boro paddy in the suit land and under such circumstances the learned District Judge came to the finding that in such view of the matter, appointment of a receiver will meet the ends of justice in this case. 

 16. For the reasons stated above, we find nothing to interfere with the impugned order of the learned District Judge.

full_judgment:
3. Briefly stated the plaintiffs case is that Hemanta Kumar Ghosh and others, the land-lords purchased in auction their aiyati interest of one Golam Ali Sk. on 4.9.34 which was sold in execution of rent decree vide rent execution case No. 1918 of 1934 and took delivery of possession on 31.1.55. This raiyati interests comprised 4.48 acres of land in a kbatian no 188. Within this raiyati interest k was an under tenancy comprising. 10 decimals of land which was annulled by the Ghosh landlords by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The plaintiff thereafter took settlement of the entire laud measuring 3.48 acres from the Ghosh landlords by executing a regd. kabuliyat dated 25th Baishak, 1342 .B.S. corresponding to 8.5.35 at a rental of Rs. 6-5 anas. Since then he has been in possession of the land on payment of rent for which he got dakhilas from the Government, The defendants constructed 3 huts of golpata in Asar, 1367 B.S. on 10 decimals of land .and got this piece of land recorded in the record of rights prepared after State acquisition. Hence the suit. 

 4. Defendant nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement to the effect that there was no auction purchase or delivery of possession and no notice was served under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, their interest was never annulled and they have been continuously in possession of the suit land althrough. 

 5. The main point for consideration before the courts below was whether the plain-tiff had any right, title, interest and possession.: in the suit land comprising 10 decimals of south east portion of plot NO. 66 of kbatian No. 188/1. This point is dependant on whether the Ghosh landlords after purchasing the raiyati interest of Golam Ali SK. in execution of the rent decree, annulled the incumbrance of the defendants by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and thereafter settled the entire raiyati interests with the plaintiff free from all encumbrances as recited in the registered Kabuliyat dated .8-5-35 executed by the plaintiff. 6. The learned Munsif after discussing the evidence on record held: defendants cannot say that their under tenancy was never annulled. On the other band the Additional Subordinate Judge on the basis of the same evidence found; “Thus upon the evidence, the story of khas possession either by the Ghash landlords or their lessee, the plaintiff has not 'been proved and that shows that the korfa of the defendants does not-stand disturbed and shall be deemed to have been continuing as before." 

 7. Mr. Sk. Razzaque Ali, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plain-tiff-appellant has urged that on the face of preponderance of evidence on record which he has referred to, in the course of his sub-mission, the lower appellate court erred in law in not holding that the tenancy of the defendants was not annulled. 

 9. The learned Counsel for the contesting respondents has further relied upon two decisions, one of the Calcutta High Court Tayefa Khatun Choudhurani vs. Sornadhan  K. Sen Rai reported in 53(1931) Calcutta Law journal page 512 and another of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, Nirode Baran Va. Devendra Mohan reported in BCR 309 (AD) in support , of his contention that , the provision of section 167 of the Bengal, Tenancy Act has not been complied with in the instant case. The facts and circumstances of these cases referred to above are quite different from those of the instant case. The Calcutta case lays down that sec.167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is intended to ,Offer a choice to the purchaser of a tenure under a rent decree either to accept the under tenure or to avoid it within a year. If the purchaser does not exercise the right to annul the encumbrance within the time allowed, by law, it must be presumed that he intends to adopt the under tenure or any other encumbrance created by the last tenant. This is a correct interpretation of the section. But in the instant case the main point for consideration is not the requirement of that section but whether or not the annulment of the encumbrance by the Ghosh landlords in accordance with the provisions of section 167 of that Act has been proved by the evidence on record. 

 10.  In the appellate Division case the question of annulment was under consideration. and both the courts below as well as the High Court Division in second appeal found on discussion of evidence that the under tenancy was not extinguished by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. That being a question of fact and decided by all the court's below the Appellate Division held that no interference was called for. 

 11. It is the case of the plaintiff that Golam Ali Sk. held the raiyati interest under the Glaosh landlord in Khatian No. 188 and under Golam Ali Kohiluddin, defendant No. 1, his brother Fatik father of defendants Nos. 2, 3 and 4 and Yousuf held an under tenancy in Khatian No.188(1). Admittedly the plaintiff could not file any paper to show directly the annulment of this under tenancy in accordance with section 167 of the Bangal Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate for the 5 appellant submits that mere non-production of the notice under section 167 or paper connected with the service of such notice by itself Would not be fatal for the plaintiff's case if it could be proved otherwise that there was service of such notice and the encumbrance was, in fact, annulled. 

 12. The under-tenancy was held by defendant No. 1 Kohiluddin Sk. his brother Fatik Sk., the father of defendant No. 2, 3 and 4 and one Yousuf Sk. It is on evidence that the interest of Yousuf Sk. was purchased by the plaintiff long before the aforesaid rent execution case. Ext. 4 is the registered kabuliyat dated 8.5.35 executed by plaintiff in favour of the ex-landlords. It has been mentioned in the recital of the kabuliyat that the plaintiff is taking settlement of the entire land measuring 3.48 acres from the said Ghosh landlords free from all incumbrance. It is interesting to note that Fatik, father of defendant No.2 to 4 was attesting witness of this kabuliyat and also identified Abdul Sk., the executant, i.e. the plaintiff herein and it is also interesting to note that only one of Fatik's sons and Fatik's brother Kohiluddin Sk. are the only contesting parties. It is true that a document is not binding on a person who is not a party to it but such a document is admissible in evidence under section 13 of the Evidence Act as an instance of assertion of right even though it is not inter parties and weight is given to the recital in an old document though not inter parties particularly when the recital in the document is acted upon. 

 13. It is further seen from the evidence that Yousuf, one of the co-sharers of Fatiq and of defendant No. 1 Kohiluddin, attested the writ of delivery of possession dated 31.1.35 (Ext. 6) made in pursuance of the auction sale referred to above. Furthermore, the plaintiff has produced dahlias (Ext. 1 series) to show that he paid rent in respect of the entire tenancy which he took settlement from the Ghosh landlord. He paid rent to the ex-landlords and after state acquisition of rent-receiving interests to the Government. 

 15. As against the dakhilas submitted by the plaintiff in support of his case and also indicating the facts of his exercise of rights of ownership of the entire land measuring 3.48 acres taken by him by way of settlement from the Ghosh landlords, the defendants could not produce any dakhila or paper to show that they ever paid any rent to anybody in respect of the under-tenancy they claim to have been holding from a long period of time. It indicates that they have been acting upon the premise of annulment of their under tenancy. 16. It is further found from the evidence on record that the plaintiff (as P.W. 1) deposed that the under-tenancy in question was annulled by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the notice was served on the land by hanging a copy there of on a bamboo slip in the disputed land and possession thereof was taken by beat of drum in the summer season and he was present at that time He further said that defendant No.1 Kohiluddin constructed hut on the disputed land in Asar, 1367 B.S. in spite of his opposition and this  was known to Opazuddin, P.W. 5 who corroborates  the plaintiff on this point. P.W. 2 Kayemuddin Sk, also spoke of the construction of huts by the defendants in. 1367 B.S. P.W. 3, Mohiuddin a former Tahsildar of the Ghosh lands proved the dakhilas issued by them. 

 19. In the instant case the deposition of P.Ws. 1; 2, 3 and 5 Coupled with the documentary evidence Exta. 1 series; 3, 4, 5 and 6 unmistakably lead to the irresistible conclusion that the under-raiyati interests of the defendants stood annulled and the defendants themselves also acted upon the promise of annulment of their interest by refraining from paying any rent in respect of that interest thereafter to anybody. In the face of all these weighty evidences it cannot be held as has been erroneously done by the lower appellate court that the under-tenancy of the defendants was not annulled.

The plaintiff's further case was that for arrear of rent, certificate cases were started against the heirs of S.A. recorded tenants and the suit property was sold in auction and the plaintiff being the highest bidder in open auction purchased it on 22-1-71 and the sale was confirmed on 23-12-72, the certificate was granted in favour of the plaintiff on 24-12-72 and the certificate officer formally delivered possession of the property to the plaintiff on 28-12-72. Thereafter Mihir Kumar Saha one of the vendors of the plaintiff filed an application for setting aside the said sale, which was ultimately withdrawn on 18-5-72 and as a result the auction sale remained confirmed. 

 2. Pursuant to the said Bainanama dated 4-3-65 the plaintiff's vendors executed the Kabala which was registered on 19-5-72. Thus the plaintiff became -/16/- annas owner and possessor in the suit property and accordingly paid rent and mutated his name in the record of rights as well as in the Paurashava. 

 4. Two sets of written-statements were filed by defendant no. 1 and the Government. In the written-statement filed by defendant no. 1, it was alleged that some of the recorded persons left for India long before 1965 and the suit property being the enemy property vested upon the Government under the provisions of Ordinance No.1 of 1964 and that Sukumar Saha Roy and Mihir Kumar Saha Roy were not in possession of the suit property and one Hari Mohan was the authorised person as caretaker of the suit property, who inducted defendant no.1 in the suit property as a monthly tenant and then the said Hari Mohan left for India. Subsequently, the said Sukumar Saha Roy sold his share to Amena who in her turn transferred the same to one Kuddus Dewan and others and the share of Mihir Kumar Saha Roy was also transferred to Nasiruddin and others. Defendant no.1 after liberation of Bangladesh being aware of the suit property as enemy property applied for lease and was in possession but as his brother was killed he fled away from the suit property and during his absence, the plaintiff forcibly entered into the suit property and thereafter on 25-4-74, the defendant No.1 applied for lease of the suit property and the impugned memorandum was passed causing eviction of the plaintiff. 

 10. The trial Court found plaintiff's title to the disputed land on the basis of purchase by Kabala executed by Mihir Kumar Saha Roy and Sukumar Saha Roy but held that the alleged auction sale and purchase was illegal as some dead persons were made parties in that certificate sale and that necessary person were not made parties. The plaintiff was found in possession of the disputed property. The lower appellate Court took the view that the plaintiff's Kabala was hit by Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 and as such plaintiff did not acquire any title on the disputed land on the basis of Kabala executed by Mihir Kumar Saha Roy and Sukumar Saha Roy. It however found plaintiff's possession and title on the basis of auction purchase. The lower appellate Court observed; "custodian cannot take without filing a suit for partition of the portion which has been declared as enemy property. In view of what I have discussed above I cannot but hold that the learned Munsif has rightly decreed the suit and I see no reason to interfere with his judgment". The learned Judge of the High Court Division though found possession in favour of the plaintiff however observed "so far auction purchase is concerned the trial Court held that the certificate being against some dead persons is nullity and the certificate sale is illegal and void. The lower appellate Court did not reverse the findings and decision of the trial Court in this respect after considering the evidence on record. There is therefore error apparent on the face of the record in the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate Court". Accordingly, he set aside the said judgment and decree and sent back the appeal in remand to the lower appellate Court for re-hearing and disposal in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made in the judgment. While sending the case on remand the learned Judge further observed "it will have to be seen whether plaintiff is entitled to the declaration without proving his legal right or character to the suit land". 

 12. In that view of the matter, we find substance in the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the Kabala in favour of the plaintiff being executed on 3-5-72 and registered on 19-5-72, is not hit by the provision of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964. There is also substance in the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that since the Government did not move the High Court Divisi6n against dismissal of their Appeal No. 202 of 1978, the Government accepted the position that the impugned Memorandum issued by Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) is illegal and void. Mr. Maksudur Rahman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of respondents 2 to 8, however, submits that although the Government did not move the High Court Division against the judgment of the lower appellate Court dismissing their appeal but the Government was made a party in Civil Revision No. 1419 of 1980 filed by defendant no.1 and the appearance of the learned Advocate for the Government was noted in the judgment. This appearance, however, does not alter the position. The lower appellate Court, although on a ground different from that of the trial Court, found prima facie title of the plaintiff in the suit land and as such there was no justification for the learned Judge of the High Court Division to observe that it would have to be seen whether plaintiff was entitled to the declaration without proving his legal right or character to the suit land. All the Courts below including the High Court Division found plaintiff in possession of the disputed land. The trial Court decreed plaintiff's suit and the lower appellate Court affirmed the decree although on a different ground. As it is found that plaintiff's Kabala is not hit by Ordinance No. 1 of 1964, plaintiff's title on the basis of purchase by Kabala has been well established and there is no reason to send the case back on remand to the lower appellate Court. The learned Judge of the High Court Division has not exercised his discretion judicially in remanding the case. There is no error of law apparent on the face of the record nor has any failure of justice been occasioned by the decision of the lower appellate Court.

2. The facts leading to this appeal in, brief are that the suit plots were recorded in the name of Peary Mohan Chakraborty and after his death it was owned and possessed by his son, Kanak Lal Chakraborty. It was the plaintiff's case that the suit land was exchanged by Kanak Lal Chakraborty with the land of Maharam Ali in Tripura State. The recorded owners executed a general Power of Attorney in favour of the plaintiff who was the uncle-in-law of the said Maharam Ali. It was further asserted that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land as a Bargadar of the said Maharam Ali. The defendant was threatening the plaintiff with dispossession on the basis of a fraudulent deed of exchange and with that and in view he also initiated a proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C. and the suit land was attached and the Officer-in-charge of Kotwali P.S. was appointed as the Receiver. Thereafter the said proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C. was dropped but the land was kept under attachment and the parties were directed to seek relief in the Civil Court. Hence the present suit by the plaintiff. 

 3. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement wherein he denied the material allegations made in the plaint. His case was that the recorded owner Peary Mohan Chakraborty sold the suit land to his nephew, Profulla Kumar Chakraborty 17/18 years ago and delivered possession to Profulla. The defendant exchanged his land in Tripura State with the land of Profulla by a deed of exchange and since then he has been in possession. 

 4. Both sides adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsif upon a consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable without any prayer for declaration of the plaintiff's title and that the defendant was in possession of the suit land at the time of attachment. On appeal, The learned Subordinate Judge reversed the findings of the learned Munsif and allowed the appeal. Hence the present appeal at the instance of the defendant. 

 9. I am in respectful agreement with the principles laid down by their lordships in the above mentioned cases and it is therefore clear that a possessory owner is also entitled to maintain his possession, be he a bargadar or even a trespasser as against the entire world except in the rightful owner. Here in the instant case, the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land as a bargadar as well as by virtue of a power of attorney executed by the recorded owner. The plaintiff does not claim any title for himself. All that he claims is the possessory right or possessory ownership in the suit land. I am therefore, of the opinion that the suit at the instance of the plaintiff is quite maintainable and is not hit by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The suit land is admittedly under attachment and is now under the custody of the court through a Receiver appointed by the court and as such the question of recovery of possession does not arise. In this view of the matter the only prayer that the plaintiff could validly make was a prayer for declaration of his right to possession of the land free of attachment and this having been done, I find that the suit was quite maintainable. This view of mine finds support from a decision of a Division Bench in the case of K. Sandarasa Iyer Vs. Sarvajana Soirklabi Vindhl Nidhi Ltd., reported in A.I.R. 1939 (Madras) at Page 853. The contention of the learned Advocate is, therefore, without any substance; 

 11. Lastly, the learned Advocate for the appellant has argued that it was not a proper judgment of reversal. I have gone through the judgment of both the courts below and I find that the learned Subordinate Judge has adverted to the findings of the learned Munsif and has reversed the same after proper appreciation of the evidence on record with his own reasoning’s which I find quite cogent and satisfactory. No illegality or irregularity could be pointed out by the learned Advocate in the said findings. 

 12. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that there were interpolations in Exhibit A, the sole basis of the defendant's claim of possession and has disbelieved the same. He was further found that there was no documentary evidence to show that Piyari Mohan, the original owner ever sold the suit land to Prafulla from whom the defendant obtained the alleged deed of exchange. Moreover, the record of rights stands in the name of Piyari Mohan and the plaintiff claims possession through the son of Piyari Mohan. In the proceeding u/s 145 Cr. P. C., the defendant's sole witness, Sikandar Ali admitted the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land and certified copy of the deposition of the said witness has been marked as exhibit 5(a) in the suit. Having regard to these facts and circumstances, I am inclined to agree with the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the plaintiff and not the defendant was in possession of the suit land prior to the attachment. The grievance of the  learned Advocate in this regard also fails. No other ground has been urged. For the reasons stated above, I find no substance in the appeal which is accordingly dismissed with costs.

After the said sale deed was registered, Syeedullah Pramanik, Mohitullah Pramanik and Shaharbi Bewa got their title extinguished to the said amount of land. It is further stated that Syed Ali Pramanik, the predecessor of the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties, was the party to the said partition deed dated 30-6-1939 and in view of thereof MRR Khatian was prepared in the name of the parties to the partition deed. As per partition deed, Syed Ali Pramanik acquired 1.28 acres of land in CS Khatian No.1388 (schedule 2 to the plaint) and 1.06 acres of land in CS Khatian No.218 (schedule No.1) totaling 2.34 acres of land and MRR Khatian Nos. 237 and 442 were correctly prepared in his name. After the demise of Syed Ali Pramanik, the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties inherited 2.34 acres of land in the partible holdings and that they have no right, title and interest in any land in CS khatian no 889 (Schedule 3). They are only entitled to 2.34 acres of land. In the above circumstances, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 5.1 In view of the foregoing rival submissions of the learned Counsels, the first and foremost contention to be resolved in this revision is whether Partition Suit No.92 of 1993 is at all maintainable in the instant form and manner with lone relief of partition, or any additional prayer for declaration of title was required to be sought besides partition. The pleadings of the parties are found to be akin to the submissions of the learned Counsel for the defendants-appellants-petitioners that the CS and SA Khatian did not properly record, the names of the predecessors of the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties. Here the learned Counsel assails the maintainability of the suit on the ground of seeking therein the solitary prayer for partition. In the case of Chinnzoy Chowdhury and others vs Sree Mridul Chowdhury and others [23 BLD (AD) 2003, page-83-87 : 55 DLR (AD) 115], both trial court and the High Court Division held the suit to be maintainable with simple prayer for partition. Some ancestral properties were the subject matter of partition in the suit. But in the appeal before the Hon'ble Appellate Division the question of maintainability had been assailed wherein His Lordship observed as follows— 

 5.2 In our instant case, the entire scenario regarding accrual of the title of plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties to suit land has been narrated in the plaint in broad details. No hurdle seems to be apparent to determine the acquisition of title by plaintiff and hence their names, whether recorded or omitted to be recorded in a particular khatian is quite immaterial, particularly when the laid down principle is that Record-of Rights does not create or extinguish any title to the lands incorporated therein. Be it mentioned, CS Khatian though being a key land record document holding significant evidential value is not conclusive proof of ownership. Thus the contention agitated on the issue of maintainability merits no substance. 

 5.3 Pleadings of the parties and the evidences led thereon show the names and numbers of praeposituses, the devolution of properties upon their deaths on their lineage and the calculation of shares according to inheritance are not disputed at all. But there are three documents, namely a sale deed dated 3-4-1946, an unregistered amicable partition deed dated 30-6-1939 and another sale deed dated 10-2-1925, all being exhibited in original during trial as Ka, Kha, and Umo respectively, which generate a new kind of controversy between the contending parties. These documents are supposed to be the catalyst which fluctuates the share of the co-sharers in the partible holdings. The trial court upon analysis of evidences, oral or documentary, adduced by the parties, determined specific decision upon each of the documents and found plaint case to preponderate over that of these petitioners in respect of those documents. In the appeal, the learned appellate court made reappraisal of the evidences over all the issues formulated by learned trial court and concurred therewith. The courts below concurrently found that Sayed ullah, the predecessor of the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties, acquired 4.10 acres of land by inheritance and 0.15½ acre by purchase totaling 4.25 acres in the holdings under partition and they as co-sharer have been in possession thereof. It appears from the record that the learned court of appeal as the last court of fact decided the question of fact and recorded its finding on evaluation of evidence on record. The findings of appellate court, in the absence of any perversity, are not liable to be disturbed in revision. Here the citation of the decisions, as referred to by the learned Counsel for the plaintiffs-respondents-opposite parties, held in the case of Abdul Gafur and others vs Abdur Razzak and others [62 DLR (AD) 2451 and in the case of Md. Amzad Ali Sheikh and others vs Koyron Bewa and others (12 LM (AD) 2022(1), page-173 apply to our instant case.

Mr Md Zakir Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants, has submitted that the learned Joint District Judge failed to consider the facts and provision of Order VII, rule 11(b) of the Code in rejecting the plaint due to non depositing of the deficit court-fees within time fixed by the Court. He has further submitted that the provision of Order VII, rule 11(b) of the Code is not mandatory rather directory as no consequence is provided in case of failure to put in deficit court-fees within the statutory period of 21 days. In support of his submission he cited a case of Begum Sultana Mazid vs Syedul Islam, reported in 10 MLR (AD) 186. He has also submitted that the learned Joint District Judge erred in law in rejecting the plaint without giving a condition to the plaintiffs to pay deficit court-fees and only on the failure of the plaintiffs to comply with any such direction from the learned Joint District Judge, the plaint ought not be rejected. 

 10. On the other hand, Mr Md Shakhawat Hussain Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents, has submitted that in fact, there is a consequence in Order VII, rule 11(b) of the Code, as the rule provides that the plaint shall be rejected if the plaintiff fails to put in requisite stamp-papers within the time fixed by the Court, in the present case, the plaintiff appellants have failed to put the requisite stamp-papers within the time fixed by the Court and the said time shall not exceed 21 (twenty one) days. Mr Khan has further submitted that the law has not curtailed the power of the Court to extend time, in an exceptional case, to deposit the deficit Court fee but the plaintiffs have failed to make out a case that the present case is an exceptional one to get time to deposit deficit court-fees rather it reveals that they got enough time than the stipulated time of 21 days wherefrom their negligence could be revealed. Mr Khan, by referring Order VII, rule 11 (b) and its proviso, has also submitted that the consequence is not mentioned in the proviso if the plaintiff fails to correct the valuation or supply requisite stamp paper within time fixed by the court but in the very first sentence of rule 11 it is mentioned that the plaint shall be rejected on account of failure of the plaintiff in some cases as stated in the rule. In support of his submission he also referred the decision reported in 10 MLR (AD) 186. He has contended that the plaintiffs have failed to deposit the deficit Court-fees within time fixed by the Court, accordingly the trial Court rightly rejected the plaint which calls for no interference by this Court. In support of his submissions he cited the Case of Haji Md Ishaque vs Rupali Bank, reported in 11 BLD 489 = 43 DLR 621. 

 16. In this regard, we need not to discuss more as our Appellate Division affirmed the decision of the High Court Division reported in 10 MLR (AD) 186 observing that the statutory period of 21 days for putting in deficit court fee is not mandatory rather the same is directory in nature as no consequence is provided in the law in case of failure to put in deficit court fee within statutory period of 21 days. 

 20. Considering the facts and relevant provisions of law and the decision of our apex court reported in 10 MLR (AD) 186, we find merit in this appeal.

 3. Facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that the petitioners and predecessor of petitioner Mohesh Chandra Bhuimali the CS recorded tenant of 2.23 acres of land of CS Khatian No. 122 of CS Plot No. 36 died leaving behind three sons namely Surendra Chandra Bhuimali, Debendra Chandra Bhuimali and Jogendra Chandra Bhuimali and by way of amicable 'partition between them Surendra Chandra Bhuimali got the above mentioned land. Thereafter, Surendra sold 15 decimals of land by registered deed No. 11519 dated 17-10-1943 in favour of Krishna Dhan Bonik and Sree Jatindra Chandra Bonik and delivered possession to them; thereafter said 15 decimals land was recorded in their name as SA Khatian No. 58, SA plot No. 89; Jatindra Chandra Bonik died leaving behind only son Onil Chandra Bonik and RS record had been prepared in their name and the said plot had been recorded in the name of Krishna Dhan Bonik and Onil Chandra Bonik as RS plot No. 123 of RS Khatian No. 40; thereafter, aforesaid Krishna Dhan Bonik by registered deed No. 7735 dated 5-8-1973 transferred 7.5 decimals of land in favour of the petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 and on the same date by registered deed No. 7736 dated 5-8-1973, Onil Chandra Bonik transferred 7.5 decimals of land in favour of petitioner No. 3, the predecessor of the petitioner Nos. 4-8 and the vendors handed over possession to them; that after receiving possession of the case land which was a ditch the petitioner Nos. 1-3 and the predecessor of petitioner Nos. 4-8 filled up the land with earth, also mutated their names and started paying rent and taxes to the government; while the aforesaid owners were in peaceful possession and enjoying of the said land, the then District Commission of Narsingdi claiming that the case land is vested land and, as such, belong to the government and threatened to evict the owners from the case land forcefully and build a tennis court there; however, such act of the District Commissioner, Narsingdi created doubt on the unconditional ownership of petitioner Nos. 1-3 and predecessor of petitioner Nos. 4-8 over the case land and, as such, on 9-5-1987 the owners as Plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 66 of 1987 in the Court of Sub Judge, Narshingdi for a declaration of title and declaration that the scheduled property is not vested property. However, learned Judge, by his judgment and decree dated 10-10-1992 dismissed the suit stating inter alia that the petitioners should file a suit for partition and not for simple declaration and being aggrieved by the judgment and decree the instant petitioner Nos. 1-3 and the predecessor of the petitioner Nos. 4-8 filed First Appeal No. 4 of 1993 in the High Court Division of the Supreme Court. 

 4. At the hearing stage of the said FA No. 4 of 1993 the defendant-respondent on 18-6-2015 filed an affidavit-in-opposition against an application by the appellant stating inter-alia that the RS Khatian and plot of the suit land has been included in the vested property list and as per the provision of অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন-২০০১, the FA No. 4 of 1993 cannot be continued and stands abated and as such said appeal was made out of list. 

 5. It is claimed that the petitioners have possessed the case property being RS Plot No. 123 of RS Khatian No. 40 since long and the same has never been enlisted as Enemy Property or vested property, inclusion of the same under the "Ka" list of the vested property through publication of the Gazette Notification dated 19-4-2012 under the অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন-২০০১, and for the first time petitioners came to know on receipt of the said application filed by the defendant Opposite party Government on 18th June 2015. 

 8. The Respondent No. 1, Ministry of Land, in its affidavit-in-opposition denied the material assertion and claims that the land in question actually belongs to the respondent No. 1 and subsequently the land in question i.e. the RS Plot No. 123 of RS Khatian No. 40 has been included in the vested property list published by Gazette Notification dated 19-4-2012. Ms Purabi Saha, Assistant Attorney General appeared on behalf of the respondent No. 1, submits that the petitioner earlier filed Title Suit No. 66 of 1987 for declaration of title and also declaration that the schedule property is not vested property, while the said suit was dismissed by the trial court and thereafter against the aforesaid judgment and decree of trial court, the petitioners preferred First Appeal No.4 of 1993 before this Court and finally filed this writ petition only to grab the property. She lastly submits that petitioners were fully aware about the Gazette Notification, they deliberately overlooked the aforesaid notification and on that plea filed this writ petition which is not maintainable in the summary proceedings. They have to follow the অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন-২০০১, the Rules made thereunder. 

 10. She submits that the land in question comprises 15 decimals of land of RS Plot No. 123 of RS Khatian No. 40 which corresponding to SA plot No. 58 of RS Khatian No. 89 but the corresponding SA Khatian No. 89 and plot No. 58 having not been included in the vested property list published in the Gazette notification dated 19-4-2012 itself shows the anomalies and discrepancies of the list itself wherein 15 decimals of land of RS Khatian No. 40 and RS plot No 123 is included in two separate serial being serial No. 301 and 302; the 15 decimals of land appears to have been declared vested property through two different vested property case being Vested Property Case No. 28/81 dated 23-5-87 and Vested Property Case No. 13/87 dated 23- 5-1987; the said piece of land has also been taken possession by the government on two separate dates; the name of the predecessor of the petitioner Krishno Dhan Bonik has not been included at the Column No. 4 মূল মালিক এর নাম পিতার নাম ও ঠিকানা of Row No. 301 or 302 as of annexure-1 of affidavit-in-opposition. However the corresponding SA khatian and plot number is not included in the vested property list at Row No. 7 and 8 at serial No. 301 and 302; Although all the RS khatian and plot numbers shown in serial No. 301 and 302 at Column No. 7 and 8 are same, the total amount of land at serial No. 301 is 0.075 acres or 7.50 decimals and on the other hand the accumulated amount of land in serial No. 302 is .74 acres or 74 decimals (as of annexures-D). Lastly she submits that inclusion of the petitioners' property in the list of vested property is also violative of the Article 42 of the Constitution. 

 12. It appears from the record that the office note of the vested property case clearly shows that the 15 decimals land of SA Plot No. 58 of SA Khatian No. 89 which corresponds the RS Khatian No. 40 of RS Plot No. 123 was never declared vested property and it had never been leased out to any person or organization rather government on several occasion planned to acquire the said land but never did so. The office note No. 82, 83 of Vested Property Case No. 13 of 87 is quoted below: 

 13. It also appears that the Government of Bangladesh i.e., defendants of Title Suit No. 66 of 87 repeatedly stated that Government of Bangladesh has no claim over SA Plot No. 58 of SA Khatian No. 89 and that the same is not vested property but throughout the trial the defendants remained silent about what is the corresponding RS Plot and Khatian of this 15 decimals of land and claimed ignorance about the status of RS Plot No. 123 of RS Khatian No. 40. The DW 1 Mr AFM Tofa Khan the then Assistant Superintendent, Vested Property, Narshingdi in cross-examination deposed that: 

 15. Heard the learned Advocates appearing of their respective parties, also considered the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent and papers annexure thereto and carefully considered the submissions made by the parties in support of their respective cases. 16. The property in question i.e., 15 decimal land of RS Plot No. 123, RS Khatian No. 40 of Mouza Bilashdi has been listed as "Ka" schedule vested property and notified in Gazette on 19-4-2012 at page No. 18548 at serial No. 301 and 302. Before, publishing the same, there was a civil suit being No. 66 of 87 wherein defendants categorically stated that they have no claim over SA Plot No. 58 of SA Khatian No. 89 and the same is not vested property but throughout the trial the defendants remain silent about what is the corresponding RS Plot and Khatian of this 15 decimals of land and claimed ignorance about the status of RS Plot No. 123 of RS Khatian No. 40. It also appears that the SA and RS recorded tenant Krishna Dhan Banik has never left India and he stayed here in this country, and he was made witness No. 2 for the plaintiff in Title suit No. 66 of 1987. 

 17. From the above fact as evident from the documents it is clear that the petitioners name has been recorded in the record of rights and they paid tips rents, they never left the country and had been enjoying the property since long. The RS record of 15 decimals land of RS Khatian No. 40 and RS Plot No. 123 itself shows that the name of the predecessor of the petitioners as the owner and not the Government.

3. The petitioner has six sons and three daughters and all of them are Bangladeshis and are engaged in different business at Syedpur under the present district Nilphamari. The petitioner was present in Bangladesh on 25th day of March 1971 and never left Bangladesh and has been continuously living in Bangladesh. The petitioner is a permanent resident of Bangladesh under the law and she is not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen of Bangladesh. She swore an affidavit of allegiance to Bangladesh before the Sub-Divisional Magistrate Nilphamari on 11.11.1972 and again swore an affidavit before the 1st Class Magistrate, Syedpur on 28.3.1985. Affidavits are annexed and marked as Annexure A & A-1 respectively to the petition. The petitioner acquired the lands measuring an area of 1.90 acres appertaining to plot numbers 665, 699, 675, 671, 672, 673, 674, 678, 609, 669/844, 676 of Khatian numbers 172, 176, 177, 178, 227, 363, 374 and 375 at mouza Saptanga PS Lalmonirhat district Lalmonirhat by registered sale deed dated 6.8.1959 which was purchased from Ambika Charan. The petitioner's name has been recorded in the record of rights and she paid rents. The deed of sale and recorded porcha and rent receipts are annexure to the petition and marked as Annexures-'B', B-1', B-2' and 'B-3' respectively. 

 10. An affidavit-in-opposition has been' filed on behalf of respondent No. 1 stating, inter aliathat the petitioner left Lalmonirhat during the War of Liberation of Bangladesh and her whereabouts were not known and, as such, the property became vested and was given on rent by the Government. The respondent No. 1 has not denied that the disputed property is owned by the petitioner but has stated that the disputed land appears to have been recorded in the name of Ambika Charan. However, it appears to us from Annexure-B that the petitioner has purchased these properties from the said Ambika Charan as early as 1959 and has been paying rent in repect of the property. There is, therefore, only one question to be decided and that is, whether the property is an abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972. The petitioner has stated that she and her family have all along been living in Bangladesh and also during the war of liberation, and she never left Bangladesh. Her husband was an Assistant Sub- Inspector of Police in 1950 and retired from the service in the year 1984 and died on 1.3.85. We can take note of the fact that the situation at Lalmonirhat from 25.3.71 till end of December may not have been favourable for the non-locals and so the petitioner and her caretaker left the property at Lalmonirhat for safety. It appears from Annexure-A' to the petition that the petitioner as early as on 11.11.72 swore an affidavit before the SDO Nilphamari that she, her husband and their children were all along living at Lalmonirhat. That her house, landed property, etc. situated at Lalmonirhat were left by her out of fear and she and her children took shelter at Syedpur and have been living there since then. She has also affirmed that all her children have decided to live in Bangladesh, not to go to any other country, that she was a Bengali national, loyal and faithful to Bangladesh. We have seen that her name appears in the voters' list and the pass-book of Habib Bank Ltd. Syedpur Branch (which was re-named Agrani Bank) from 1971 to 1977 shows that she had been operating her bank account and living in Bangladesh. In the circumstances it cannot be said that the petitioner's whereabouts were not known and that her property was abandoned under President's Order 16 of 1972.

2. The facts, relevant for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that the plaintiffs [hereinafter referred to as the appellants] instituted Title Suit No.43 of 1993 in the Court Assistant Judge, Amtoli, Borguna for declaration of the title and recovery of khas possession stating, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Abdus Sattar and others. The suit land was sold in auction and the same was purchased by plaintiff No.3 on 30.06.1986 who sold out 6 decimals of land to plaintiff No.1 on 14.02.1987 by registered deed. Plaintiff Nos.1 and 3 have been possessing the same by mutating their names in the khatian and paying rent to the Government. Plaintiff No.2 took settlement of 10 decimals of land from plot Nos.921 and 934 recorded in khas khatian No.1 registered by kabuliat dated 12.11.1986 from the Government. In this way, the plaintiffs became the owners of 22 decimals of land. On the 11th day of Falgoon, 1396 B.S. defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. The plaintiffs requested defendant No.1 to vacate the land, but he did not pay any heed. Hence, the plaintiffs instituted the suit. 

 3. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation contending, inter alia, that the suit land appertaining to PS Khatian No.4 of Mouza-Amtoli originally belonged to one Zaminder Zadunath Saha Chowdhury and others who settled 1.81 acres of land to their tenants and kept 1.47 acres of land in their khas possession. One Sukh Lai Saha and others were the owners of the land of PS Khatin No.7 and they settled 2.93 acres of land to the tenants and kept 2.59 acres of land in their khas possession. Zadunath Saha and others through their Naeb Shailendra Nath Sahaettled the land to one Tazem Ali Howlader, the predecessor of defendant No.l. Shailendra Nath executed a salami receipt on 5 Baishakh, 1359 BS on behalf of the Zamindars receiving taka 100 as salami from Tazem Ali Howladar. Tazem All Howlader erected dwelling homestead and planted trees etc in the said land. In this way, his father had been a tenant under the Zamindar with regard to 66 decimals of land including the disputed land and thereafter, on 15.01.1960 his father orally gifted him the disputed land by delivering possession. Defendant No.1 has been possessing the disputed land since 1960. During revisional survey 1.87 acres of land of PS khatian Nos.4, 7, and 12 including the 66 decimals of land which were given pattan to his father Tazem Ali Howladar was wrongly recorded in Hal Plot No.934 of Khatian No.1 in the name of Government. The plaintiffs have had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. 

 9. Ms. Sayeda Nasrin, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant, submits that the suit land was recorded in the name of the Government under khas khatian No.1 during SA operation and it vested in the Government and thereafter, the Government settled the suit land in favour of plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 by registered kabuliat vide Certificate Case No.827 of 1980-81 and Lease Case No.02 of AM-1985-86 and thereafter, they mutated their names and paid rent to the Government for the suit land. She further submits that the appellant got settlement of the suit land from the Government by registered kabuliat and got physical possession from the Government and this fact was proved by the plaintiffs by producing both documentary and oral evidence. She further submits that both the Courts below con-currently found the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land pursuant to the settlement case and certificate case and delivery of possession was given by the Government and the concurrent findings of fact as arrived at by both the Courts below are based on material evidence on record. It is finally submitted that there was no misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence on record and the concurrent findings of fact of both the Courts below cannot be interfered by the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. 

 10. Per contra, Mr. Shahidul Islam, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent No.1, contends that the plaintiff-appellant totally failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land within 12 years of institution of the suit. He further contends that the fact of settlement allegedly granted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Barguna in favour of the plaintiffs father vide exhibit-2[Certified copy of Kabuliat dated 12.11.1986] having not proved and allegedly having granted settlement for an unspecified area of .07 decimals out of 1.87 acres of land of Plot No.934, the suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession was not tenable in Law. He adds that exhibit-3[Certified copy of Boinama of Certificate Case No.827 of 1980-81 and dakhalnama] cannot be construed to be a document of handing over possession in favour of the plaintiff upon an unspecified 07 decimals of land out of 1.87 acres of land when the defendants' two storied dwelling house has been constructed upon a part of Plot No.934. He further contends that Pw-1, in his cross-examination, deposed that 'আমাদের settlement দেয়ার অর্থ দখল দেয়া। যে তারেখেই settlement দেয়া সেই তারিখেই Surveyor আমাদের মেপে জমি বুঝিয়ে দিয়ে আসে।' It is an evidence on oath which clearly disclosed that the plaintiffs have instituted the suit for recovery of khas possession followed by dispossession being out of possession and was not maintainable. He further contends that the evidence adduced by Dw-1 proved it beyond doubt that the defendant has been possessing his homestead, constructed upon a part of the suit plot continuously since 1960. He finally contends that there is no evidence in support of handing over possession in favour of the plaintiffs in the suit land within period from 30.06.1986 to 14.02.1987 and the settlement from the Government dated 12.11.1986 having not proved, the evidence on record proved it beyond doubt that the plaintiffs instituted the suit being out of possession. 

 11. Heard the contentions of learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the relevant materials and other connected papers along with the judgment and decree of the high Court Division on record. 

 12. The claim of the plaintiff-appellants is that they are the owners of the land by Nilam purchase and by purchasing with consideration money vide registered kabala and kabuliyat from the owners of the land, i.e. from the Government as khas land lease and they possessed the land. Devastating Tornedo and flood washed away their house, so the land remained vacant. When WAPDA cut mud from there, a ditch was made therein where the defendant erected houses illegally, forcibly dispossessing the plaintiffs from 'Ka' scheduled land on 11 Falgoon, 1396 BS. A local salish was held wherein the defendants admitted that they would hand over possession. The land in question has properly been recorded in the name of the plaintiffs when the defendant has failed to mutate his name and his rather also failed to mutate his name in the disputed khatian. The plaintiffs claimed that they have been able to prove their right, title and interest in the suit land by producing parchas, boinama, dakhalnama, kabuliyat, rent receipts which are public documents. In support of their contention, they cited the cases: Brahma Nand Puri-Vs-Neki Puri, reported in AIR1965SC1506 and Vijay Pullarwar-Vs-Shri Hanuman Deostan, (2019)11SCC718. 

 14. Defendant No.1 also claimed that during Revisional Survey operation, 26 decimals of land of P.S.Khatian Nos.4, 7 and 12 is neither recorded in the name of any landlord nor in any other name at all, but recorded in the names of Amrita Lal, Abdul Aziz and others, Kali Bilash and Keshab Lal and others in S.A. Khatian Nos.22/261/411 and 427 correctly. 1'87 acres of land of PS Khatian Nos.4, 7 and 12 including the 66 decimals of land which were given pattan to his father, Tazem Ali Hawlader wrongly recorded in Hal Plot No.934 of Khatian No. 1 in the name of Government. Having taken the opportunity of the wrong record, the Revenue Officer of Amtali Upazila declared for pattan on 01.11.1393 B.S. and to save the possession of defendant No.1, he filed Title Suit No. 34 of 1987 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge and on transfer, it was renumbered as Title Suit No.8 of 1992 which was heard and dis-missed on 15.08.1992 by the learned Assistant Judge, Bamna Upazila, Borguna. Against the judgment and order, defendant No.1 preferred Title Appeal No.56 of 1992 in the Court of District Judge, Borguna which is still pending. 

 16. On perusal of the documents on record, it appears that 12 decimals of land of Plot No.935 of SA Khatian No.789 under Amtalimouza belong to Abdus Sattar, Birendra Bijoy Das and others. The aforesaid land was auctioned on 30.06.1986 and plaintiff No. 3 purchased the same. On 14.02.1987, plaintiff No.3 by a registered deed of sale transferred six decimals of land of Plot No.935 to plain-tiff No. l. Plaintiff Nos.3 and 1 mutated their names. Bijendra Bijoy Das, father of plaintiff No.3 achieved pattan of 3 decimals of land of Plot No.921 and 7 decimals of land of Plot No.934 in total 10 decimals of land from khas khatian No.1 of the Government through Settlement Case No.2(Am) of 1985-86. A Kabuliyat deed was registered on 12.11.1986 after having salami of taka 1750 and a new khatian No. 1326 was created in the name of Birendra Bijoy Das. The plaintiffs exhibited original parcha of SA khatian No.1326, certified copy of Kabuliyat dated 12.1.1.1986, the boinama and dakhalnama of certificate case No. 827(Am) of 1980-81, DCR of payment of salami taka 1.750 dated 10.11.1986, certified copy of SA Khatian No.789 and certified copies of order sheet of Settlement Case No.2(Am)/ 85-86.In the instant suit, the plaintiffs have produced documentary evidence, most of which are public in nature, regarding their title to the suit land. They also produced documentary evidence dhakhalnama and rent receipts in support of their possession to the suit land before dispossession. Simultaneously, they produced oral evidence in support of their title and possession followed by dispossession from the suit land. It appears that Pw-1 consistently deposed in support of the plaint that they took possession of the suit land in accordance with certificate case, boinama, dakhalnama, sale deed, and kabuliyat but on 23'02/1990 corresponding to 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.E. Defendant No.1 dispossessed them from the suit lard by force. Pw-1 did not depose contrary to his statement during cross-examination. Pw-2 and Pw-3 duly corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 regarding the plaintiffs' title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land. It appears that Pw-2 materially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 to the effect that on 11 Falgoon, 1396 B.S. defendant No.1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. Likewise, Pw-3 substantially corroborated the testimony of Pw-1 that during 1396 B.S. defendant no 1 dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. It appears that the plaintiffs have primarily been able to prove their title and possession (before dispossession) to the suit land and they have discharged their initial burden of proof. Now it is the turn of defendant No.1 to discharge his onus of proof. In terms of Section 102 of the Evidence act, 1872, the initial onus to prove its claim is always on the plaintiff and if he discharges that onus and makes out a case which entitles him to a relief, the onus shifts to the defendant to prove these circumstances, if any, which would disentitle the plaintiff to the same [Bharat Alumnium Co.-V- Maharashtra Alumnium Co., 2009 DLT 489]. In a suit for possession based on title once the plaintiff has been able to create a high degree of probability so as to shift the onus on the defendant, it is for the defendant to discharge his onus and in the absence thereof, the burden of proof lying on the plaintiff shall be held to have been discharged so as to amount to proof of the plaintiffs title [R. V. E. Venkatachala Gounder -V- Arulmigu Viswesaraswaini and V. P. Temple, AIR 2003 SC 4548]. Let us have an overview of the defendant's case to see defendant No.1 has been able to discharge his onus of proof. 

 17. The disputed land is presently situated at Amtali Upazila of Borguna District which was formerly included in the subdivision of Patuakhali. Defendant No.1 in support of his title to the suit land produced an unregistered salami receipt dated 5 Baishakh, 1359. BS and Dakhila dated 15.08.1360 BS. The trial Court and the Appellate Court were of the view that at date of execution of the salami receipts on 5 Baishakh, 1359 BS corresponding to 18th April 1952 AD Zamindari system was not prevalent because of the coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the SAT Act) and, therefore, Zamindars had no right to give pattan of their land at that time. But the High Court Division took a different view on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act stating that Part-V of this Act came into force in the Sub-Division of Patuakhali on 5th August, 1954 AD. The view taken by the High Court Division on the point of coming into force of Part-V of the SAT Act appears to be correct since Part-V of the SAT Act came into force in entire area of Patuakhali Sub-Division of the District of Bakcrganj with effect from the date of publication of the notification in the Dacca Gazette, vide Notification No.9918-LR., date 8th July 1954, published in the Decca Gazette, date 5th August, 1954, Part-I, p. 890 (SAT ACT DLR by Obaidul Huq Chowdhury, Fifth Edition-2015, page 242- 243].Hence, in the Subdivision of Patuakhali Zamindars had right to give pattan of their land by receiving salami before 5th August, 1954. But the question pertaining to this case is whether Naeb Shailendra Nath Saha executing the salami receipt on behalf of the Zamindars gave the same to the father of defendant No.1, Tazem Ali Hawlader and delivered possession of the suit land to him or not? The salami receipts and rent receipts were marked as exhibits with objection. Salami receipt and dakhila are private documents and those will not be admissible in evidence as genuine documents on the mere production of the same. The genuineness of the salami receipt has to be determined in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. The Appellate Court held that the salami receipt/lease document is not genuine itself since it is rubbed and has cut marks and the back page of it is covered by white paper. This view of the Appellate Court regarding the title document of defendant No.1 seems to be based on proper appreciation of the documentary evidence on record in the light of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In the case of Ajufannessa @ AjiBibi and others-Vs-Safar Miah and others, 30 D.L.R (AD) 41 it was held that "A private document can-not be taken notice of and marked as an Exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may, however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a person, as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a landlord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. In this case, both of the courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or procedure which had affected the merits of the case." The ratio of this case was again reiterated in the case of Md. Jashimuddins Kanchan -Vs- Md. Ali Ashraf (42 DLR (AD) 289]. The High Court Division did not reverse this finding of the Appellate Court that the genuineness of the salami receipt is highly doubtful. Since the tide document of the father of defendant No.1 is highly doubtful, subsequent transfer of the same property to defendant No.1 by oral gift is also doubtful. Defendant No.1 claimed that during 1961 his house at the disputed land was destroyed by cyclone for which he repaired the same with his own expense. But he deposed,  “১৯৬১ সালে আমি ৬ষ্ঠ শ্রেণীতে পড়তাম। তখন আমার ব্যক্তিগত আয়ের উৎস ছিলনা।" This portion of the deposition of Dv-1 suggests that the claim of defendant No.1 regarding his possession of the suit property from 1960 onward is apparently baseless. It appears that father of defendant No.1 and thereafter, defendant No.1 did not take any time worthy step whatsoever for correction of the record of rights. The possession of the defendant No.1 in the suit land cannot be traced back to any valid title whereas the possession (before dispossession) of the plaintiffs in the suit land can be traced back to valid title which coupled with attending facts and circumstances reasonably gives rise to the presumption that the plaintiffs were dispossessed from the suit land by defendant No.1 by force. 

 19. Upon perusal of the Judgment of the High Court Division it appears that the High Court Division on erroneous belief decided the case keeping in view of section-9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. But the pleadings of the parties clearly indicate that this case is brought under section-8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 read with Article 142 of schedule-1 to the Limitation Act, 1908 and, therefore, the plaintiffs case file the suit for recovery of possession within 12 years from the date of dispossession. The finding by the High Court Division to the effect that the notice by the government to defendant No.1 to vacate possession cast a substantial doubt in believing the plaintiffs' case does not seem to be correct since possession of defendant No.1 can never be adverse to the government without defendant No. 1 is 60 years continuous adverse possession as per article 149 of schedule-1 of the Limitation Act, 1908 which is absent in the present case. 18. The trial Court as well as the Appellate Court arrived at concurrent finding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title and possession following by dispossession from the suit land. It appears that the findings of the trial court as well as the Appellate Court are based on the proper appreciation of evidence on record both oral and documentary. It is well settled position in law that under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court cannot re-appreciate the evidence and cannot set aside the concurrent findings of the Courts below by taking a different view of the evidence. The High Court is empowered only to interfere with the findings of fact if the findings are per-verse or there has been a non-appreciation or non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the Courts below. Simply because another view of the evidence may be taken is no ground by the High Court to interfere in its revisional jurisdiction [Masjid Kacha Tank, Nahan-Vs-Tuffail Mohammed, AIR 1991 SC 455]. The civil cases are decided on the basis of preponderance of probability. Civil cases are decided on the basis of pre-ponderance of evidence while in a criminal case the entire burden lies on the prosecution and proof beyond reasonable doubt has to be given [Vishnu Dutt Sharma-V-Daya Sapra 13 SCC (2009) page 729]. In view of the facts, circumstances and proposition of law discussed above, we are of the view that the preponderance of probability regarding title and possession (before dispossession) of the plaintiffs to the suit land is clearly in favour of the plaintiffs and, therefore, the High Court Division made serious error of law in making the rule absolute which occasioned failure of justice.

Facts leading, to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the respondent herein as plaintiff filed the Other Class Suit No.899 of 1984 seeking declaration that he is the exclusive owner in possession of the suit land on the averments that Samir Gaine was the owner in possession of the suit land and he died leaving behind two sons, namely, Jomir, Sobir and a daughter, Suborna Bewa, and later on Jomir died leaving behind his brother Sobir and sister Suborna and then Sobir died leaving one unmarried daughter Sorodini and sister Suborna and then Sorodini also died unmarried and thus, Suborna became the owner of the suit property and she, by deed of hiba-bil-Ewaz dated 30-4-1958, corresponding to 17 Baishakh, 1365 BS, transferred the suit property to the plaintiff and further the plaintiff also acquired 10 decimals of land by way of Korfa Pattan from Jotindranath Sil and also acquired 0.47 acre of land by way of exchange from Belo Bewa and Sadibullah in lieu of 0.10 acre of land and thus, the plaintiff became owner of the suit property but the same had been wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant which castes a cloud upon the title of the plaintiff. 

 3. The defendant contested the above suit by filling written statement denying material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that, Suborna, the mother of the plaintiff and the defendant, was the owner of the suit property and she decided to transfer the suit land to both of them in equal halves by way of sale but the plaintiff fraudulently procured a deed of hiba-bil-Ewaz in his favour showing transfer of the entire suit land in his favour and thus, the above deed of hiba-bil-Ewaz is void and the plaintiff also did not acquire 0.10 acquire of land from Jatindra Nath Sil by way of Korfa Pattan dated 27 Kartik, 1352 BS and also not get 47 decimals of land by way of exchange from Belo Bewa and Sadibullah. The plaintiff and the defendant are co-sharers in the suit property in equal halves and Suborna, by inheritance, got the suit property and subsequently, she having been remarried, left her former place and thereafter, for her own necessity she had decided to sell the suit property and both the plaintiff and defendant agreed to purchase the same in equal shares and then the defendant, who is a illiterate person, asked the plaintiff though for taking necessary steps to get the sale deed registered but on the day of registration, the plaintiff himself did not go to the registry office but managed to get the suit land transferred in his name making the defendant understood that a sale deed had been executed and registered in their joint names and the record of rights also stand in their joint names in equal share and on that basis, the defendant also owned and possessed the suit property on payment of rents regularly. His further case is that his brother also inherited 0.10 acre of land out of 0.20 acre and subsequently, 7.85 acres of land including the said 0.20 acre of land was put in auction for failure of payment of rent by the tenant and then the father of the plaintiff and the defendant took "Korfa" Pattan of the same in the name of the plaintiff and the defendant and then the record of right was duly prepared in the name of the plaintiff and the defendant in equal halves and thus, the acquisition of 0.47 acre of land by the plaintiff, on the basis of exchange as claimed by the plaintiff, is also false and concocted and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. On conclusion of the trial, the Trial Court, considering the evidences and documents on record, dismissed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 24-1-1987. 

 9. Mr Golam Robbani, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submit that the High Court Division committed error in arriving at the finding that the Courts below dismissed the suit on misreading and misconstruction of evidence and on erroneous view of the provisions of sections 58, 65 and 73 of the Evidence Act and further the High Court Division without at all considering that in a suit for declaration of title, the onus lied upon the plaintiff to prove his title by producing evidence and the Courts below found that the plaintiff could not discharge his onus of declaration of title over the suit property. He further submits that the plaintiff over the suit land have been sought for declaration of title by the plaintiff on the basis of deed of hiba-bil-Ewaz dated 30-4-1958 but he in his deposition stated that he did neither go to Registry Office at the time of registration of the said deed nor he has given the Holy Quran to his mother as a consideration for the gift and he merely stated that he gave Taka 30 to PW 2 to purchase the Holy Quran whereas PW2 in his deposition could neither say the price of the Holy Quran alleged to have been given to him by the plaintiff nor could produce the receipt showing purchase of the Holly Quran and accordingly, the learned Courts below rightly found that the deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaz has not been proved. He next submits that the High Court Division, on misreading the evidence on record erroneously held that the defendant, having admitted the existence of the said hiba-bil-Ewaz deed, the plaintiff, in view of the provision of section 58 of the Evidence Act, was not required to prove said deed and the High Court Division also committed an error of law in not considering the fact that the land measuring an area 47 decimals of land purported to have acquired by the plaintiff on the basis of exchange with Belo Bewa and Sadibullah has not been proved in view of the fact that the plaintiff has neither produced any documents in support of the above exchange nor impleaded the heirs of the said Belo Bewa and Sadibullah in the suit. He finally submits that the Appellate Court being a final Court of facts found that the deed of Korfa Settlement is not an old one as written in 1352 BS and it has been written for purpose of the suit depriving the defendant from his legitimate share and even Jotindra Nath, the Vendor of the said deed has not brought before the Court to prove the execution of it and the High Court Division committed an error of law in holding that the deed has been executed by the Vendor placing reliance on the evidence of PW 4 and committed serious illegality in making the Rule absolute and thereby set-aside the judgments and decrees of the Courts below and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. 

 11. We have heard Mr Golam Robbani, the learned Advocate for the appellants. Perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 

 13. Now let us carefully scan the evidence on record, ascertain the facts and circumstances of the cases, and decisions of the three (03) Courts below, whether judgment and order of High Court Division is justified or erred which calls for interference by this Division. 

 23. In the instant case, on conscientious searching into the judgments of the Trial Court and lower Appellate Court it become obvious to us that the Trial Court reached into the decision as to that the pivotal assertions of the plaintiffs that he owned the suit land through Hiba-bil-Ewaz deed, Korfa deed and exchange with Belo Bibi and Sadibullah was disproved on the basis of proper appreciation of the evidences on record. The lower Appellate Court affirmed the same findings on apposite evaluation of the materials on record. 

 24. Our considered view is that High Court Division on misreading the evidence on record erroneously held that the defendant, having admitted the existence of the said Hiba-bil-Ewaz deed, the Korfa deed is valid and the respondent-plaintiff got some suit land with exchange from Belo Bibi and Sadibullah. 

 25. As such, this Division finds no non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence on record or an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice or such finding is found to have resulted from glaring misconception of law or misconception, misapplication or misapprehension of law in the judgments and decisions of the Courts below. 

 26. Rather, we find that the High Court Division committed error of law in disturbing the concurrent findings of facts arrived at by both the Courts below and on misreading of the evidence on record. Hence, we compelled to approve the submission of the learned Senior Counsel that the High Court Division gave appalling discovery upon non-consideration of the findings of facts recorded by the Courts below.
